topic.name: Mental addition and subtraction (age 6+)
topic.description: Add and subtract a two-digit number and ones mentally and using concrete/pictorial representations
evidence: Calculate 36 + 7 = 43 using objects or mentally
Calculate 52 − 4 = 48 using a number line or mentally
Explain bridging through 10 when adding ones to a two-digit number
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out '36 + 7' or '42 − 5' in their head — keeping the tens in place and only adjusting the ones?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Add and subtract a two-digit number and ones (36 + 7, 52 − 4), mentally and with concrete/pictorial support, bridging through a multiple of ten. Ages 6–7.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'add and subtract numbers using concrete objects, pictorial representations, and mentally, including: a two-digit number and ones'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.4 add within 100 including a two-digit and a one-digit number, using place value and the relationship between addition and subtraction; extended by 2.NBT.5.
• Operational details: the key skill is bridging the tens boundary — partition the ones to reach the next (or previous) decade, then add/subtract the rest (36 + 7 → 36 + 4 = 40, + 3 = 43; 52 − 4 → 52 − 2 = 50, − 2 = 48). Ground in base-ten blocks and the number line so the new ten is seen forming. Contrast with cases that don't cross a ten (43 + 5) so children bridge only when needed.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — adds ones without crossing a ten (43 + 5) and with blocks when crossing. Tier B (age 7) — bridges 36 + 7 and 52 − 4 mentally via the decade. Tier C (age 7+) — explains why the tens digit changes and chooses to bridge only when the ones cross a multiple of ten.
bestPractices: Teach bridging explicitly: partition the ones to land on the decade, then add/subtract the remainder.
Use base-ten blocks so ten ones visibly regroup into a new ten (and vice versa when subtracting).
Use the empty number line to show the two-part jump to and past the decade.
Mix bridging and non-bridging items so children decide when a boundary is crossed.
Connect the mental bridging steps to later column methods (regrouping).
keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks (ones regrouping into a ten)
Empty number line with a jump to the decade then on
Ten-frames / partially filled frames showing the ones
Hundred square (move along a row, drop to next row at the boundary)
Part-whole splitting the ones (7 as 4 + 3)
commonMisconceptions: Adding the ones digits and ignoring the new ten (36 + 7 → 33 or '313').
Counting on/back in ones and slipping by one at the tens boundary.
Failing to change the tens digit when the ones cross a multiple of ten.
Bridging when it isn't needed, or not bridging when it is.
For subtraction, stopping at the decade (52 − 4 → 50) or miscounting past it.

learn.summary: Children aged 6–7 add and subtract a two-digit number and ones by bridging through a multiple of ten: partition the ones to land on the decade, then add or subtract the remainder (36 + 7 → 36 + 4 = 40, + 3 = 43; 52 − 4 → 52 − 2 = 50, − 2 = 48). Core activities use a manipulable number line and base-ten blocks — with ten-frames and a hundred square as alternative views — so the new ten is seen forming and the tens digit updates for a visible reason, with mixed bridging and non-bridging items (43 + 5) so children decide when a boundary is actually crossed. Fluency practice, a static anchor image, and a narrate-your-method conversation are retained as complementary approaches with distinct purposes.

activities.title: Bridge the decade on a number line with a base-ten mat
feedback: If the answer keeps the original tens digit (e.g. 36 + 7 → 33 or '313'), show the ten ones regrouping into one new ten on the mat and re-run the jump through 40 so the tens digit visibly changes.
If the answer is one off (e.g. 42 or 44), point out counting single steps across the boundary; partition the ones to land exactly on 40 first, then add the rest.
For subtraction, if the child stops at 50 or lands on 49/47, model bridging back to 50 first, then taking the remaining 2 to reach 48.
For a non-bridging item like 43 + 5, confirm that the ones do not cross a decade so no bridge is needed, reinforcing when bridging applies.
activities.rationale: Bridging is a two-part jump, and a manipulable number line plus a regrouping mat lets the child reach the decade and then complete the jump while seeing ten ones become a new ten; ten-frames and a hundred square offer the same structure in other concrete/pictorial forms. Live feedback can catch the count-in-ones slip and the ignore-the-new-ten error as they occur. Non-bridging items prevent over-applying the strategy.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils add and subtract a two-digit number and ones using concrete, pictorial and mental methods.
1.NBT.4 covers adding within 100 including a two-digit and a one-digit number using place value, with regrouping of ten ones into a ten.
Bridging through ten by partitioning is a core mental strategy; digit-separation errors (ignoring the regrouped ten) are common.
learnerActions: Work 36 + 7 by first jumping from 36 to the next decade (40), then completing the jump with the remaining ones (to 43).
On a base-ten mat, watch four loose ones combine with the existing ones to make a whole new ten-stick as the jump reaches 40, so the tens digit change has a visible cause.
Switch to subtraction mode for 52 − 4: jump back to the decade first (52 − 2 = 50), then take the remaining 2 to reach 48.
Mix in non-bridging items such as 43 + 5 and decide for each item whether the ones cross a decade before choosing to bridge.

Optionally view the same bridging in another representation: a ten-frame filling up to a complete ten of ones, or a hundred square where you move along a row and drop to the next row as you cross the decade, so the new ten is seen forming in more than one way.
State out loud which decade you bridge through and why the tens digit does or does not change.
activities.intendedInsight: When adding makes the ones fill up to a whole ten, a new ten is formed and the tens digit increases by one; when subtracting takes away more ones than there are, a ten is broken into ones and the tens digit decreases by one (52 − 4 = 48). Partitioning the ones to reach the decade makes this regrouping explicit for both addition and subtraction.

activities.title: Fluency practice: fill in, draw the jump, choose the decade
feedback: If a learner picks the results distractor that ignores the regrouped ten (e.g. 33 for 36 + 7), return to a regrouping representation to show why the tens digit must change and re-run the jump through 40.
If the drawn jump skips the decade stop, prompt the learner to mark the decade first, then the remainder.
Confirm correct recognition when a non-bridging item is answered without an unnecessary bridge.
activities.rationale: A fixed practice sequence consolidates the method and surfaces the characteristic errors through targeted distractors, but it cannot provide the live regrouping feedback of the manipulative, so it is best used after the hands-on work.
sourceClaims: Bridging through ten by partitioning is a core mental strategy; digit-separation errors (ignoring the regrouped ten) are common.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in results such as 36 + 7 = ___ mentally or with a jotting.
Draw the two-part bridging jump on an empty number line to show reaching the decade and then continuing.
Choose which decade you bridge through for a given calculation, with decade options as the choices (for 36 + 7 the decade is 40).
In a separate results question, identify the correct total, where a distractor such as 33 for 36 + 7 reflects the ignore-the-new-ten error (keeping the original tens digit).
Include at least one non-bridging item so you practise recognising when no bridge is needed.
activities.intendedInsight: Once the bridging strategy is understood, spaced and varied practice builds fluency in partitioning the ones and updating the tens digit accurately.

activities.title: Anchor image: a worked bridging number line
feedback: If the learner cannot say why the jump pauses at 40, highlight that the first jump completes a ten and point to the labelled new ten.
Prompt the learner to connect the picture back to doing their own jump on the manipulative.
activities.rationale: A static worked number line anchors the appearance of bridging and labels the regrouped ten. It supports understanding of the structure, though the count itself still needs to be rehearsed in a doing activity; treat this as a reference rather than practice of the procedure.
learnerActions: Study a number line showing 36 → 40 → 43 with the regrouped ten labelled, revealing each step in turn.
Describe in your own words why the jump stops at 40 before continuing to 43.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear worked picture shows what a bridging jump looks like and names the new ten, giving a reference model for the two-part method.

activities.title: Narrate your method: how did you get across the ten?
feedback: If the explanation describes counting single steps, guide the child to describe partitioning the ones to reach the decade first.
If the child cannot justify why the tens digit changes, revisit the regrouping of ten ones into a new ten.
Confirm reasoning when the child correctly identifies that a non-bridging item needs no bridge.
activities.rationale: A talk-through surfaces the child's method and misconceptions, complementing the hands-on and practice activities; it is a way to assess and reinforce the procedure being practised, though recognition in talk does not by itself guarantee independent production.
learnerActions: Work a bridging item and a non-bridging item, then explain aloud how you got across the ten (or why you did not need to).
Answer questions such as 'Why does the tens digit change here?' and 'For 43 + 5, did you need to cross a ten? How do you know?'
Show 52 − 4 on the number line and say where you stopped on the way.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the decade step and the reason the tens digit changes reveals whether the child is partitioning to bridge or merely counting in ones.

constraints: Ground the strategy in base-ten blocks and the number line (with ten-frames or a hundred square as alternative representations) so the new ten is seen forming (and un-forming when subtracting) before expecting mental calculation.
Always mix bridging and non-bridging items (e.g. 43 + 5) so children learn to bridge only when the ones cross a decade and do not over-apply the strategy.
A fixed practice sequence consolidates fluency but does not provide live regrouping feedback; use it after hands-on manipulative work.
A static worked image anchors what bridging looks like but does not rehearse the count; it is a reference, not a substitute for doing the procedure.

Checkpoint tiers: Tier A (age 6) adds ones without crossing a ten and with blocks when crossing; Tier B (age 7) bridges 36 + 7 and 52 − 4 mentally via the decade; Tier C (age 7+) explains why the tens digit changes and chooses to bridge only when the ones cross a multiple of ten.
Connect the mental bridging steps to later column methods (regrouping) as children progress.

responseLevels.gap: Adds/subtracts the digits with no regard to place, or cannot get across the tens boundary.
responseLevels.full: Bridges through the decade by partitioning the ones, updates the tens digit correctly, and recognises when no bridge is needed.
responseLevels.partial: Reaches answers by counting in ones across the boundary — slow and error-prone — without partitioning to bridge.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out — mentally or on the number line — and talk me through each: 36 + 7; 52 − 4; 43 + 5.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Two items cross a tens boundary and one does not. A child with place-value bridging partitions the ones to hit the decade and updates the tens digit; a child treating the digits separately gives the tell-tale 33 for 36 + 7, and a count-in-ones child slips by one at the boundary. The non-bridging item checks they don't over-apply bridging.

topic.name: Addition and subtraction strategies (age 7+)
topic.description: Explain why addition and subtraction strategies work, using place value and the properties of operations
evidence: Explain why adding tens and ones separately gives the correct total
Describe why a compensation strategy works (e.g. 'I added 1 too many, so I subtract 1')
Use place-value language to justify a written method step by step
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} works out '67 + 24' by splitting it into '60 + 20' and '7 + 4', can they explain to you in words *why* that approach gives the right answer?

pedagogy.summary: This topic asks children to JUSTIFY why addition and subtraction strategies work, using place value and the properties of operations — the step from doing a strategy to explaining it. Two justifications are central: partitioning ('add tens and ones separately, then recombine') works because a number is composed of tens and ones and addends may be split, reordered and regrouped without changing the total (commutativity/associativity); and compensation ('add 100 for 99, then take 1 away') works as an equivalent transformation — you adjusted by a known amount and undo it. The goal is reasoning voiced in place-value language, not more correct answers.
bestPractices: Ask 'why does that work?' routinely, and press for reasons beyond 'that's the rule' — model place-value language back to the child
Ground justification in materials first (base-ten shows the whole is conserved when partitioned) then move to verbal argument
Make the properties explicit: order and grouping of addends don't change the total; use this to justify partitioning
For compensation, track the adjustment quantitatively — 'I added one too many, so I subtract one' — and why the direction is forced
Use talk moves (revoice, 'do you agree and why?', counterexamples) so explanations are built collaboratively
keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks (whole conserved under partitioning)
Number line (compensation: overshoot then step back)
Part-whole diagram (the number as tens + ones)
Worked strategy with each step annotated by its reason
Bar model (equivalent transformations preserve the total)
commonMisconceptions: Restating the procedure or citing authority ('the teacher said') instead of giving a reason
Doubting that splitting/reordering preserves the total (fearing something is lost when a number is broken up)
Compensation direction error: adding 100 for 99 then adding 1 (not seeing 100 is one too many)
Explaining WHAT was done but not WHY it is valid

learn.summary: Children justify WHY addition and subtraction strategies work, using place value and the properties of operations — the step from executing a strategy to explaining it. Two justifications are central: partitioning ('add tens and ones separately, then recombine') is valid because a number is composed of tens and ones and addends may be split, reordered and regrouped without changing the total (commutativity/associativity); and compensation ('add 100 for 99, then subtract 1') is an equivalent transformation — you adjusted by a known amount and undo the surplus. The target is reasoning voiced in place-value language, not more correct answers. A dialogic 'prove-it' routine is well-suited as the primary vehicle because producing a justification requires the child to articulate their reasoning, which an open spoken exchange is well-suited to elicit; written annotation, manipulatives and spot-the-flaw tasks serve as complementary scaffolds and probes.

activities.title: Talk with a 'prove-it' partner who never accepts a bare rule
feedback: When the child only restates the steps, press 'but why doesn't splitting change the total?' — revoice any seed of a reason and build on it rather than supplying the full answer.
Model place-value language back: 'so 46 IS 40 and 6, and putting them back together gives the whole.'
For a compensation direction slip (adding 1 instead of subtracting), ask 'how much more is 100 than 99?' so the child tracks the surplus of one.
If the child thinks a different split (35 + 2) might break the method, have them add the parts and recombine to confirm the whole is unchanged.

Accept any genuine answer; the only thing not accepted is 'that's the rule' or 'the teacher said' — keep asking for the reason. Surface the reasoning for discussion rather than scoring it right/wrong.
activities.rationale: The objective is producing a justification, which requires the child to articulate their reasoning; an open 'why?' prompt that accepts answers but never a bare rule is well-suited to pushing the child to explain why splitting and compensation are valid. Talk moves (revoicing, pressing for reasoning, agree/disagree, counterexamples) move children from asserting to justifying, and justifying order/grouping of addends rests on commutativity/associativity.
sourceClaims: Productive mathematical discussion is built through talk moves (revoicing, pressing for reasoning, agree/disagree, counterexamples) that push children from asserting to justifying.

Year 2 pupils show that addition can be done in any order (commutative) but subtraction cannot, use the inverse relationship, and check by adding numbers in a different order — establishing commutativity and associativity; recording in columns supports place-value reasoning.
learnerActions: Solve 46 + 37 by adding tens and ones separately (40 + 30 = 70, 6 + 7 = 13, 70 + 13 = 83), then say the answer aloud.

When your partner (teacher, peer, or an in-role character) asks 'but why doesn't breaking 46 into 40 and 6 lose anything?', explain in your own words why splitting and recombining keeps the same total.
Try splitting 37 a different way — e.g. 35 + 2 instead of 30 + 7 — and explain whether the method still works and why, to show the reasoning transfers to a new split.
Solve 46 + 99 by adding 100 and then adjusting; when asked 'why take one BACK rather than add one?', explain how much too much 100 is compared with 99 and why the surplus must be removed.
Respond to a counterexample your partner offers (e.g. a friend who split 46 into 40 + 6 but only added the 40 and forgot the 6) and say whether that mistake means splitting itself is unreliable.
activities.intendedInsight: A remembered procedure becomes an owned explanation: the number IS its tens and ones, so like parts can be added and recombined without loss, and this holds whichever way you split; adding 100 for 99 adds exactly one too many, so you subtract one to land on adding exactly 99.

activities.title: Show the whole is conserved: partition with materials, compensate on a number line
feedback: If the child fears something is lost when a number is split, recombine the base-ten pieces in front of them to show the whole is conserved.
If the overshoot step-back is unclear, mark 99 and 100 on the line and point out 100 is one step beyond 99.
Prompt the child to voice the reason — the materials make the conserved whole visible and seed the explanation, but the child still needs to say why it is valid.
activities.rationale: Grounding justification in materials first lets the child see the whole conserved under partitioning and see compensation as overshoot-then-step-back, giving concrete footing before the verbal argument. These representations seed the explanation but do not by themselves make the child voice the reason, so pair them with the 'why?' prompt.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils show that addition can be done in any order (commutative) but subtraction cannot, use the inverse relationship, and check by adding numbers in a different order — establishing commutativity and associativity; recording in columns supports place-value reasoning.
learnerActions: Using base-ten blocks, a part-whole diagram, or a bar model, split 46 into 40 + 6 and check that the pieces still make 46 — nothing is lost when you break it up.
Rearrange the order and grouping of the parts (e.g. 6 + 40, or group the tens first) and confirm the total is unchanged.
On a number line, add 46 + 99 by jumping 100 forward, then step back 1; highlight the extra +1 you overshot by.
Say out loud why you step back rather than forward.
activities.intendedInsight: Partitioning preserves the total because the parts still compose the same whole and any order/grouping of addends gives the same sum; compensation is 'overshoot then step back' by the known surplus.

activities.title: Annotate a worked strategy with the reason for each step
feedback: If a label only restates the action ('added the tens'), ask 'why is that step valid?' and look for the place-value reason.
A static annotated strategy is useful reference, but reading a finished annotation does not by itself show the child can reason — follow it with the child explaining a fresh example aloud.
activities.rationale: A worked strategy with each step annotated by its reason makes the hidden place-value logic visible and gives a model for what a justification contains, while making clear that reading a finished annotation is a scaffold rather than independent reasoning.
learnerActions: Take a written worked method for 46 + 37 (40 + 30 = 70; 6 + 7 = 13; 70 + 13 = 83).
Label each step with WHY it is allowed, not just what was done (e.g. '46 is 40 and 6', 'the order of adding the parts doesn't change the total', 'recombining the parts gives the whole').
Do the same for a compensation method (46 + 99 = 46 + 100 − 1) and name the surplus of one and its undoing.
activities.intendedInsight: Every step of a strategy has a place-value reason; a justification names those reasons, not just the actions.

activities.title: Spot the flawed reasoning / pick the valid justification
feedback: After a selection, always ask the child to explain why the chosen justification is valid — recognising the right answer does not on its own show they can produce the reasoning.
For the 'add 1' error in the chain, re-anchor on 100 being one more than 99, so one must be taken back off.
activities.rationale: Choosing the valid justification or spotting the flaw in a reasoning chain can probe understanding of justification and target the common compensation-direction error. Selection tasks cannot capture an open explanation, so use them to probe and surface errors, then move to the child constructing their own reason.
learnerActions: Read two or three explanations of a compensation step and choose the one that correctly justifies subtracting 1 after adding 100.
Find the error in a written reasoning chain (e.g. one that adds 1 instead of subtracting it) and say what has gone wrong.
Explain in your own words why the correct justification is correct.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising valid versus invalid reasoning sharpens the child's sense of what counts as a justification, especially the forced direction of the compensation adjustment.

constraints: The goal is reasoning voiced in place-value language, not more correct answers; do not score the discussion right/wrong — surface reasoning for discussion.

Manipulatives, number lines, bar models and annotated strategies seed and model the explanation but do not themselves make the child articulate WHY — pair them with an explicit request for the child's reason.
Justification can be produced in speech or in writing; the dialogic routine is well-suited to eliciting it but is not the only valid medium.

Selection tasks (choose the valid justification, spot the flaw) assess and probe recognition; recognising a correct justification does not elicit independent construction of one, so follow them with the child explaining in their own words.
Compensation direction must be tracked quantitatively: 100 is one MORE than 99, so adding 100 adds exactly one too many and one must be subtracted; watch for the error of adding 1.
The compensation direction error (adding 1 instead of subtracting) should appear only as a flaw to be identified, never presented as a valid option.

Prerequisites to revisit if reasoning is shaky: three-digit place value / composition of number (if the child doubts splitting preserves the total), and the compensation strategy itself (if the compensation logic is absent).
Subtraction is not commutative even though addition is — do not let 'any order works' be over-generalised to subtraction.

probeDeeper: Does it matter whether you add the tens or the ones first? Why not?
You added 100 instead of 99 — exactly how much too much did you add, and how do you undo it?
Would splitting still work if you split 37 into 35 + 2 instead of 30 + 7? Explain why.

Compensation works because 100 is one more than 99, so adding 100 adds one too many and you subtract one to get back to adding exactly 99 — an equivalent transformation.

errorPatterns.pattern: Restates the procedure or appeals to authority ('that's how you do it', 'the teacher said') with no reason
errorPatterns.nextMove: In discussion, press 'but why doesn't splitting change the total?'; revoice any seed of a reason and build on it. Do not score — keep drawing out the justification.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child describes the steps again when asked WHY, or defers to a rule without explaining

errorPatterns.pattern: Doubts that splitting/reordering preserves the total — worries breaking the number up loses something
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss with base-ten showing the whole is conserved under partitioning and that any order/grouping of addends gives the same total; reteach three-digit place value if the composition idea is shaky.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child is unsure the partitioned method must give the same answer, or thinks order could matter

errorPatterns.pattern: Compensation direction error — says add 100 for 99 then ADD 1, or can't justify the 'take 1 away'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss on a number line: 100 is one MORE than 99, so one step must come back off; track the surplus explicitly. Reteach the strategy if the compensation logic is absent.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child adjusts the wrong way, or cannot say how much too much was added

responseLevels.gap: Restates the steps or cites authority; gives no reason, or believes splitting could change the total.
responseLevels.full: Justifies with place value AND the properties — the number is composed of tens and ones so like parts add and any order/grouping works; compensation is an equivalent transformation (added too many, subtract the surplus) — and transfers the reasoning to a new split or number.
responseLevels.partial: Offers a partial reason — e.g. 'because 46 is 40 and 6' — but cannot yet justify why recombining the parts is valid, or gets the compensation direction without explaining it (lists the parts without explaining how operating on them preserves the total).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Discuss, don't mark: 'When you add 46 + 37 by working out 40 + 30 = 70 and 6 + 7 = 13 and then combining, why is it OK to break the numbers up like that and still get the right total?' Then: 'To add 46 + 99, someone adds 100 and then takes 1 away — why is that allowed, and how do they know to take 1 away rather than add it?' Listen for place-value and properties reasoning.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The probe separates a child who can JUSTIFY (invoking place-value composition and the properties, and tracking the compensation adjustment) from one who merely restates the steps or cites a rule. The partial-to-full boundary is exactly the move from listing the parts ('46 is 40 and 6') to explaining why operating on the parts and recombining is valid. Surfaced for discussion, not scored right/wrong.

pedagogy.summary: Mentally adding or subtracting ones to a three-digit number rests on one insight: only the ones digit changes, UNLESS the calculation bridges a ten (then the tens digit changes too, and possibly the hundreds). Children apply their secure within-20 bonds at the end of a larger number, keeping the hundreds and tens as an untouched 'anchor'. It is taught with place-value apparatus and a number line so the local change is visible against the stable larger part.

learn.summary: Year 3 pupils mentally add or subtract ones to a three-digit number. The core insight: only the ones digit changes UNLESS the calculation bridges a ten, in which case the tens digit (and possibly the hundreds) also changes. Children anchor the hundreds and tens as a stable 'larger part' and operate only on the ones, reusing secure within-20 make-ten bonds for the bridging cases. Contrasting a non-bridging case directly with a bridging case is what refines the rough rule 'only the ones change' into the accurate 'only the ones change unless we cross a ten'.

activities.title: Anchor the larger part, spin only the ones
feedback: If the child changes the wrong digit (e.g. gives 345+3 as 375, adding to the tens): re-anchor with the chart — the 3 is three ones, so it joins the ones. Name the value of each digit before adding.
Reinforce by asking which column the added amount belongs to, every time, until anchoring is automatic.
activities.rationale: Anchoring the larger part and operating only on the ones makes the local nature of the change explicit; naming place value directly counters the wrong-digit error. A coded or physical chart where only the ones row moves makes this concrete, while base-ten blocks, a bead string or a partitioning jotting (345 = 340 + 5) show the same stable-anchor idea in other media.
learnerActions: Show 345 on a place-value chart (e.g. a Gattegno chart) with the hundreds, tens and ones rows visible.
Work 345 + 3: change only the ones from 5 to 8, keeping '34_' fixed, and say aloud which digits stayed the same and which changed.
Name the value of each digit before adding (the 3 you add is three ones, so it joins the ones), to guard against adding to the wrong column.
Predict, before calculating, which digits will change.
activities.intendedInsight: A change to the ones stays local: the hundreds and tens act as an untouched anchor, so for a non-bridging case only the ones digit moves.

activities.title: Bridge a ten with make-ten bonds
feedback: If the child fails to bridge (e.g. 345+7 given as 342, keeping the 2 and dropping the extra ten, or strings digits as 3412): rebuild with make-ten on the number line — 345 to 350, then +2 — and connect it to the within-20 bond they already know.
Highlight that keeping the tens digit at 4 cannot be right because the answer passed 350.
activities.rationale: Bridging reuses within-ten make-ten bonds, and multiple representations (number line, hundred-square, place value, symbolic) connect the mental strategy. Showing the ones filling to the decade then the remainder makes visible why the tens digit moves. The cascading chart and number-line toggle are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required apparatus.
sourceClaims: Bridging a ten reuses within-ten 'make ten' bonds; multiple representations (number line, place value, symbolic) connect the mental strategy.
learnerActions: Work 345 + 7 on a marked number line (or a hundred-square segment near the decade): jump +5 to land on 350, then +2 more to reach 352.
Connect this to the within-20 bond already known: split 7 into 5 + 2, so 345 + 7 = 345 + 5 + 2.
Notice the moment the tens digit changes (4 becomes 5 as you cross 350) — this is the exception to 'only the ones change'.
Optionally watch a place-value chart where the ones roll past 9 and cascade a carry of +1 into the tens, with a number-line toggle showing the same jump onto 350 then stepping to 352.
activities.intendedInsight: When a calculation crosses a ten, the ones 'fill up' to the next decade and the tens digit also changes; make-ten bonds the child already knows handle the split.

activities.title: Contrast non-bridging and bridging side by side
feedback: If the child insists only the ones can ever change, point to the bridging case where the tens visibly moved past a decade, and ask them to re-predict.
Praise correct predictions that name the crossing of a ten as the reason the tens digit changes.
activities.rationale: Contrasting a non-bridging case with a bridging case isolates exactly when more than the ones digit changes, which is the heart of this skill. Prediction-before-calculation surfaces the misconception for discussion. Rapid mixed items can rehearse and check the skill but mainly confirm rather than build the insight.
learnerActions: Place 345 + 3 and 345 + 7 next to each other and predict, for each, which digits will change before calculating.
Calculate both, then state which digits actually changed and why they differed.
Articulate the refined rule: 'only the ones change, unless we cross a ten'.
Try a mixed set of items sorted by whether they bridge, predicting each time.
activities.intendedInsight: Directly comparing a case where only the ones change with one that bridges turns the rough rule into the accurate rule and exposes the 'only the ones ever change' overgeneralisation.

activities.title: Bridge downwards when subtracting
feedback: If the child does 'five take two is three' and gives 463 (subtracting the smaller from the larger within the column): show on the number line that 462 − 5 must move down past 460 — take 2 to reach 460, then 3 more. Sanity-check that subtracting makes the number smaller.
Reinforce the direction check as the first move on any subtraction that bridges.
activities.rationale: The smaller-from-larger error can produce an answer larger than the start, as with 462 − 5 → 463, though not always (464 − 7 → 463). A number-line model travelling down past the decade corrects it. A direction check, plus a check that the tens digit dropped, catches it. Answers across the set: 345+3 = 348 (only ones change), 345+7 = 352 (bridges up, tens change), 462−5 = 457 (bridges down, tens change).
sourceClaims: Bridging a ten reuses within-ten 'make ten' bonds; multiple representations (number line, place value, symbolic) connect the mental strategy.
learnerActions: Work 462 − 5 on a number line (or hundred-square segment near the decade), moving DOWN: take 2 to reach 460, then 3 more to land on 457.
Check direction first: subtracting should make the answer smaller than 462, so an answer above 462 is wrong.
State which digits changed (the tens digit drops from 6 to 5) and why.
Thinking aloud, do 345 + 3, 345 + 7 and 462 − 5 in turn, saying which digits change after each.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtracting across a decade moves the number down past the ten, so the tens digit drops. A direction check catches the smaller-from-larger error when it gives an answer above the start (462 − 5 → 463), but it cannot catch every case. Checking that the tens digit dropped, because the answer passed below 460, makes the check complete.

constraints: The target is mental calculation: apparatus (place-value/Gattegno chart, number line, hundred-square segment, base-ten blocks, bead string, partitioning jottings) are scaffolds to make the local-versus-bridging change visible, to be faded as the child calculates reliably in their head.

Multiple-choice or rapid mixed items (e.g. 345+7 with a 342 distractor) chiefly check whether the child bridges and catch the 'only ones change' overgeneralisation; they do not by themselves build the bridging insight, which needs the child to construct and explain the steps.
A static tap-to-reveal chart can show which digit changes but does not let the child follow the carry cascade; pair it with a number line or manipulation if the bridging mechanism is the goal.
Prerequisites: secure within-20 make-ten bonds and confident place-value naming of hundreds/tens/ones digits; reteach these if the wrong-digit or no-bridge errors persist.
Partial mastery looks like handling the non-bridging case and bridging only with a number line or apparatus, not yet reliably in the head, and possibly missing direction on subtraction.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Add and subtract a two-digit number and tens (45 + 30, 82 − 40) mentally and with concrete/pictorial support, recognising that only the tens digit changes. Ages 6–7.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'add and subtract numbers using concrete objects, pictorial representations, and mentally, including: a two-digit number and tens'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.5/1.NBT.6 (mentally find 10 more/less; subtract multiples of 10) and 2.NBT.8; adding/subtracting a multiple of ten changes only the tens.
• Operational details: build directly from '10 more/10 less' — adding 30 is three jumps of ten, so the ones stay fixed and the tens digit changes by 3. Use base-ten blocks (add/remove ten-sticks, ones untouched) and a hundred square (move vertically). The insight is that the ones digit is invariant.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — finds 45 + 10 then 45 + 30 by repeated tens. Tier B (age 7) — computes 45 + 30 and 82 − 40 mentally in one step. Tier C (age 7+) — explains that only the tens digit changes and predicts the result before calculating.
bestPractices: Build from '10 more/10 less' to adding/subtracting several tens at once.
Use base-ten blocks: add or remove ten-sticks while the ones pile stays untouched.
Use a hundred square with vertical moves (down = +10, up = −10).
Draw attention to the invariant ones digit as the key check.
Contrast with adding ones (which changes the ones) so children don't confuse the two.

Hundred square with vertical jumps
Empty number line with jumps of ten
Place-value (Gattegno) chart sliding the tens
Arrow cards separating tens and ones

Adding the tens digit to the ones (45 + 30 → 48 or 75... e.g. treating 30 as 3 ones).

learn.summary: For ages 6–7: add and subtract a two-digit number and a multiple of ten (e.g. 45 + 30, 82 − 40) mentally and with concrete/pictorial support, building from '10 more/10 less'. The key insight is that adding or subtracting whole tens leaves the ones digit fixed and, while the answer stays between 0 and 99, changes only the tens digit (crossing 100, e.g. 85 + 30 = 115, also changes the hundreds). The classic error is treating the added tens as ones (45 + 30 → 48) or changing both digits. A deliberate contrast with adding ones (45 + 3) keeps the two procedures distinct.

activities.title: Add and remove tens while the ones stay put
feedback: If a learner answers 48 for 45 + 30, show that 30 is three ten-sticks, not three single ones: place the three ten-sticks with the tens and leave the ones pile of five untouched, so 45 + 30 = 75.
If the ones digit changes after adding tens (e.g. 45 + 30 → 70 or 78), point to the ones column on the hundred square and confirm it stays 5 through every vertical jump.
If the tens digit is off by one ten (65 or 85 for 45 + 30), count the ten-jumps aloud together and track them on fingers so exactly three tens are added.
When the learner correctly keeps the ones fixed, ask them to predict the next item before acting to confirm the reasoning, not just the answer.
activities.rationale: A manipulable base-ten mat and hundred square make the invariant ones digit visible as tens are added or removed, which targets the common place-value confusion between adding tens and adding ones. A 'predict then act' step shifts focus from counting to reasoning about place value.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils add and subtract a two-digit number and tens using concrete, pictorial and mental methods.
Adding multiples of ten leaves the ones digit invariant; confusing add-tens with add-ones is a common place-value error.
learnerActions: Start with a base-ten representation of 45: four ten-sticks and five single ones, with the numeral 45 shown alongside.
Before acting, predict the answer to 45 + 30 and say which digit you think will change.
Add three more ten-sticks one at a time for +30, saying the running total aloud: 45 → 55 → 65 → 75, and notice that the five single ones never move.
Switch to subtraction: start from 82 (eight ten-sticks, two ones) and remove four ten-sticks for 82 − 40, reaching 42, with the two ones untouched.

Repeat the same moves on a hundred square numbered with 1 at the top: for +30 move three rows straight down (45 → 55 → 65 → 75); for −40 move four rows straight up (82 → 72 → 62 → 52 → 42), watching that the ones column stays the same.
Immediately afterwards do 45 + 3 with single ones to feel the difference: now the ones pile changes and the tens stay the same.

Optionally, show the same tens move on other representations of place value — an empty number line with jumps of ten, a Gattegno place-value chart where the tens row slides while the ones stay, or arrow cards that separate the tens and ones — to reinforce that only the tens change.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting a multiple of ten moves only the tens; the ones digit is invariant. Adding ones is a different move that changes the ones instead.

activities.title: Fluency practice: one-step add/subtract tens
feedback: If a fluency answer alters the ones digit, send the learner back to the base-ten or hundred-square representation to re-see the fixed ones before continuing.
Reinforce correct one-step answers by asking the learner to state which digit changed and why.
activities.rationale: Speeded recall practice is proposed to help cement the one-step move once the invariant-ones insight is secure; it practises fluency rather than building the underlying place-value understanding, so it is best used after the manipulative work.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in items such as 45 + 30 = ___ and 82 − 40 = ___, aiming to answer in one step.
Answer 'which digit changes?' questions for an add-tens item, resisting a distractor answer that alters the ones digit.
Work through a short sequence of +10 steps (e.g. 45, 55, 65, 75) and then a −10 sequence, saying each total.
Mix in an occasional add-ones item (45 + 3) so you have to decide which digit changes each time.
activities.intendedInsight: The one-step mental move for adding/subtracting tens can become more automatic, while deliberate contrast with adding ones keeps the two procedures from merging.

activities.title: Explain and predict the invariant digit
feedback: If the learner cannot explain the invariance but gets answers by repeated +10 steps, name what they are doing: each +10 is one step down the hundred square (with 1 at the top) with the ones unchanged, so adding three tens keeps the ones fixed.
If the learner confuses the add-tens and add-ones items, revisit the deliberate 45 + 30 versus 45 + 3 contrast with concrete materials.
activities.rationale: Prompting prediction and explanation surfaces the place-value reasoning and can distinguish a learner who understands invariance from one relying only on repeated counting; the contrast item is the discriminating check.
sourceClaims: Adding multiples of ten leaves the ones digit invariant; confusing add-tens with add-ones is a common place-value error.
learnerActions: Work out 45 + 30; 82 − 40; and 45 + 3 mentally and state which digit changed each time.
Explain why only the tens change when adding or subtracting tens, and why the ones change for 45 + 3.
Predict the ones digit of 82 − 40 before calculating, then check.
Show 45 + 30 on a hundred square and describe which way you move and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to articulate why the ones stay fixed (because whole tens are being added) demonstrates secure place-value reasoning beyond getting the right number.

constraints: Build from an existing '10 more/10 less' skill: adding 30 is three jumps of ten, so the ones stay fixed and, when the total stays below 100, the tens digit goes up by three.

Include a contrast with adding ones (e.g. 45 + 3) so learners do not merge the add-tens and add-ones procedures; this contrast is strongly recommended and is the basis of the diagnostic discrimination between the two moves.
Fluency/fill-in practice reinforces speed but does not by itself build the invariant-ones understanding; use it after concrete and pictorial work.
A static highlighted hundred square can anchor the idea but does not let the learner practise the move; treat it as an anchor, not the main activity.
Live digit updates, dragging ten-sticks, and vertical hundred-square jumps are helpful ways to make the mechanism concrete but are optional illustrations, not required mechanisms.
Base-ten sticks and hundred squares are pictorial/concrete models of place value; keep attention on what each represents (tens vs ones) rather than the material itself.

pedagogy.summary: Adding and subtracting two two-digit numbers is introduced through concrete and pictorial regrouping before any formal column method. The central idea is composing a ten when the ones exceed nine (34+27) and decomposing a ten when there are too few ones to subtract (63−28). Base-ten blocks make the exchange physical; number lines and partitioning jottings connect it to recording. This is where 'carrying' and 'borrowing' are given meaning as exchange rather than taught as digit tricks.
bestPractices: Establish the exchange principle with base-ten blocks: ten ones can be fairly swapped for one ten, and one ten for ten ones (NRICH: exchange/unitising)
Partition both numbers into tens and ones, combine like with like, then compose/decompose a ten as needed (NCETM Spine 1.15/1.16)
Use a number line for subtraction as finding a difference (count up 28→63) as an alternative to take-away
Move concrete → pictorial → jotting for the SAME calculation so the recording mirrors the action
Ask the child to explain their strategy and why 34+27 is not 511 — the recombination is where meaning is tested
keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks with a place-value mat (compose/decompose a ten)
Number line (jumps for adding; count-up for difference)
Part-whole / partitioning jottings (30+20 and 4+7)
Bar model (comparison and missing-part subtraction)
Hundred square
commonMisconceptions: Failing to compose the ten: adding tens (50) and ones (11) and writing them side by side (511) or keeping 51

learn.summary: Ages 6–7 add and subtract two two-digit numbers (e.g. 34+27, 63−28) by giving meaning to 'carrying' and 'borrowing' as fair exchange: ten ones can be swapped for one ten and vice versa. Learners partition into tens and ones, combine like with like, then compose a ten when the ones exceed nine, or decompose a ten when there are too few ones to subtract. Concrete base-ten work and pictorial jottings for the SAME calculation let the recording mirror the physical action, so regrouping is felt as a swap rather than rehearsed as a digit trick.

activities.title: Exchange on a place-value mat: compose and decompose a ten
feedback: If the child writes 511 or keeps 51: have them physically swap ten of the eleven ones for one ten-rod on the mat, then re-read the result; name it — 'ten ones is the same as one ten'.
If the child does the ones of 63−28 as 8−3 and answers 45: show on the mat that 3 ones cannot give 8, so a ten must be broken open first (63 = 50+13); check by adding 45+28, which gives 73, not 63.

If the child breaks rods apart to recount everything in ones: do not stop them handling the blocks or drill exchange in isolation — treating a rod as one 'ten' is a maturing shift; each time they exchange, read both ways aloud together, 'that's ten ones AND one ten', so unitising develops.

Probe: 'You made eleven ones — can you swap some for a ten? Show me.' 'For 63−28 you needed more ones — where did the extra ones come from?' 'Would 34+25 still need an exchange? Why not?' (For 34+25 the ones are 4+5=9, below ten, so no exchange is needed.)
activities.rationale: The concept being taught is exchange, so the learner should perform the regroup, not just watch it. Partitioning into tens and ones and composing/decomposing a ten is the standard mastery progression, and pairing the concrete action with a matching jotting makes the recording mirror the exchange. Reading a ten-rod as both 'ten ones' and 'one ten' builds unitising.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils add and subtract two two-digit numbers using concrete objects, pictorial representations and mentally, and recording in columns supports place value and prepares for formal written methods.
Two two-digit numbers are added by partitioning one or both into tens and ones; subtraction partitions the subtrahend into tens and ones, decomposing a ten where the ones are insufficient.

Exchange — fairly swapping ten ones for one ten (and vice versa) — and unitising a ten as a single entity are the ideas underpinning regrouping; such resources can be used diagnostically to assess whether place value is genuinely understood.
learnerActions: Set out 34 + 27 on a place-value mat using base-ten blocks (or draggable on-screen tens and ones).

Pile the ones together to find there are eleven; because that is ten or more, perform a 'make a ten' action that swaps ten loose ones for one ten-rod moved into the tens column, leaving one loose one, then read the answer as 61 (not 511, not 51).
Set out 63 − 28; find there are not enough ones to give eight, so take a ten-rod and break it into ten loose ones, so 63 is now 50 and 13.
Hand over eight ones (13−8=5) and subtract the tens (50−20=30) to reach 35.
Record each physical step as a matching jotting: 30+20=50, 4+7=11, exchange → 61; and 63 = 50+13, 13−8=5, 50−20=30 → 35.
Say aloud why 34+27 cannot be 511 ('ten ones is the same as one ten, so the extra ten joins the tens').
activities.intendedInsight: Composing a ten (addition) and decomposing a ten (subtraction) are the same exchange run in opposite directions; 'carrying' and 'borrowing' are fair swaps between ones and tens, not separate digit tricks.

activities.title: Subtraction as finding a difference on a number line
feedback: If jumps don't land cleanly, suggest jumping first to the next multiple of ten (28 → 30) before the big jump.

If the count-up answer differs from the take-away answer, check both: revisit the ones step on the mat for a missed exchange, and re-add the jumps on the number line, since either method may hold the slip.
Ask: 'Which method did you find easier for 63 − 28, counting up or taking away? Why?'
activities.rationale: A number line presents subtraction as finding a difference (count up 28→63) as an alternative to take-away, giving a complementary model and a self-check; a bar model and hundred square are further optional representations. This is offered as an alternative representation, not a replacement for the exchange work. A number line is a pictorial method, but no cited source directly validates the count-up-as-difference principle, so no source claim is attached.
learnerActions: Place 28 and 63 on a number line.
Count up from 28 to 63 in convenient jumps (e.g. 28 → 30 is 2, 30 → 60 is 30, 60 → 63 is 3).
Total the jumps (2 + 30 + 3 = 35) and state 63 − 28 = 35.
Compare this count-up answer with the take-away/exchange answer from the mat and confirm they agree.
Optionally model the same subtraction with a bar model (whole 63, known part 28, missing part found as the difference) or on a hundred square, as further representations of the same difference.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtraction can be read as the difference between two numbers found by counting up, which offers a second route to the same answer and a self-check against the smaller-from-larger error.

activities.title: Annotated worked example and targeted consolidation
feedback: For a chosen '511'/'51': return to the eleven-ones-make-a-ten step and have the learner state where the extra ten goes.
For a chosen '45': have the learner break a ten in 63 to make 50+13 and redo the ones step, then check by adding.
Encourage the learner to narrate the exchange aloud each time, since the explanation is where understanding is tested.
activities.rationale: A staged annotated example can show the partition and exchange as a reference, and a set of two-digit ± two-digit items consolidates and catches the 511 and smaller-from-larger errors — but reference and recognition rehearse rather than build the exchange insight, so they follow the hands-on exchange rather than replace it. Recognising a correct answer does not by itself elicit independent production of the exchange. Asking the child to explain why 34+27 is not 511 is where the recombination meaning is tested.
sourceClaims: The 'smaller-from-larger' subtraction error is a classic systematic buggy algorithm.
Two two-digit numbers are added by partitioning one or both into tens and ones; subtraction partitions the subtrahend into tens and ones, decomposing a ten where the ones are insufficient.
learnerActions: Study a worked example of 34+27 and 63−28 where the partition and exchange step are revealed one stage at a time (e.g. reveal 4+7 becoming 'one ten and one'; reveal the tens as 30+20+10).
Explain in your own words what happened at the exchange step before moving on.
Then work a short set of two-digit ± two-digit items, including 34+27 and the decomposition of 63 into 50+13, choosing or writing the answer and giving the exchange reasoning.
When a '511', '51' or '45' answer appears, say why it is wrong rather than only marking the correct one.
activities.intendedInsight: A clearly staged worked example makes the partition and exchange visible for reference, and a focused problem set surfaces whether the compose-a-ten and smaller-from-larger errors have really been overcome.

constraints: Build the skill from repeated hands-on exchange with base-ten blocks and a place-value mat before any formal column method; introduce 'carrying'/'borrowing' only as names for the exchange already performed.
Move concrete → pictorial → jotting for the SAME calculation so the recording mirrors the action; do not jump straight to abstract digit manipulation.
A static annotated worked example or tap-to-reveal reference can show the steps but does not let the child perform the regroup; use it as reference alongside, not instead of, hands-on exchange.

A set of items that includes the common wrong answers 511/51 and 45 can consolidate and expose errors, but recognition-only responses do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the exchange; pair with the learner performing and recording the swap.
When describing whether an exchange is needed (e.g. 34+25 vs 34+27), check the ones sum directly — exchange is needed only when the ones reach ten or more (4+5=9 needs none; 4+7=11 does).
Treat a ten-rod being recounted as ten separate ones as a developmental stage in unitising, not an error to drill away; keep reading it both ways aloud.

The place-value mat is essentially planar (tens and ones, place value), so these activities do not propose a third dimension or spoken-only delivery as the main medium for the exchange insight; this is a design preference, not evidence that 3D or dialogue cannot teach it, and talk is still used so the child can explain their strategy.

A bar model (comparison and missing-part subtraction) and a hundred square remain available as further optional representations and should not be presented as replacements for the base-ten exchange work.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two cited sources are marked unverified in the source row (NCETM Spine 1.15/1.16 partitioning claim; Brown & Burton 1978 / VanLehn 'Mind Bugs' 1990 on the smaller-from-larger buggy algorithm); treat their support as provisional.

Arithmetic self-check: 34+27 → 30+20=50, 4+7=11, 50+11=61 (not 511, not 51). 63−28 → 63=50+13, 13−8=5, 50−20=30, so 35; number-line count-up 28→30→60→63 gives 2+30+3=35. The smaller-from-larger error 8−3=5 yields the incorrect 45, and 45+28=73≠63. These confirm the answers used; 511/51/45 appear ONLY as named incorrect responses to diagnose, never as valid answers.

The legacy source framed digit-based side-by-side work as something hands-on exchange 'cannot fake' and spoken discussion as unable to substitute for exchange; these comparative-necessity claims are softened here to scoped affordances/limits rather than asserted as established efficacy.

No source directly supports subtraction read as a difference found by counting up on a number line; it is a pictorial method and a self-check, so the number-line activity carries no source claim rather than citing the broad DfE pictorial/mental claim as if it validated the count-up principle.

The source misconception 'misaligning tens and ones when recording without a place-value mat' is addressed implicitly by consistent use of the place-value mat and matched jottings across the first activity.

probeDeeper: You made eleven ones — can you swap some of those for a ten? Show me what you do.
For 63 − 28 you needed more ones than you had — where did the extra ones come from?
Explain to me why 34 + 27 isn't five hundred and eleven.
What if it were 34 + 25 instead of 34 + 27 — would you still need to exchange? Why not?

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't compose the ten — 'thirty and twenty is fifty, four and seven is eleven, so five hundred and eleven' (or keeps 51)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child physically swap ten of the eleven ones for one ten-rod on the mat, then read the result. Name it: ten ones is the same as one ten.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child records 50 and 11 but never exchanges the eleven ones for a ten; writes 511 or 51

errorPatterns.pattern: Smaller-from-larger in subtraction — '63 take 28: eight take three is five', answering 45
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the mat, show 63 cannot give 8 ones from only 3, so a ten must be broken open first (63 = 50+13). Check by adding 45+28.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The ones column of 63−28 is done as 8−3 with no decomposition; answer 45

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts every cube in ones and loses the ten-structure — treats a ten-rod as ten separate things to recount rather than one ten
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT stop them handling the blocks or drill exchange in isolation — treating a rod as one 'ten' is a maturing shift. Keep pairing the two readings aloud ('that's ten ones AND one ten') each time they exchange, so unitising develops.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child base-ten blocks and paper and set two calculations to work with the blocks and record: 34 + 27, then 63 − 28. Watch what they do at the ones in each case.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 34+27 requires composing a ten from eleven ones; a child who answers 511 or 51 has added the parts but not exchanged. 63−28 requires decomposing a ten; the smaller-from-larger child answers 45. Doing both correctly shows exchange is understood in both directions, which side-by-side digit work cannot fake.

topic.name: Adding within 100
topic.description: Add within 100 using strategies based on place value, including adding a two-digit and one-digit number, and a two-digit and a multiple of 10
evidence: Calculate 46 + 7 using place value (46 + 4 + 3 = 53)
Calculate 38 + 40 = 78 using tens understanding
Relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out sums like '47 + 8' or '35 + 50' by thinking about the tens and ones separately rather than counting up one at a time?

pedagogy.summary: Adding within 100 is taught as strategy work grounded in place value, not as an early column algorithm. Children partition, use known number bonds, and bridge tens: 46+7 becomes 46+4+3, 38+40 adds tens to tens leaving ones untouched. The concrete-pictorial-abstract progression (base-ten blocks, bead strings, number lines → jottings) makes the tens boundary visible before it is recorded symbolically.
bestPractices: Extend within-20 'make ten' bonds to numbers within 100 — 46+7 uses the same partition of 7 into 4+3 that 6+7 does (NCETM Spine 1.13: known within-ten facts applied to a two-digit + single-digit number)
Keep tens and ones distinct: for 38+40, add the multiple of ten to the tens and leave the ones alone, so the child feels tens land on tens
Use multiple connected representations for the same calculation — bead string, part-whole diagram, number line, and symbolic jotting — so the strategy transfers
Secure fluent partitioning of numbers to ten first; it is the explicit prerequisite for independent bridging
Ask the child to relate the mental strategy to a written record and justify it, not just state the answer (curriculum: explain the reasoning)
keyRepresentations: Bead string / 100-bead frame (bridging a ten made visible)
Base-ten blocks (tens rods and ones)
Number line with jumps (partition the added amount into a jump to the next ten, then the rest)
Part-whole model (partition the addend, e.g. 7 = 4 + 3)
Hundred square (move along for ones, down for tens)
commonMisconceptions: Treating a multiple of ten as ones: 38+40 done as 38+4=42
Not bridging the ten: 46+7 done as 6+7=13, keeping the 3 and losing the extra ten (answer 43), or concatenating to 413
Adding the added amount to the wrong part (ones added to the tens digit)
Persisting with count-all/count-on-in-ones instead of using place value

learn.summary: Children aged 6-7 add within 100 using place-value strategies, not a column algorithm. They partition addends, use known number bonds to bridge a ten (46+7 as 46+4+3), and add tens to tens leaving the ones untouched (38+40=78). A concrete-pictorial-abstract progression (bead strings, base-ten blocks, number lines, then jottings) makes the tens boundary visible before it is recorded symbolically. The crossing-a-ten moment and the tens-onto-tens move are the two insights to build and check.

activities.title: Watch a ten compose when you cross the boundary
feedback: If the child computes the ones as 13 but writes only the 3 (answer 43) or strings digits as 413, return to make-ten within 20 on a bead string so the extra ten is seen composing, then carry that exact move up to 46+7. The crossed ten must not disappear.

If the child counts on in ones (54, 55, ... 62 for 53+9), do not ban the counting or penalise slowness: it is valid and matures as make-ten becomes automatic. Model the make-ten jump alongside their count so the efficient move becomes the natural one.
Praise relating the spoken strategy to the partition: 'you split 7 into 4 and 3 to land exactly on the ten'.
activities.rationale: Known within-ten facts and partitioning transfer to a two-digit-plus-single-digit sum; the make-ten bridging strategy depends on fluent partitioning of numbers to ten, and letting the child act on the boundary turns bridging into something observed rather than told. A live manipulative where loose ones visibly compose a ten (with a running count) makes the regroup concrete; this is one effective way to expose the structure, not the only possible one. Equivalent physical bead strings or base-ten blocks serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils add and subtract using concrete objects, pictorial representations and mentally, including a two-digit number and ones, a two-digit number and tens, and two two-digit numbers; recall facts to 20 and derive related facts to 100.

Known within-ten facts and partitioning are applied to add a single-digit number to a two-digit number; the make-ten bridging strategy requires fluent partitioning of numbers to ten, and strategies are connected across multiple representations (tens frames, part-whole, number line, symbolic).
Unitising (treating one ten as a single entity) and exchange are the ideas children must grasp to calculate with numbers beyond ten; a digit's value depends on its position.
learnerActions: Start with 46 shown on a bead string or in a base-ten workspace
Add single ones one at a time, saying the running total aloud (47, 48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53)

When the added one makes ten loose ones, see that they complete a ten (on a bead string, the next block of ten beads is filled; with base-ten blocks, swap the ten ones for a ten-rod), so the count goes 49, then 50, then on to 53
Re-tell what happened: 'I added 4 to reach 50, then 3 more to make 53', and link it to the partition 7 = 4 + 3
Repeat for 53 + 9 (bridge to 60 by adding 7, then +2)
activities.intendedInsight: Bridging a ten is not an arbitrary rule: the extra ten is physically composed from ten ones, and the make-ten partition (7 = 4 + 3) is the same move used within 20 applied at 46.

activities.title: Tens land on tens: add a multiple of ten
feedback: If the child gives 38 + 40 = 42 (adding 4 to the ones, saying 'four tens is a four'), rebuild with ten-rods: forty is four tens and joins the three tens already there. Confront the size mismatch — 42 is only just above 38, so it cannot be right after adding forty.
Reinforce order-independence: adding the 8 first or the 40 first both give 78.
activities.rationale: The curriculum expects adding a two-digit number and a multiple of ten; keeping tens and ones distinct prevents the common error of adding a multiple of ten as if it were ones. Base-ten rods make the place-value distinction tangible.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils add and subtract using concrete objects, pictorial representations and mentally, including a two-digit number and ones, a two-digit number and tens, and two two-digit numbers; recall facts to 20 and derive related facts to 100.
Unitising (treating one ten as a single entity) and exchange are the ideas children must grasp to calculate with numbers beyond ten; a digit's value depends on its position.
learnerActions: Start with 38 shown with three ten-rods and eight ones
Add four ten-rods, watching them join the tens while the eight ones stay untouched
State the total as 70 + 8 = 78, and say why the ones did not change
Check by a different order: add 30 + 40 = 70 first, then the 8 — confirm it gives the same 78
Contrast with the wrong move: 'is 38 + 40 the same as 38 + 4? why not?' — notice 42 is only 4 more than 38, far too small after adding forty
activities.intendedInsight: A multiple of ten joins the tens, not the ones; four tens combine with three tens to make seven tens, leaving the ones unchanged.

activities.title: Partition the addend with a part-whole picture
feedback: If the child splits 7 into something that does not reach 50 (e.g. 2 and 5), ask which part gets them exactly to the next ten from 46.
A labelled picture shows the structure but does not let the child perform the regroup themselves; pair it with hands-on bridging (first activity) so the felt move and the structure connect.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal or labelled part-whole diagram makes the partition and the ten-crossing explicit. It teaches the structure of the strategy; because the learner does not act on the boundary, it works best alongside, not instead of, hands-on regrouping.
sourceClaims: Known within-ten facts and partitioning are applied to add a single-digit number to a two-digit number; the make-ten bridging strategy requires fluent partitioning of numbers to ten, and strategies are connected across multiple representations (tens frames, part-whole, number line, symbolic).
learnerActions: Look at 46 + 7 with 7 shown in a part-whole model
Split the 7 into 4 (the amount needed to reach the next ten) and 3 (the rest)
Mark where the calculation crosses a ten (at 50) and label it 'this is where we cross a ten'
Say the two jumps: 46 + 4 = 50, then 50 + 3 = 53
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing the partition that lands exactly on the next ten is what makes bridging efficient; the structure of the strategy can be seen even before acting it out.

activities.title: Connect the strategy to a written record and explain it
feedback: Efficient work: 46+7 by partitioning 7 into 4+3 (46+4=50, then +3=53); 38+40 by adding tens (30+40=70, then +8=78) leaving the ones untouched; 53+9 by bridging (53+7=60, then +2=62) or 53+10-1.
If the child only states answers, ask them to link the jotting to the number line and say why each step works.
activities.rationale: The curriculum asks pupils to relate the strategy to a written method and explain their reasoning; using multiple connected representations for the same calculation helps the strategy transfer. Consolidation items (fill-the-blank partitions such as 46 + ? = 50, 50 + ? = 53, and choosing the correct partition of 38+40 rather than the common 42 error) check retention after the insight is built.
sourceClaims: Known within-ten facts and partitioning are applied to add a single-digit number to a two-digit number; the make-ten bridging strategy requires fluent partitioning of numbers to ten, and strategies are connected across multiple representations (tens frames, part-whole, number line, symbolic).
learnerActions: For each of 46+7, 38+40, 53+9, carry out the mental strategy and write a matching jotting (e.g. 46 + 4 = 50, 50 + 3 = 53)
Show the same calculation as a number-line jump (a jump to the next ten, then the rest)
Explain aloud why the method works, not just the answer
Answer probes: 'Show on the number line why 46 + 7 lands on 53'; 'For 38+40, would adding the 8 first give the same answer? How do you know?'; 'What changes if it were 46 + 40 instead of 46 + 4?'
activities.intendedInsight: The mental strategy, the number-line jump, and the written jotting are the same story told three ways; being able to justify the reasoning is part of the objective.

constraints: Teach as strategy work grounded in place value, not as an early column algorithm.
Secure fluent partitioning of numbers to ten first; it is the explicit prerequisite for independent bridging.

Fill-the-blank and multiple-choice items rehearse, check and consolidate the strategy and suit practice after the insight is built; they do not let the child enact the ten-crossing regroup by hand, so pair them with the hands-on activity (and the part-whole scaffold) rather than using them to first build the strategy.
A labelled or tap-to-reveal part-whole picture shows the structure but does not let the child perform the regroup; it is a scaffold to pair with hands-on bridging, not a replacement.
Do not ban counting-on in ones or penalise slowness; it is a valid developmental strategy that matures as make-ten becomes automatic. Model the efficient jump alongside the child's count.

Optional interactive supports (dragging ones that compose a ten at the boundary, a running count, sliding ten-rods onto the tens, a toggle mirroring the action as a number-line jump and jotting) make the mechanism concrete but are examples, not required mechanisms; equivalent physical bead strings and base-ten blocks serve the same purpose.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources have NOT been re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The NCETM Spine 1 source (Segments 1.11 & 1.13) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim with corresponding caution.

The source row rated a third spatial dimension and in-role dialogue as poor fits with reasoning that extra dimensions 'add nothing' and 'talk is not the bottleneck'. These are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and are not asserted here. Addition within 100 is a quantity-and-place-value idea that does not require a third spatial dimension, and spoken explanation remains valuable for the 'explain your reasoning' objective.

The 'explain your reasoning' objective is drawn from the broader DfE curriculum; the specific quoted DfE claim does not state it, so its support rests mainly on the multiple-representations claim rather than a direct quotation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put these three in front of the child one at a time and ask them to work each out, thinking aloud and jotting if they wish: 46 + 7, then 38 + 40, then 53 + 9. Watch closely what happens on the two that cross a ten.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two items that cross a ten (46+7, 53+9) separate a child who bridges using place value from one who mishandles the boundary and drops or concatenates the extra ten; 38+40 separates a child who adds tens to tens from one who adds the '4' of forty to the ones. pedagogy.summary: This topic is about APPLYING addition and subtraction to real problems — including two-step problems, money, and measures — and choosing between a mental method and a written one. The mathematical challenge is less about calculating and more about modelling: reading the situation, deciding what operation each step needs, and picking an efficient method. Bar models and part-whole diagrams are the key tools for representing the structure before computing.
bestPractices: Teach the child to represent the situation first (bar model / part-whole) before choosing numbers or method — structure before calculation
For two-step problems, make the intermediate result explicit ('how much after spending, before finding?')
Discuss method choice: some problems are quicker mentally (35p−12p), some warrant a jotting/written method — build the judgement

Bar models and part-whole diagrams represent the structure before any computing.

activities.title: Build the story as a bar model (money two-step)
feedback: If the child answers 23p for the money problem, point to the third part of the story: 'then found 5p' — ask 'is 23p the final answer, or is there another step?' and have them add the last bar.
If the answer has no unit or mixes cm and p, ask 'how many WHAT?' and require a labelled answer, keeping coins or a ruler in view.
If they reach for an operation before drawing, ask them to show who has what as a bar first, before choosing to add or subtract.
activities.rationale: Representing the relationships between quantities with a strip/bar diagram, rather than attending to surface features, supports genuine problem solving; making the intermediate result explicit directly addresses the common error of doing only the first step.
sourceClaims: Genuine problem solving is reasoning about a problem's structure, 'not the execution of memorized rules or shortcuts, such as using key words'; teaching students to represent the relationships between quantities with visual representations (strip/bar diagrams), rather than attending to surface features, improves problem solving (Recommendation 3, STRONG evidence).
learnerActions: Take the problem 'I had 35p, spent 12p, then found 5p — how much now?' and draw a bar to represent the starting 35p.
Cut 12p off the bar for the spending, and label the segment that is left — write 35−12=23 and mark 23p as the intermediate result.
Add a 5p bar for 'then found 5p' and compute the final total: 23+5=28p. Label the answer with its unit.
Repeat with a lengths story, e.g. 'a ribbon is 45cm, I cut off 18cm — how long is left?', drawing and labelling the bar and giving the answer in cm (45−18=27cm).
activities.intendedInsight: Drawing the situation turns a confusing word problem into visible parts; seeing the middle number (23p) appear is what stops a child from stopping after step one, and labelling keeps the units correct.

activities.title: Compare problems that defeat keyword guessing
feedback: If the child chooses an operation from a cue word, have them draw both people's bars first: in the first problem Tom's bar is longer, so we add; in the contrasting problem Sam's bar is shorter, so we subtract.
Ask 'could more than ever mean subtract?' to surface that keywords are unreliable and the drawn structure is the guide.
activities.rationale: Some compare and start-unknown structures are where keyword strategies often fail. Children solve them more reliably by modelling the situation. Setting the Sam/Tom problem, where 'more than' does mean add, beside a problem where 'more' needs subtraction makes the keyword strategy visibly break down.
sourceClaims: Word-problem difficulty follows the problem's semantic structure: result-unknown (join/separate) problems are easier than compare and start-unknown structures, on which keyword strategies systematically fail; children solve most reliably by modelling the situation.

learnerActions: Solve 'Sam has 24 stickers. Tom has 8 more than Sam. How many does Tom have?' by drawing Sam's bar and building Tom's bar as Sam's amount plus 8 more.
State the operation you used (24+8=32) and explain why 'more than' here means add, even though 'more than' can sometimes cue the wrong choice.

Try a contrasting compare problem where the cue word misleads, e.g. 'Tom has 32 stickers. He has 8 more than Sam. How many does Sam have?' Draw both bars and notice that, even though it says 'more', Sam's bar is shorter, so you subtract (32−8=24). Modelling, not the cue word, tells you whether to add or subtract.
activities.intendedInsight: The operation comes from the situation, not from a trigger word; a bar model makes compare problems (where keywords can mislead) solvable by showing the structure.

activities.title: Mental or written? Choosing an efficient method
feedback: If the child always writes everything out, ask whether 35p−12p really needed paper, and invite a mental attempt.
If a larger problem goes wrong in the head, suggest a jotting or a number-line count-on and compare which felt more reliable.
activities.rationale: The curriculum expects pupils to use both mental and written methods; building the judgement of when each is efficient is part of the objective rather than defaulting to one.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils solve problems with addition and subtraction using concrete objects, pictorial representations and mental and written methods, including problems involving numbers, quantities and measures.
learnerActions: For each problem decide: can I do this quickly in my head, or should I jot it down? Then solve it.
Compare 35p−12p (quick mentally) with a larger measures problem such as 45cm−18cm that may be easier with a jotting or bridging step.
Build a short anchor chart of 'when I use mental' versus 'when I jot/write', and justify one of your choices aloud.
activities.intendedInsight: Method choice is a judgement about efficiency, not a rule; small, friendly numbers often suit mental work while larger or multi-digit ones may warrant a written method.

activities.title: Talk through the structure before solving
feedback: If the child jumps to an answer, pause and ask them to re-tell the story in their own words and count the steps.
Keep the discussion on eliciting structure and steps — avoid simply supplying the answer so the child still does the modelling.
activities.rationale: Spoken elicitation of 'what we know / what we need' keeps attention on the problem's structure rather than on cue words, but talk alone does not provide the manipulable diagram or practice volume, so it is paired with actually building and computing the model rather than offered as a substitute.

learnerActions: With a partner or adult, answer three questions about a new story: what is happening, what do we know, and what do we need to find?
Say how many steps the problem has before computing anything, and name the intermediate quantity for a two-step problem.
Only then draw the bar model and solve, checking your spoken plan against your diagram.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the structure first guards against grabbing an operation prematurely and against stopping halfway through a two-step problem.

constraints: Represent the situation first (bar model or part-whole) before choosing numbers or method — structure before calculation.

Use problem vocabulary (total, difference, more/less, change) so the operation is drawn from the situation, not from keywords.
