topic.name: Subtracting multiples of 10
topic.description: Subtract multiples of 10 (10–90) from multiples of 10 using place value strategies
evidence: Calculate 70 − 30 = 40
Use base-ten blocks to show 80 − 50 = 30
Explain that subtracting tens is like subtracting the tens digits
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly work out '80 − 50' or '70 − 40' in their head by thinking about how many tens are left?

pedagogy.summary: Subtracting multiples of ten (70−30) is taught through unitising: a decade number is a count of tens, so 70−30 is seven tens minus three tens, and the answer is four tens. The known single-digit fact (7−3=4) is reused at the scale of tens. Ten-rods, bead strings and number lines that jump in tens make this visible, so the '0' in the answer carries meaning rather than being appended as a trick.
bestPractices: Build on 'the multiples of ten represent one-to-nine tens': treat 70−30 as 7 tens − 3 tens (NCETM Spine: derived facts, e.g. 30+70 from 3+7)
Reuse the known within-ten fact explicitly — connect 7−3 to 70−30 so the child sees the same subtraction at a larger unit
Represent with ten-rods and with a number line that jumps in tens, so subtraction of tens is a small number of large jumps
Ask the child to explain that subtracting tens is like subtracting the tens digits because each unit is a ten — meaning behind the zero
Contrast 70−3 with 70−30 to expose whether the child is tracking the unit
keyRepresentations: Ten-rods / base-ten tens (remove whole rods)
Bead string in tens or 100-bead frame
Number line with jumps of ten
Hundred square (move up in tens)
Place-value chart showing the tens column
commonMisconceptions: Dropping the ten-unit: subtracting 7−3=4 and answering 4 instead of 40
Treating the zero as a spelling trick ('add a zero') with no unit meaning
Counting back in ones (70,69,68…) and losing track
Confusing 70−3 with 70−30 because the unit isn't tracked

learn.summary: Teach subtracting multiples of ten (e.g. 70−30) through unitising: a decade number is a count of tens, so 70−30 is seven tens minus three tens = four tens. The known fact 7−3=4 is reused at the scale of tens, so the '0' in 40 carries real place meaning rather than being appended as a trick. Removable tens-materials, bead strings, and number lines that jump in tens make this visible; contrasting 70−3 with 70−30 exposes whether the child is tracking the unit.

activities.title: Removing whole tens from a tens-only mat
feedback: If the child answers 4 for 70 − 30, point to the four rods and ask 'is each of these one, or ten?' — rebuild the answer as four tens = 40.
If the child says 'you just add a zero', ask them to show the four tens on the mat and explain why the answer is four tens and not four ones.
Confirm good reasoning by asking the child to check: add the three removed rods back and see that seven tens (70) returns.
activities.rationale: Unitising — treating 'one lot of ten' as a single object that can be removed whole — is the crux of calculating with numbers larger than ten, and removable tens-materials let the child act on tens as units while watching the count change in ten-steps. An optional linked number line jumping in tens can mirror the rod action.
sourceClaims: Unitising — engaging with 'one lot of ten' as a single entity operated on as one object — is essential for calculating with numbers larger than ten.
learnerActions: Lay out seven ten-rods (or ten-sticks/strips of ten) to represent 70.
For 70 − 30, physically remove three whole rods and say the running count aloud: 70 → 60 → 50 → 40.
Name what is left as 'four tens, which is 40', pointing at the four rods rather than counting individual cubes.
Say the matching single-digit fact: 'seven tens minus three tens is four tens, just like 7 − 3 = 4.'
Repeat for 80 − 50 (eight rods, remove five, leaving three = 30) and 90 − 60 (nine rods, remove six, leaving three = 30), each time removing whole rods and stating the answer in tens.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtracting multiples of ten is the same subtraction as the known single-digit fact, spoken in units of ten; the zero in the answer is a real placeholder showing zero ones, which keeps the 4 in the tens place. It is not decoration.

activities.title: Contrasting 70 − 3 with 70 − 30
feedback: If the child gives the same answer for both, ask them to lay the two removed amounts side by side (three rods vs three cubes) and compare.
Praise reasoning that references the unit: 'three tens is thirty, three ones is only three.'
activities.rationale: Contrasting 70−3 with 70−30 exposes whether the child is tracking the unit rather than mechanically subtracting digits, directly addressing the confusion between the two.
sourceClaims: Unitising — engaging with 'one lot of ten' as a single entity operated on as one object — is essential for calculating with numbers larger than ten.
learnerActions: Work 70 − 30 by removing three whole ten-rods; record the answer (40) and the running count.
Rebuild 70 with seven ten-rods, then unbundle (or exchange) one ten-rod for ten single cubes; use these to work 70 − 3 by removing three single cubes.
Compare the two results: 70 − 30 = 40 (a big change) versus 70 − 3 = 67 (a small change).
Explain in words why removing three tens changes the number far more than removing three ones.
activities.intendedInsight: The size of the unit being removed matters: subtracting tens and subtracting ones are different because each ten is worth ten ones.

activities.title: Linking the known fact on a reference chart
feedback: If the child writes the answer but reads it as ones, re-read it together as 'four tens'.
Reinforce by asking which single-digit fact each decade subtraction is 'borrowing'.
activities.rationale: A reference layout that pairs the within-ten fact with the decade fact makes the reuse of known facts explicit. This is a scaffold for consolidation and does not by itself let the child act on removing tens, so it works best after hands-on removal.
sourceClaims: Derived-fact reasoning for decade calculations reuses known within-ten facts at the scale of tens (e.g. 86−50 via 80+6−50 = 30+6).
Year 2 pupils derive facts to 100 from facts to 20, e.g. using 3+7=10 to calculate 30+70=100 and 100−70=30; they understand multiples of ten and the value of each digit.
learnerActions: Look at 70 and state that it is '7 tens'.
Alongside 7 − 3 = 4, write 7 tens − 3 tens = 4 tens = 40.
Do the same for other decade pairs (e.g. 8 − 5 = 3 beside 80 − 50 = 30), reading each as a statement about tens.
activities.intendedInsight: Each decade subtraction reuses a single-digit fact at the scale of tens, so the known fact gives the answer directly.

activities.title: Decade subtraction practice with the dropped-unit trap
feedback: If 4 is chosen, return to the rods: four tens, not four ones.
If the correct answer (40) is chosen but the explanation is 'add a zero', ask them to justify it in tens.
activities.rationale: A short practice set rehearses the strategy and surfaces the dropped-unit error with a targeted trap; it is best placed after hands-on and reference work, which do more to first build the underlying idea.
learnerActions: Complete a short sequence of decade subtractions (e.g. 70−30, 60−40, 90−50), writing each answer.
For 70 − 30, choose the correct answer from options that include 4 as a tempting wrong answer, and explain why 4 is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the tens strategy and catch the common error of dropping the ten-unit.

activities.title: Optional: rhythmic count-back in tens
feedback: Keep this chant focused on jumping in tens for fluency; counting back in ones is still a valid strategy and should not be marked wrong, but for this particular chant gently restart in tens so the ten-jump becomes automatic.
activities.rationale: Rhythmic chanting can reinforce the decade count-sequence and support fluency. It supports but does not build the unitising insight, so it is a supplement to the hands-on work rather than the primary teaching.
learnerActions: Chant the tens count-back sequence aloud with a rhythm: '70, 60, 50, 40' for 70 − 30.
Match the number of jumps to the number of tens being removed.
activities.intendedInsight: The tens count-sequence becomes fluent and the 'jump in tens' becomes a natural move.

constraints: The reference chart and reveal-style layouts are consolidation scaffolds: they link 7−3 to 70−30 but do not let the child remove tens and watch the count change, so they do not by themselves build the unitising action.

Practice sequences and choice items rehearse the strategy and can surface errors such as the dropped ten-unit, so they are well suited to consolidation and checking, and are less likely than hands-on removal to first establish the unitising idea.
Chanting supports the count-sequence; on its own it does not establish why the answer is four tens.

Paper strips, rods, or card tens have slight physical thickness and are approximations of abstract tens; keep attention on 'each piece is worth ten', and an idealised on-screen counter is a model of the tens count, not the tens themselves.
Do not forbid or mark wrong a child who counts back in ones — it is a valid strategy that matures; model the ten-jump alongside it.
Keep the 'subtract the tens digits, keeping the ten-unit' shortcut scoped to decade−decade subtraction; it is not a general rule for cases needing regrouping.

pedagogy.summary: Formal columnar addition and subtraction to three digits is the compact, efficient written algorithm. It should be introduced only once children understand composing/decomposing concretely, and taught as a bridge FROM the expanded method (writing partial sums) TO the compact one, so each carried or exchanged digit still means a real ten or hundred. The skill has three parts: correct place-value alignment, the carry/exchange mechanic, and checking with estimation or the inverse.
bestPractices: Bridge expanded-to-compact: start with partitioned partial sums, then compress, so the compact carries keep their meaning (NCETM; DfE Appendix 1)
Insist on place-value alignment — use a column grid or squared paper so ones sit under ones
Keep base-ten/place-value counters available alongside the written method during the transition, especially for exchange
Teach subtraction exchange as decomposition ('take a ten, make ten ones'), not a memorised 'borrow', and rehearse across-zero cases
Always check: estimate first (round) and verify with the inverse (DfE Year 3)
keyRepresentations: Column grid / squared paper with H-T-O headings
Place-value counters alongside the algorithm
Expanded written method (partial sums) as the stepping stone
Base-ten blocks for the exchange step
Number line / estimation for the check
commonMisconceptions: Place-value misalignment: writing digits ragged so ones and tens are added together
Smaller-from-larger: subtracting the smaller digit from the larger in each column regardless of position (83−25→62 pattern, now at three digits)
Carry omitted or mis-placed: forgetting to add the carried ten/hundred to the next column
Borrow-across-zero errors when the adjacent column is 0 (502−276)

learn.summary: Teach formal columnar addition and subtraction to three digits as a compact written algorithm that keeps its place-value meaning. Introduce it only after children can compose/decompose concretely, and bridge from the expanded method (partial sums) to the compact one so each carried or exchanged digit still stands for a real ten or hundred. The skill has three parts: correct place-value alignment, the carry/exchange mechanic, and checking with estimation or the inverse. Pair written work with place-value counters during the transition, and rehearse the hard across-zero exchange explicitly.

activities.title: Carry and exchange with counters beside the columns
feedback: If digits are added across different columns, rebuild on a headed H-T-O grid so ones sit under ones; connect each column to its counter so alignment has a reason.
If the across-zero step stalls, model the cascade with counters slowly and narrate: one hundred becomes ten tens, then one ten becomes ten ones.
If a carry is dropped, have the child write the small carried digit and say what it is ('one ten') before adding the next column.
Confirm success when the estimate is close to the answer (about 500–550 for the addition, about 220 for the subtraction) and 226 + 276 returns 502.
activities.rationale: Linking the written carry/exchange to the quantity it represents keeps the compact algorithm meaningful; a live counter panel that moves as the child records the digit is one effective way to make the mechanism concrete, not the only way.
sourceClaims: Columnar methods are developed by bridging from an expanded written layout (partial sums) to the compact algorithm so that carried digits retain their place-value meaning.

Year 3 pupils are taught to 'add and subtract numbers with up to 3 digits, using formal written methods of columnar addition and subtraction; estimate the answer to a calculation and use inverse operations to check answers' (statutory).
learnerActions: Set out 347 + 185 in columns on squared paper or a headed H-T-O grid, ones under ones.

Add the ones: 7 + 5 = 12. Write the 2 in the ones column and the carried 1 above the tens; alongside, exchange ten of the 12 one-counters for a single ten-counter and place it in the tens column, so the written '1' and the real ten move together.
Add the tens: 4 + 8 + 1 = 13. Write 3, carry 1 hundred, and exchange ten of the 13 ten-counters for a single hundred-counter, placing it in the hundreds column.
Add the hundreds: 3 + 1 + 1 = 5, giving 532.

Now set out 502 − 276. To take 6 from 2 in the ones you need more ones, but the tens column is 0: first break one hundred into ten tens (502 becomes 400 + 90 + 12 after the cascade), then break a ten into ten ones.
Estimate first by rounding (≈ 350 + 200 = 550, or 300 + 200 = 500, for the addition; ≈ 500 − 280 = 220 for the subtraction) and check the subtraction by adding 226 + 276 back to 502.
activities.intendedInsight: A carried or exchanged digit is a real ten or hundred moving between columns, not a meaningless mark; across a zero you must decompose a hundred into tens before you can get a ten, then a ten into ones.

activities.title: Bridge from expanded partial sums to the compact column
feedback: If the compact and expanded answers disagree, line up each partial sum with its column to find the mislaid ten or hundred.
If the child cannot explain a carry, return to the partial sum (12 = 10 + 2) to show the ten being carried.
activities.rationale: Starting from partitioned partial sums and then compressing keeps the compact carries meaningful rather than memorised, following the expanded-to-compact bridge.
sourceClaims: Columnar methods are developed by bridging from an expanded written layout (partial sums) to the compact algorithm so that carried digits retain their place-value meaning.
learnerActions: Solve 347 + 185 first in the expanded written layout, writing each partial sum: 7 + 5 = 12, 40 + 80 = 120, 300 + 100 = 400.
Add the partial sums (12 + 120 + 400 = 532) and notice where the extra ten and the extra hundred come from.
Rewrite the same calculation in the compact column, carrying the 1 ten and 1 hundred, and check the answer matches 532.
Say aloud what each carried digit in the compact version stands for, pointing back to the partial sum it came from.
activities.intendedInsight: The compact algorithm is a shorthand for the expanded method; every carry corresponds to a partial sum crossing into the next place.

activities.title: Spot the error in a worked column
feedback: For misalignment, re-copy onto grid paper with place-value headings.
For smaller-from-larger, show that 2 ones cannot give 6, so a ten (via the hundred here) must be broken open first; check by adding the answer back.
For borrow-across-zero, rehearse several across-zero cases with counters and narration.
activities.rationale: Critiquing wrong worked examples targets the stable, documented bugs directly; practice builds accuracy but should sit alongside meaning-building work rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: Smaller-from-larger and borrow-from-zero are among the most common systematic, STABLE subtraction bugs: in Brown & Burton's data (1325 students) 'smaller-from-larger' (subtract the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position — the '437−284=253' pattern) was used by 54 students, and 'borrow-from-zero' (change the 0 to a 9 but fail to continue borrowing leftward) was the single most common bug at 107 occurrences; ~40% of students showed consistently buggy behaviour. Errors that look careless are the surface manifestation of a systematic wrong procedure.
learnerActions: Examine a worked example where the digits are set out ragged (for example the 5 of 185 placed under the 4 of 347) and identify what has gone wrong and why the answer is unreliable.
Examine a worked across-zero subtraction where a 9 or 0 has been written at the empty tens column without decomposing a hundred, and explain the correct cascade.
Rework each flawed example correctly on a headed grid and state what the fixed carry or exchange represents.
Complete a few mixed column calculations for fluency, estimating first and checking with the inverse.
activities.intendedInsight: Many errors that look careless are the surface of a systematic wrong procedure (misalignment, smaller-from-larger, borrow-across-zero); naming the bug helps avoid it.

activities.title: Explain your steps aloud
feedback: Accept explanations that name real quantities ('one ten', 'a hundred broken into ten tens'); redirect vague 'you just carry it' answers back to the counters.
If the inverse check fails, revisit the exchange step that produced the wrong ones or tens.
activities.rationale: Explaining each step surfaces reasoning and meaning; used as a supplement it exposes misconceptions but does not by itself supply the volume of aligned written practice the skill needs.
learnerActions: After solving a column calculation, answer: 'Point to the little 1 you carried — what does that 1 actually stand for?'
For 502 − 276, explain: 'There were no tens to take from — how did you get them?'
Justify the estimate: 'Round 347 + 185 — is your answer sensible?'
Verify: 'Add your subtraction answer to 276 — does it come back to 502?'
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why a carry or exchange happens exposes whether the procedure is understood or merely copied.

constraints: Introduce the compact algorithm only after children can compose and decompose numbers concretely.
Keep base-ten blocks or place-value counters available alongside the written method during the transition, especially for exchange.
Teach subtraction exchange as decomposition ('take a ten, make ten ones'), not a memorised 'borrow', and rehearse across-zero cases.
Always estimate first by rounding and verify with the inverse operation; any close rounded estimate (not an inflated one) serves the sanity-check.
Insist on place-value alignment using a column grid or squared paper so ones sit under ones.
Error-spotting and repeated drill rehearse and check accuracy but do not on their own build the place-value understanding; pair them with meaning-focused work.
Explain-aloud discussion is a supplement for reasoning; it cannot replace sufficient aligned written practice.
A worked annotated example is useful reference but cannot catch a child's own alignment slips; have the child produce calculations too.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent re-review self-audit of arithmetic: 347 + 185 = 532 (ones 7+5=12 write 2 carry 1; tens 4+8+1=13 write 3 carry 1; hundreds 3+1+1=5). 502 − 276 = 226 (decompose to 400+90+12; 12−6=6, 90−70=20, 400−200=200). Expanded partial sums 12+120+400=532. Inverse check 226 + 276 = 502. All confirmed.

A prior candidate error had the addition estimate as ≈500+200=700, which mis-rounds 347 and is far from 532; the corrected activity uses ≈350+200=550 or ≈300+200=500, and the success feedback now accepts either (about 500–550). The ≈500−280=220 subtraction estimate is sound.
The NCETM/DfE Appendix 1 bridging claim is marked verified:false in the row; treat as unconfirmed.

The original row's catalog-fit judgements ('3D adds nothing', quiz 'rehearses rather than builds understanding') have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements and are not asserted as universal laws.

probeDeeper: Point to the little 1 you carried — what does that 1 actually stand for?
For 502 − 276 there were no tens to take from — how did you get them?
Estimate 347 + 185 by rounding — is your answer sensible?
Check 502 − 276 by adding your answer to 276 — does it come back to 502?

errorPatterns.pattern: Place-value misalignment — writes the digits ragged so, say, the 5 of 185 lines up under the 4 of 347
errorPatterns.nextMove: Provide a column grid/headed H-T-O paper and rebuild; connect each column to its place-value counter so alignment has a reason, not just a rule.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Digits not aligned by place value on the page; unlike columns added together

errorPatterns.pattern: Smaller-from-larger — in 502−276 does 6−2 in the ones ('six take two is four') rather than exchanging
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to concrete decomposition; show 2 ones cannot give 6, so a ten (here, via the hundred) must be broken open first. Check by adding the answer back.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ones column done as larger-minus-smaller with no exchange; often a suspiciously 'clean' subtraction

errorPatterns.pattern: Carry omitted or misplaced — in 347+185 forgets to add the carried ten/hundred to the next column
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: have the child write the small carried digit explicitly and say what it is ('one ten') before adding the next column. This is a tracking lapse.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Column sums correct but the carried digit is dropped or added to the wrong column; answer off by 10 or 100

errorPatterns.pattern: Borrow-across-zero — in 502−276 tries to take a ten from the empty tens column, fabricating a digit instead of decomposing the hundred first
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model the cascade with counters: a hundred becomes ten tens, then a ten becomes ten ones. Rehearse several across-zero cases slowly with narration.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child stalls at the zero or writes 9/0 there without decomposing a hundred to feed it

responseLevels.gap: Misaligns digits, drops carries, does smaller-from-larger, or stalls at the zero; the algorithm produces unreliable answers.
responseLevels.full: Aligns correctly, carries and exchanges accurately including across a zero, explains what each carried/exchanged digit represents, and checks with estimation or the inverse.
responseLevels.partial: Executes the algorithm correctly on the straightforward addition but stumbles on the across-zero exchange, or gets answers without being able to say what a carried/exchanged digit means; check step omitted.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to set out and solve two calculations in columns on squared paper, then check each: 347 + 185, then 502 − 276. Watch how they align the digits, handle the carry, and manage the exchange across the zero.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 347+185 requires two carries; an omitted or misplaced carry, or ragged alignment, shows immediately. 502−276 forces exchange across a zero — the borrow-across-zero and smaller-from-larger bugs surface, and a child running the algorithm without understanding cannot resolve the empty column.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Adding numbers
topic.description: Add up to four two-digit numbers using strategies based on place value and properties of operations
evidence: Add three or four two-digit numbers by grouping tens and ones
Look for pairs that make multiples of 10 to simplify addition
Explain the strategy used to combine multiple addends
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} add up four two-digit numbers — like '14 + 23 + 32 + 19' — by grouping them cleverly, rather than just plodding through from left to right?

pedagogy.summary: Adding up to four two-digit numbers is where the properties of operations become a practical tool: because addition is commutative and associative, children may reorder and regroup the addends to make the work easier — hunting for pairs that make a multiple of ten, then partitioning the rest into tens and ones. The efficiency insight (look before you leap) matters as much as accuracy; the composing of several tens at once is the new demand over two-addend work.
bestPractices: Teach 'look for pairs that make ten (or a multiple of ten)' before adding — reorder using commutativity/associativity (extends adding three one-digit numbers)
Partition all addends into tens and ones, sum the tens, sum the ones, then recombine — composing as many tens/hundreds as needed
Encourage jottings to keep track when combining many ones, to prevent accumulation slips
Discuss which grouping was smartest and why, so the properties are used deliberately not accidentally
Use manipulatives/ten-frames so 'making a ten' from a pair is seen, then move to numbers
keyRepresentations: Ten-frames / bead strings (spotting pairs that make ten)
Draggable number cards (reorder addends to pair)
Part-whole / column jottings (tens together, ones together)
Number line (cumulative jumps)
Base-ten blocks (composing several tens)
commonMisconceptions: Adding strictly left-to-right and missing pairs that make ten (not using commutativity to simplify)
Losing track when combining many ones, or forgetting to compose more than one ten (ones sum to 23, only one ten carried)
Believing the addends must be added in the given order (no reordering allowed)
Miscounting during a long running total

learn.summary: Children add up to four two-digit numbers by using the commutative and associative properties as a practical tool: reorder and regroup addends to find pairs that make a multiple of ten, then partition the rest into tens and ones, sum each, and recombine. The 'look before you leap' efficiency insight matters alongside accuracy, and composing several tens at once is the new demand over two-addend work. The strongest version lets the child physically reorder addends and see pairs combine into round numbers; recognition tasks and static ringed examples are useful rehearsal and reference, but because they do not themselves require the child to reorder addends they check the strategy more than they elicit the independent habit of looking for pairs first.

activities.title: Snap the pairs that make a tidy number
feedback: If the child adds left-to-right without scanning, don't reteach addition: ask 'before you start, can you see any two that make a tidy number?' and let them re-experience the shortcut.
When two cards combine into a round number (e.g. 15 and 25 becoming 40), name it: 'those two made exactly 40, so now you only have round numbers left.'

If the child insists the numbers must stay in the written order, demonstrate with counters that the total is the same in any order, and connect it to adding three one-digit numbers where pairing to ten was allowed.

OPTIONAL: on a screen version, cards whose sum is a multiple of ten can snap into a labelled '40' or '20' block, remaining tens and ones can auto-partition and recombine to show the composed tens, and a side-by-side 'left-to-right vs paired' race can make the efficiency gain visible. These are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required features.
activities.rationale: Physically reordering and watching pairs fuse into round numbers rewards spotting the number bond and makes the commutative/associative strategy deliberate rather than accidental. Reordering to check and simplify is the curriculum route by which these properties are established at this stage.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils add three one-digit numbers and, building on this, add numbers including combining several addends; adding numbers in a different order is used to check and establishes commutativity and associativity.
Choosing an efficient order of addition (identifying two addends that make ten) uses the associative and commutative laws; children need not use the formal terms at this stage.
learnerActions: Take four addends to add, e.g. 15, 8, 25, and 12, arranged as cards that can be physically moved (paper cards, counters on a tray, or draggable on-screen tiles).
Before adding anything, scan the four numbers and decide which two, placed together, would make a multiple of ten.
Pair 15 with 25 to make 40, and 8 with 12 to make 20, then add the two round numbers: 40 + 20 = 60.
Repeat with 24, 17, 6, 13 (24+6=30 and 17+13=30, giving 60) and say aloud which pair you spotted first and why.
Try one example by adding strictly left-to-right, then again by pairing first, and compare how much easier the paired route felt.
activities.intendedInsight: Because addition can be done in any order and grouping, reordering to make pairs that total a multiple of ten turns a fearsome four-number sum into an easy sum of round numbers. The properties of operations are a lever, not an abstraction.

activities.title: Partition into tens and ones, and compose the tens carefully
feedback: If the answer is off by exactly ten, the child likely composed one ten from the ones and dropped a second: have them pool all the ones again and count how many full tens they can make.
Encourage jottings to track the running total of ones so slips don't accumulate.
If the tens are right but the total drifts, slow the recombination step and check how many tens came out of the ones.
activities.rationale: Composing several tens at once is the genuinely new demand of four-addend work; pooling all ones before exchanging and making the exchange visible with base-ten targets the specific 'dropped a composed ten' error.
learnerActions: Take all four addends and split each into its tens and its ones: for 15, 8, 25, 12 the tens are 10, 0, 20, 10 (the single-digit 8 has no tens) and the ones are 5, 8, 5, 2.
Add all the tens together (10 + 0 + 20 + 10 = 40), then pool ALL the ones together before exchanging.

From the pooled ones, exchange every full ten you can: here 5 + 8 + 5 + 2 = 20, which makes two tens and no leftover ones; if the ones had totalled 23 you would make two tens (not one) and keep 3 ones.
Recombine the composed tens with the tens you already had (40 + 20 = 60) and check it matches the paired-up method.
Use base-ten blocks or ten-frames so that making more than one ten from the ones is something you can see, not just carry in your head.
activities.intendedInsight: When many ones are combined they can compose more than one ten. Pooling all the ones and exchanging every full ten before recombining is a reliable way to make sure no composed ten is lost. If a composed ten is dropped, the answer comes out ten too small, or more than ten too small if several tens are dropped.

activities.title: Explain and defend the smartest grouping
feedback: If the child can solve but can't explain, ask them to point to the pair that made a round number and say the new, simpler sum it created.
Accept informal language; the formal terms 'commutative' and 'associative' are not required at this stage.
If the child spots pairs only when prompted, praise the find and ask them to scan unprompted on the next sum to build the habit.
activities.rationale: Articulating the strategy distinguishes a child using the properties deliberately from one who adds accurately but never looks for simplifying pairs; reasoning about reordering is how the curriculum establishes commutativity and associativity.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils add three one-digit numbers and, building on this, add numbers including combining several addends; adding numbers in a different order is used to check and establishes commutativity and associativity.
Choosing an efficient order of addition (identifying two addends that make ten) uses the associative and commutative laws; children need not use the formal terms at this stage.
learnerActions: After solving a four-addend sum, say which two numbers you added first and why that order made the work easier.
Answer 'you added them in a different order than they're written — does that change the answer, and how do you know?'
Given 19 + 4 + 1 + 6, decide which you would add first and justify it (19 + 1 makes 20, then + 4 + 6 reaches 30).
Pick a sum where no neat pair exists and explain what you do then (partition into tens and ones).
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining the chosen grouping makes the properties a conscious, reusable strategy and shows that reordering never changes the total.

constraints: Prerequisite: pairing numbers to make ten (as in adding three one-digit numbers) and exchanging ten ones for a ten; revisit these if a child insists order is fixed or loses a composed ten.

Recognition-style tasks (matching pairs that make ten, choosing the smartest first step, filling blanks in running totals) rehearse and check the strategy and can catch left-to-right grinding, but because they do not require the child to reorder the addends themselves they do not on their own elicit the independent habit of looking for pairs first; pair them with tasks where the child reorders the addends.
A static worked example with the pairs ringed is useful reference but does not let the child try reordering; use it alongside, not instead of, hands-on regrouping.
Manipulatives (ten-frames, bead strings, base-ten blocks) should make 'making a ten' and composing several tens visible before moving to numbers alone.
Keep sums engineered so tidy pairs exist when teaching the strategy, but also include a sum with no neat pair so the child learns the fallback of partitioning into tens and ones.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched and the listed source claims retain their original verification status (one marked verified, one not). Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The original 'worked correct answer' example lists ones such as 5+8+5+2=20 for the first sum (composing two tens), consistent with the 'ones can exceed ten' point; retained as-is.

The original row asserted '3D adds nothing' and 'talk cannot supply the manipulation-and-feedback practice the strategy needs'. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened: spoken discussion is used productively in the explain/defend activity, and the hands-on reordering is proposed on its affordances (physical regrouping and feedback) rather than as the only possible medium.

Comparative efficacy wording in the summary was tightened to the observable limit that recognition/static tasks do not require the child to reorder; no claim of tested superiority of any medium is made.

probeDeeper: Before adding, did any two of these numbers jump out as making a tidy total? Which?
You added them in a different order than they're written — does that change the answer? How do you know?
Your ones added up to more than ten — how many tens did you make from them?
If I gave you 19 + 4 + 1 + 6, which would you add first, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: 60 and 60. Efficiently: 15+25=40 and 8+12=20 → 60; 24+6=30 and 17+13=30 → 60. Alternatively partition all into tens and ones (tens 10+20+... , ones summed and composed). Both reach 60; the strategy question is whether pairs are spotted.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds strictly left-to-right, never scanning for pairs that make ten — '15 and 8 is 23, and 25 is 48…'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach addition; prompt 'before you start, can you see any two that make a tidy number?' and let them re-experience the shortcut. Build the looking-first habit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child works in given order with no pause to look for bonds; the skill of pairing is available but not deployed

errorPatterns.pattern: Loses a composed ten when combining many ones — ones total 23 but only one ten is carried, or the running total drifts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child pool ALL the ones first and exchange as many tens as possible before recombining; use base-ten so multiple composed tens are visible.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The tens are right but the answer is off by ten; the child composed one ten from the ones and dropped the second

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes the numbers must be added in the order written — resists reordering
errorPatterns.nextMove: Demonstrate with counters that the total is the same in any order; connect to adding three one-digit numbers where pairing to ten was allowed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When invited to reorder, the child says you can't, or that it would change the answer

responseLevels.gap: Adds left-to-right, drops composed tens, or insists order is fixed; answers unreliable and slow.
responseLevels.full: Scans for pairs making multiples of ten, reorders confidently using the properties, composes multiple tens correctly, and explains why the chosen grouping was efficient.
responseLevels.partial: Adds accurately by partitioning but doesn't yet look for pairs to simplify, or spots pairs only when prompted.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set two calculations and watch how the child tackles each, thinking aloud: 15 + 8 + 25 + 12, then 24 + 17 + 6 + 13. Notice whether they look for pairs that make a multiple of ten before adding, and how they combine the ones.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Both sums are engineered so pairs make tidy multiples of ten. A child who uses commutativity spots the pairs and finishes quickly and accurately; a child who grinds left-to-right is slower and far more likely to slip when the running total's ones exceed ten. Watching the ORDER they add in exposes whether the properties are a live tool.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Addition and subtraction within 1000
topic.description: Add and subtract within 1000 using concrete models, drawings, and strategies based on place value; understand composing and decomposing tens and hundreds
evidence: Add two three-digit numbers using base-ten blocks or drawings, composing a ten or hundred when necessary
Subtract three-digit numbers, decomposing a ten or hundred when necessary
Relate the concrete/drawn strategy to a written method and explain why it works
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} add or subtract numbers in the hundreds — like '347 + 256' — by thinking about hundreds, tens, and ones separately, or drawing a diagram to help?

pedagogy.summary: Adding and subtracting within 1000 extends the compose/decompose-a-ten idea to a second boundary — composing a hundred from ten tens and decomposing a hundred into ten tens. It is taught concretely and pictorially (base-ten blocks, place-value counters, drawings) BEFORE the compact column algorithm, so that 'carrying' and 'borrowing' across two columns are understood as exchange, not digit rituals. The DfE places this in Year 3 as the conceptual foundation for formal columnar methods.
bestPractices: Work concrete→pictorial→written for the SAME calculation so the recording mirrors the exchange (NCETM Spine 1.17: strategies across the hundreds boundary combine bridging-ten with unitising)
Make both boundaries explicit: ten ones → one ten, and ten tens → one hundred; and the reverse for subtraction
Use place-value counters or base-ten on a H-T-O mat so an exchanged unit physically moves one column left/right
Deliberately include 'exchange across a zero' cases (e.g. 402−137) since these are the hardest and most error-prone
Check with estimation and the inverse operation (DfE Year 3)
keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks (ones, ten-rods, hundred-flats) on a place-value mat
Place-value counters on a H-T-O grid
Part-whole / partitioning drawings (256 = 200+50+6)
Number line for count-up subtraction across hundreds
Expanded written layout bridging to compact columns
commonMisconceptions: Smaller-from-larger subtraction across any column (e.g. ones done as larger-minus-smaller)
Failing to compose a hundred: ten or more tens left in the tens place (170+80 recorded with 15 in the tens column)
Borrow-across-zero errors: decomposing when the adjacent column is 0 (402−137) done incorrectly
Treating each column independently with no exchange, so carried/borrowed units vanish

learn.summary: Year 3 learners add and subtract within 1000 by extending the compose/decompose-a-ten idea to a second boundary: ten tens make a hundred, and a hundred can be broken back into ten tens. Taught concretely then pictorially then in writing for the SAME calculation, so 'carrying' and 'borrowing' across two columns are understood as exchange, not digit rituals. Across-a-zero subtraction (e.g. 402−137) is the hardest, most error-prone case and deserves deliberate attention.

activities.title: Double exchange on a place-value mat: 256 + 167
feedback: If twelve tens are left sitting in the tens column, prompt: 'You have twelve tens — can you swap ten of them for a hundred? Show me on the mat.' Physically swap ten ten-rods for one hundred-flat and watch it slide to the hundreds column.
If a carried unit disappears, point back to the rod/flat that moved and ask where its mark is in the written record.
Check with estimation: 260+170 is about 430, so 423 is reasonable.
activities.rationale: Working concrete→pictorial→written for one calculation lets the recording mirror the physical exchange; making BOTH boundaries explicit (ten ones→one ten and ten tens→one hundred) addresses the compose-a-hundred misconception directly.
sourceClaims: Strategies for calculating across the tens boundary combine with unitising to calculate across the hundreds boundary; exchange (ten ones for one ten, ten tens for one hundred) is the unifying structure.

Year 3 pupils add and subtract numbers with up to three digits using formal written methods, add/subtract mentally, estimate and use inverse operations to check, and apply partitioning related to place value (e.g. 146 = 100+40+6, 146 = 130+16).
learnerActions: Lay out 256 and 167 with base-ten blocks (or place-value counters) on a H-T-O mat.
Combine the ones: 6+7=13. Exchange ten ones for one ten and move that ten into the tens column (leave 3 ones).
Combine the tens: 5+6+1(carried)=12 tens. Exchange ten tens for one hundred and move it into the hundreds column (leave 2 tens).
Combine the hundreds: 2+1+1(carried)=4. Read the result: 423.
Record the matching written steps beside the blocks — first in an expanded layout, then in compact columns — so each written mark names a physical exchange.
activities.intendedInsight: Carrying across two columns is the same exchange move repeated at a second boundary: ten ones become one ten, and ten tens become one hundred.

activities.title: Cascade across a zero: 402 − 137
feedback: If the child does 7−2 ('seven take two is five') instead of exchanging, return to decomposition within 100 first (the same move one column up), then rebuild 402−137 so a unit must be broken open before subtracting.

If the child fabricates a digit (9 or 0) at the zero column without decomposing, model the two-step cascade with blocks: a hundred becomes ten tens, THEN a ten becomes ten ones. Slow it down and have the child narrate each step.
Compare: 'What if it were 452−137 instead of 402−137 — which is easier, and why?' to surface why the zero is the hard part.
activities.rationale: Across-a-zero cases are deliberately included because they are the hardest and expose borrow-across-zero and smaller-from-larger bugs; building and narrating the cascade shows why the procedure works rather than rehearsing a ritual.
sourceClaims: Borrow-across-zero and smaller-from-larger are classic systematic subtraction bugs.

Year 3 pupils add and subtract numbers with up to three digits using formal written methods, add/subtract mentally, estimate and use inverse operations to check, and apply partitioning related to place value (e.g. 146 = 100+40+6, 146 = 130+16).
learnerActions: Build 402 with blocks on the mat (4 hundreds, 0 tens, 2 ones).
Try to subtract the ones (2−7): there aren't enough, and there are no tens to borrow — notice the empty tens column.
Break one hundred into ten tens (now 3 hundreds, 10 tens, 2 ones).
Break one of those tens into ten ones (now 3 hundreds, 9 tens, 12 ones). This is 402 written as 300+90+12.
Narrate each exchange aloud before recording it, so the two-step cascade is spoken and written in order.
activities.intendedInsight: When a column is empty you cannot borrow directly; you must first decompose the next higher unit to fill it, then decompose again — a cascade, not a one-step borrow.

activities.title: Annotated worked example: reveal each exchange step
feedback: If a prediction is wrong, ask the learner to redo the step with physical blocks before moving on, since this format shows the exchange but does not let the child perform it.
Reinforce naming: 'ten tens is one hundred, exactly as ten ones is one ten.'
activities.rationale: A step-revealing worked example gives a reference model and prompts prediction, but it is a scaffold: it does not let the child perform the double regroup, so it should follow or accompany hands-on work.
learnerActions: Study a worked addition and a worked across-zero subtraction with each exchange step hidden until requested.
Before revealing, predict what happens to a pile of ten tens, or where a borrowed ten in an empty column comes from.
Reveal the step (e.g. the tens pile becoming one hundred and some tens; the zero column being fed from a decomposed hundred) and compare it with your prediction.
Explain in your own words why the unit moved one column over.
activities.intendedInsight: Each written exchange step corresponds to a specific regrouping of units; a step-by-step reference makes the structure of the double regroup visible.

activities.title: Consolidation practice with across-zero and compose-a-hundred checks

Children partition into tens and ones, compensate, use known facts, and exploit the inverse relationship. Fluency is built on secure single-digit recall and strategy-based adding within 100; the goal is flexible, justified computation, not speed alone.
bestPractices: Teach a repertoire and the judgement to choose: partitioning for 46+37, counting-up/finding-the-difference for near numbers like 71−68, compensation for numbers near a ten
Use the inverse relationship to check (add the answer back) and to solve missing-number problems
Partition the subtrahend into tens and ones for two-digit subtraction, decomposing a ten where the ones are insufficient (NCETM Spine 1.16)
Contrast two methods on the same calculation and ask which was quicker and why, to build strategic flexibility
Keep concrete/pictorial support (base-ten, number line) available so regrouping stays meaningful, not a memorised digit ritual

learn.summary: Fluent addition and subtraction within 100 means computing accurately AND choosing an efficient strategy for the particular numbers, not running one algorithm for everything. Learners partition into tens and ones, compensate near a ten, use known facts, count up to find a difference between close numbers, and exploit the inverse to check. The target is flexible, justified computation, built on secure single-digit recall. The core activity places the same calculation on two tools so the learner feels why the smart method depends on the numbers; supporting activities add strategy-selection practice, a worked strategy reference, and spoken justification.

activities.title: Same calculation, two tools: feel which method fits the numbers
feedback: If the borrow and the count-up look equally fast to you, count the steps in each: counting up from 68 to 71 covers a difference of just three, while the borrow takes several steps. Closeness of the numbers is the signal to count up.
If 46+37 came out as 73, show exactly where the extra ten went: 6+7 makes 13, which is one ten and three. That one ten joins the 70 to make 80, and the 3 ones make the total 83.
If you reached for the same written method on every pair, pause first and read the numbers: are they close (count up), near a ten (compensate), or a known fact you can just recall?
activities.rationale: Presenting the identical calculation on a number line and a base-ten workspace side by side lets the learner directly compare strategies on the same numbers, which is the comparison that strategy selection depends on. Auto-composing/decomposing a ten keeps the regroup visible so it is not reduced to a memorised digit ritual. Optional timing/animation of both methods and drag-to-count on the number line make the efficiency gap concrete; these are illustrative supports, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Two-digit subtraction is done by partitioning the subtrahend into tens and ones (decomposing a ten where needed), and strategy choice varies with the numbers — e.g. counting up from 67 to find 94−67, or counting back for 64−25.

Year 2 pupils recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive related facts to 100, use the inverse relationship to check calculations, and partition numbers in different ways (e.g. 23 = 20+3 and 10+13) to support subtraction.
learnerActions: Take 71 − 68 and first work it on a base-ten column workspace: there are not enough ones, so decompose a ten, cross out, and carry through the several steps of the borrow.
Now work the same 71 − 68 on a number line: count up from 68 to 71 and see the difference is just three.
Place the three-hop count-up beside the multi-step borrow and say which was quicker and why.
Switch to 46 + 37 on the base-ten side: combine 40+30 and 6+7, compose the thirteen ones into one ten and three, and add that ten in so the total is 83, not 73.
Finish by looking at a fresh pair of numbers and stating, before you start, which method you will use and why.
activities.intendedInsight: The efficient method depends on the numbers: when the numbers are close, counting up the difference beats a columnar borrow; regrouping must be composed or decomposed deliberately so the extra ten is never silently dropped.

activities.title: Check with the inverse and solve missing-number problems
feedback: If adding the answer back does not return to the start, either the subtraction or the checking addition has an error—often a dropped or mis-recombined ten; rework both with place-value support.
If you treated the missing-number problem as unrelated to subtraction, notice that 46 + ? = 83 is answered by 83 − 46 = 37.
activities.rationale: Using the inverse to check and to solve missing-number problems targets the common gap of treating the two operations as unrelated, and is named directly in the Year 2 curriculum.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive related facts to 100, use the inverse relationship to check calculations, and partition numbers in different ways (e.g. 23 = 20+3 and 10+13) to support subtraction.
learnerActions: After computing 83 − 25, add your answer back to 25 and confirm it returns to 83.
Given a missing-number problem such as 46 + ? = 83, use subtraction (83 − 46) to find the unknown, then add back to check.
State in words how addition and subtraction undo each other for the pair you just solved.
activities.intendedInsight: Addition and subtraction are inverse operations, so adding an answer back is a reliable self-check and lets you turn a missing-number problem into the operation you find easier.

activities.title: Match the calculation to the smartest strategy (selection practice)
feedback: If you chose 62 for 83 − 25, you likely did 5 − 3 in the ones column; you cannot take 5 from 3, so 83 must give up a ten (becoming 70 + 13) first, giving 58. Check by computing 62 + 25, which comes to 87, not 83.
If you matched a slow method to close numbers like 71 − 68, reconsider: close numbers signal counting up the difference.
activities.rationale: A selection/matching task with 62 offered as the tempting wrong answer rehearses strategy choice and catches the smaller-from-larger bug. This format checks and reinforces selection rather than building flexibility through sustained varied doing, so it supplements, not replaces, the two-tool work.
sourceClaims: The 'smaller-from-larger' subtraction error is a classic, systematic buggy algorithm — the child subtracts the smaller digit from the larger within each column regardless of position (the '437−284=253' pattern). In Brown & Burton's 1325-student data it was used by 54 students; such bugs are stable, not careless (~40% of students consistently buggy).

Two-digit subtraction is done by partitioning the subtrahend into tens and ones (decomposing a ten where needed), and strategy choice varies with the numbers — e.g. counting up from 67 to find 94−67, or counting back for 64−25.
learnerActions: Across a mixed set of additions and subtractions, pair each calculation with the most efficient strategy (partition, compensate near a ten, count up the difference, or recall a known fact).
For 83 − 25, choose the correct answer (58) and explain why 62 is wrong.
Say aloud what feature of the numbers made you pick that strategy.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading the numbers first—how close they are, whether they sit near a ten, whether a fact is known—tells you which method is efficient before you compute.

activities.title: Worked strategy reference to consult
feedback: If the reference method differs from yours, identify which numbers triggered it—that trigger is the point to remember.
Use the reference to locate a slip (e.g. a dropped ten) rather than to replace doing the calculations yourself.
activities.rationale: A static reveal-the-method chart displays worked examples clearly but cannot exercise the choosing itself, so it is a reference scaffold alongside active practice, not a substitute for it.
learnerActions: Reveal, for each calculation type, its most efficient method and a short reason: partitioning for 46 + 37, counting up for 71 − 68, compensation for numbers near a ten.
Compare a worked example with your own jotting on a similar pair to see whether your recombination kept the regrouped ten.
activities.intendedInsight: Each strategy has a signature of numbers it suits; a worked example makes the method and its justification explicit.

activities.title: Justify your method aloud
feedback: If you cannot give a reason beyond 'that's how I always do it', look again at the numbers for a feature (closeness, nearness to a ten, a known fact) that favours a particular method.
If prompted to try counting up and it proves faster, note that for next time.
activities.rationale: Spoken justification prompts a learner to articulate strategy choice, which supports metacognition; on its own it cannot supply the volume of varied practice fluency needs, so it accompanies the computational activities.
learnerActions: After solving a pair, explain to a partner or adult why you chose your method for those particular numbers.
Respond to a prompt such as: 'You borrowed for 71 − 68—can you see a quicker way to find the gap between 68 and 71?' and try the alternative.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify a strategy choice out loud consolidates the habit of reading the numbers before computing.

constraints: Fluency is a doing skill: recognition, matching, and tap-to-reveal reference formats check or display strategy but do not by themselves build flexible computation; keep substantial varied practice of actually computing.
Keep concrete/pictorial support (base-ten blocks, number line, hundred square, and bar model for comparison subtraction) available so regrouping stays meaningful rather than a memorised digit ritual.
The smaller-from-larger bug is stable and systematic, not careless; confront it with place-value regrouping and an inverse check (62 + 25 = 87 ≠ 83) rather than simply marking it wrong.
Spoken justification alone cannot supply the volume of practice needed; use it to consolidate choice, not to replace computation.
Timing/animation, drag-to-count, and auto-exchange are optional supports that make the efficiency gap and the regroup visible; they are illustrative, not mandatory mechanisms.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Go back to place-value regrouping with base-ten blocks: 83 must give up a ten to make enough ones (as 70+13) before the ones can be taken. Confront by checking 62+25.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The ones column of 83−25 is done as 5−3 with no decomposition of a ten; answer 62

errorPatterns.pattern: Partitions correctly but loses the regrouped ten — '46 and 37: seventy and thirteen… seventy-three'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the recombination, don't reteach the method: have the child compose the 13 into 'one ten and three' and add that ten to the seventy. This is a lapse, not a missing concept.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct partial sums (70 and 13) but the final recombination drops the extra ten, giving 73 instead of 83

errorPatterns.pattern: Reaches for the same written method regardless of the numbers — column-subtracts 71−68 with full borrowing instead of counting up
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the algorithm; put the count-up and the borrow side by side on the same pair and ask which was quicker and why, building the habit of looking at the numbers first.

responseLevels.gap: Smaller-from-larger or dropped-ten errors; answers are unreliable whenever regrouping is needed.
responseLevels.full: Efficient and accurate on all four, selects the method to suit the numbers (counts up for 71−68, partitions for 46+37), keeps regrouping correct, and checks using the inverse.
responseLevels.partial: Accurate with one preferred method (e.g. always partitions) but does not adapt to the numbers; slow or stumbles where counting up would be far easier; needs prompting to check.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set these four one at a time and watch the child work each, letting them choose their own method and jot: 46 + 37, then 83 − 25, then 60 − 24, then 71 − 68. Pay particular attention to which method they reach for on 71 − 68.

Children reuse a single-digit fact (3+2 hundreds) at the scale of hundreds. It is the cleanest demonstration of place-value invariance — the local part left untouched — and is taught with a place-value chart and hundred-scaled number line. (Bridging a thousand is a later topic, so within-1000 cases do not bridge.)
bestPractices: Anchor the tens and ones; operate only on the hundreds — 345+200 keeps '_45' and works 3+2 hundreds
Reuse the known single-digit fact at the scale of hundreds (3 hundreds + 2 hundreds = 5 hundreds)
Use a place-value chart to show only the hundreds row changing

learn.summary: Year 3 learners mentally add and subtract hundreds to/from a three-digit number with answers below 1000, where only the hundreds digit changes and the tens and ones stay fixed. The core insight is place-value invariance: a known single-digit fact (3+2 hundreds) is reused at the scale of hundreds while the other columns are left untouched. Work with a place-value chart, a number line marked in hundreds, base-ten hundred-flats, partitioning jottings (345 = 300 + 45), and place-value counters on an H-T-O grid; contrast with +tens/+ones (using examples that need no regrouping) so children generalise that an added amount lands in its own column when that column does not go past 9. With answers below 1000 these cases never bridge a thousand.

activities.title: Freeze the tens and ones: only the hundreds move
feedback: If the learner alters the 45 in 345+200, re-anchor on the chart: 200 is two hundreds, so it joins the hundreds. Cover or grey out the tens and ones to show they cannot change, then re-read 545.
If the learner disturbs the tens/ones in subtraction, physically hold or cover the '62' of 762 and only operate on the hundreds.

If the answer to 762−400 comes out as 462, this is most likely a single-digit fact slip (the learner found 4 hundreds instead of 7−4=3 hundreds): rehearse 7−4 on its own, then reapply at the hundreds scale to get 362. The tens and ones were kept, so place value does not need reteaching.
Prompt: 'Is 762−400 bigger or smaller than 762? Should it be?' to catch direction-of-operation errors.
activities.rationale: The objective is place-value invariance, so the activity makes the stable columns visible and asks the learner to predict and name what stays fixed before checking. A manipulable or clearly staged chart lets the learner act on the hundreds while the tens and ones remain visibly still; a static reveal can show the same contrast but does not let the learner operate the pieces.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils add and subtract mentally a three-digit number and hundreds.
Place-value understanding lets a known single-digit fact be reused at the scale of hundreds, with the other columns left invariant (unitising).
learnerActions: Show 345 on a place-value chart (hundreds, tens, ones). Add 200 and watch only the hundreds change from 3 to 5, giving 545 — say aloud that the '45' tail is unchanged.
Now do 762 − 400 on the same chart: the hundreds drop from 7 to 3 while the '62' stays put, giving 362.
Before revealing each answer, point to the tens and ones and state that they will not change, then check after.
Repeat with 518 + 300, predicting the answer (818) and naming which digits stay the same.
Articulate the rule in your own words: the amount you add or take away is a number of hundreds, so it lands only in the hundreds column.
activities.intendedInsight: When the answer stays below 1000, adding or subtracting hundreds changes only the hundreds digit; the tens and ones are invariant because the added amount belongs to the hundreds column.

activities.title: Same place-value idea, one column along
feedback: If the learner moves the change to the wrong column, restate where each amount belongs (200 = hundreds, 20 = tens) and re-anchor on the chart.

If the learner thinks a different column should change when switching between +hundreds and +tens, clarify that adding tens and adding hundreds are simply different amounts, each landing in its own column — there is no rule reversing, just a different column changing.
activities.rationale: Contrasting +hundreds with +tens/+ones helps the learner generalise beyond a single case and prevents the 'change any digit' error. Juxtaposition makes the invariance principle explicit across columns.
sourceClaims: Place-value understanding lets a known single-digit fact be reused at the scale of hundreds, with the other columns left invariant (unitising).
learnerActions: Place a +hundreds example (345 + 200) beside a +tens example (345 + 20) and work both.
For each, say which single column changes and read off the two different answers (545 vs 365).
State the shared principle: when the column does not go past 9 (no regrouping), the added amount changes only its own column and leaves the others alone.
Try a mixed set, e.g. 345+200, 345+20, 345+2, naming the changing digit each time before answering.
activities.intendedInsight: The place-value rule generalises: whether you add hundreds, tens, or ones, the added amount changes only its own column as long as that column does not go past 9 (no regrouping), as in 345+200, 345+20 and 345+2.

activities.title: Explain what stays the same
feedback: Full understanding: answers quickly in the head, keeps tens and ones untouched, and explains that only the hundreds change because the added amount is a number of hundreds.

Partial: reaches answers with the chart or number line but is unsure which digits stay fixed, or makes single-digit hundreds slips — revisit the invariance naming step and rehearse the hundreds facts.
Gap: changes the tens/ones or lands the hundreds in the wrong column and cannot say what stays the same — return to the chart activity with the tens and ones covered.
activities.rationale: Articulating which digits stay fixed surfaces whether the learner understands invariance or is guessing, and separates a conceptual gap from a mere single-digit fact slip. Reasoning-focused discussion complements, rather than replaces, the hands-on chart work.
learnerActions: Work 345 + 200, 762 − 400, and 518 + 300 mentally, thinking aloud.
After each, answer: which digits changed and which stayed exactly the same, and why?
Answer the probes: How is 762−400 like 7−4, and what is different? If it were 345+20 instead of 345+200, which digit would change?
Explain in a sentence why the tens and ones do not change.

activities.title: Contrast a non-bridging and a bridging case on a place-value chart

If the child leaves eleven tens for 372 + 40 (writing 3(11)2 / 3112) or keeps the hundreds unchanged, show on the tens number line that the jump crosses 400; use make-ten at the scale of tens (add 28 to reach 400, then 12), or exchange ten ten-rods for one hundred with base-ten blocks.

Bridging a multiple of ten (here a hundred) reuses the make-ten strategy at a larger scale, built on finding 10/100 more or less and on unitising tens.
learnerActions: Start with 345 on a place-value chart and add 40 mentally: before calculating, predict which digits will change and which will stay the same.
Confirm that only the tens change (4 tens + 4 tens = 8 tens), giving 385, with the hundreds (3) and ones (5) unchanged.
Now try 372 + 40, again predicting first: notice the tens reach eleven, so a hundred is composed and the hundreds digit ticks up — resolve to 412 (reach 400 by adding 28, then add the remaining 12).
Say aloud how 372 + 40 is like 7 tens + 4 tens = 11 tens, and point to where the extra hundred comes from.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting tens changes only the tens digit UNLESS the running total of tens crosses a hundred, in which case a hundred is composed (or decomposed) and the hundreds digit changes too — the same kind of exception children already met when crossing a ten.

activities.title: Bridge a hundred downwards when subtracting
feedback: If the child keeps the hundreds at 4 for 431 − 50, show on the tens number line that the jump must cross below 400, and decompose a hundred into ten tens with blocks.
If the child does 5 − 3 in the tens (smaller-from-larger, giving 421), check by adding back: 421 + 50 = 471, not 431, and 421 is only 10 less than 431. Then redo by crossing 400.
Confirm 381 and ask the child to explain where the hundred was decomposed.
activities.rationale: Subtraction that bridges down is the same unitising/make-ten idea applied in reverse; an amount check (is the answer exactly 50 less, and does adding 50 back return the start?) and a tens number line expose the common 'smaller-from-larger' and 'hundreds don't move' errors.
sourceClaims: Bridging a multiple of ten (here a hundred) reuses the make-ten strategy at a larger scale, built on finding 10/100 more or less and on unitising tens.
learnerActions: Work out 431 − 50 mentally, first predicting whether the hundreds digit will change.
Check the size: subtracting 50 should make the answer exactly 50 less than 431, which takes it below 400. Is your answer below 400, and does adding 50 back give 431?
Use a number line marked in tens to show the jump crosses below 400 (431 − 31 = 400, then − 19 more = 381).
If using base-ten blocks, decompose one hundred into ten tens before removing five tens.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtracting tens can bridge a hundred downwards, decomposing a hundred into ten tens; the hundreds digit then decreases, and the result must be smaller than the start.

activities.title: Predict and sort: will the hundreds digit change?
feedback: If a bridging item is sorted as non-bridging: for addition items add the tens together (e.g. 7 tens + 4 tens = 11 tens, which exceeds nine tens); for subtraction items check whether the tens removed exceed the tens in the number (e.g. 431 has 3 tens but 5 tens are removed), which forces crossing below a hundred.
Use a mixed-item check with a 3(11)2-style wrong answer for 372 + 40 (shown as 3112, or as 312 when the hundred is dropped) to surface the overgeneralisation, then re-explain via composing a hundred.
Praise reasoning that correctly anticipates the hundreds change, not just correct final digits.
activities.rationale: Asking children to predict which digits change before calculating, and contrasting bridging with non-bridging items, targets the specific misconception that the hundreds never move; recognition/sorting here supports reasoning but should follow, not replace, the mental construction work.
learnerActions: For a mixed set of items (e.g. 345 + 40, 372 + 40, 462 − 30, 431 − 50), predict for each whether the hundreds digit will change before calculating.
Sort the items into 'bridges a hundred' and 'does not bridge a hundred'.
Calculate each mentally, then check your sort against the answers (385, 412, 432, 381).
Explain in your own words the rule: only the tens change unless the calculation crosses a hundred.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding in advance whether a calculation bridges a hundred builds the discriminating judgement that prevents the over-generalisation 'only the tens digit ever changes'.

constraints: Multiple-choice or sort-and-check tasks can rehearse and surface the bridging over-generalisation, but they check reasoning rather than build the mental method; keep them after the child has constructed answers mentally.

A static tap-to-reveal chart can show which digit changes as a reference, but it cannot animate the cascade of composing a hundred; pair it with number-line or blocks work so the bridging move is actually traced.

Base-ten blocks and chart/number-line models are approximations and representations of the quantities, not the mental calculation itself; the objective is reliable mental computation, so fade the supports as the child becomes secure.
The 'only the tens digit changes' heuristic is explicitly conditional: always make the bridging exception part of the rule, in both addition and subtraction directions.

pedagogy.summary: Extending the formal columnar algorithm from three to four digits. The mathematics is unchanged — align by place value, and compose (carry) or decompose (exchange/borrow) between adjacent columns — but four digits add a thousands column and, crucially, harder exchange chains, including borrowing across one or more zeros (4002-1367). The DfE also requires checking with estimation (rounding) and the inverse, so approximate reasonableness is taught alongside exact procedure.
bestPractices: Keep the base-ten exchange rationale explicit — a carry is 'ten of these make one of those', a borrow is the reverse — do not let it become a symbol-pushing trick
Estimate first by rounding (4002-1367 is about 4000-1400 = 2600) so a place-value slip is caught
Deliberately include one across-zero subtraction — it is the most diagnostic and most-failed case
Use place-value column headers / grid paper so digits of unequal length align correctly (878 under 3456)
Check every answer with the inverse operation
keyRepresentations: Place-value columns with Th/H/T/O headers
Base-ten blocks including the thousand cube (exchange made physical)
Part-whole bar model
Empty number line for the rounding estimate

Smaller-from-larger bug — subtracts the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position

Fails to compose — leaves a two-digit result in a column instead of carrying

learn.summary: Year 4 pupils extend the formal columnar algorithm from three to four digits: aligning by place value, composing (carrying) when a column total reaches ten or more, and decomposing (borrowing/exchanging) when a top digit is too small — including the hardest case, borrowing across one or more zeros (e.g. 4002-1367). The DfE also requires checking answers by rounding to estimate and by using the inverse operation, so approximate reasonableness is taught alongside the exact procedure. The exchange rationale must stay explicit (a carry is 'ten of these make one of those'; a borrow is the reverse) rather than becoming a symbol-pushing trick.

activities.title: Cascade the thousand: borrow across two zeros with base-ten quantities
feedback: If the child stalls at the zeros or writes a garbled middle (e.g. 3745 or 2735), model exchanging one thousand downward through the columns with base-ten blocks (thousand to ten hundreds to ten tens to ten ones) BEFORE touching the written digits.
If they change the 0 to a 9 but stop borrowing from the next column left, show that the thousand being broken up is what supplies those nines — the 9s and the final 12 all come from one thousand.
If the estimate and exact answer disagree wildly, check for a place-value misalignment rather than redoing blindly.
Confirm success when they treat 4002 as 3 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 12 ones and reach 2635 with both checks agreeing.
activities.rationale: Borrow-from-zero is the single most common systematic subtraction bug in a large diagnostic dataset, and multi-zero minuends compound it across adjacent columns; making the exchange a visible movement of grouped quantities targets exactly where a symbol-only procedure tends to break down. A dynamic or hands-on model lets the child observe the cascade as the thousand-block splits into ten hundreds, then ten tens, then ten ones — the regrouping seen in motion rather than only as a finished state, while a printed worked example can still serve as a static reference.
sourceClaims: Borrow-from-zero is the single most common systematic subtraction bug in Brown & Burton's 1325-student data (107 occurrences): when borrowing from a column whose top digit is 0, the student changes the 0 to a 9 but fails to continue borrowing from the next column left; related zero bugs include STOPS/BORROW/AT/ZERO and MOVE/OVER/ZERO/BORROW. Smaller-from-larger (54 students) and these zero-borrow bugs are stable, not careless — ~40% of students showed consistently buggy behaviour. Multi-zero minuends (e.g. 4002) compound the zero-borrow bug across adjacent columns.
Composing/decomposing tens, hundreds and thousands (exchange) is the conceptual basis of the columnar algorithm; DfE Appendix 1 sets out the formal written methods this progression cross-references.
learnerActions: Set up 4002 - 1367 in place-value columns with Th/H/T/O headers, aligning from the ones column on the right.
Build 4002 physically (or on a screen model): four thousand-blocks and two ones, with empty hundreds and tens.
Try to subtract 7 ones from 2 ones; notice there is nothing in the hundreds or tens to exchange from, so the exchange must come from the thousands.

Exchange one thousand-block into ten hundred-blocks, then one hundred into ten tens, then one ten into ten ones — watching the single thousand ripple down through the two empty columns until the ones column holds 12.
Record each changed digit in the written algorithm in step with the blocks (4002 becomes 3 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 12 ones) and finish the subtraction to reach 2635.
Round both numbers to make an estimate (about 4000 - 1400 = 2600). Ideally do this before the exact working in the steps above. Then compare the estimate with the exact answer 2635.
Check with the inverse: confirm 2635 + 1367 = 4002.
activities.intendedInsight: Borrowing across zero is not a special rule: when an adjacent column is empty you continue the exchange one column further left, and a single thousand can cascade down through the zeros to free up ones. The written digits are a record of quantities actually regrouped.

activities.title: Align and compose: mixed-length columnar addition and subtraction
feedback: If the child lines 878 under the left of 3456, or 483 under the wrong columns of 6250, reinstate place-value headers or grid paper and anchor every number from the ones column on the right.
If they write a two-digit entry such as 14 in the ones column of 3456+878, show that ten ones make one ten carried to the next column.

If they subtract the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position (e.g. treat the ones 0-3 as 3 and the tens 5-8 as 3 in 6250-483), stop and exchange concretely: you cannot take 3 ones from 0 ones without exchanging a ten. After that exchange only 4 tens are left, and you cannot take 8 tens from 4 tens without exchanging a hundred.
Confirm success when the ones sit under the ones, carries and exchanges are shown, 3456+878=4334 and 6250-483=5767, and both the estimate and the inverse support each answer.
activities.rationale: Mixed-length alignment and the compose/smaller-from-larger errors are distinct, stable bugs from the borrow-across-zero case, so they deserve their own practice; grid paper and place-value headers give a concrete anchor, and estimation plus inverse checking are statutory.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils are taught to 'add and subtract numbers with up to 4 digits using the formal written methods of columnar addition and subtraction where appropriate' and to 'estimate and use inverse operations to check answers to a calculation' (statutory).
