Smaller-from-larger (54 students) and these zero-borrow bugs are stable, not careless — ~40% of students showed consistently buggy behaviour. Multi-zero minuends (e.g. 4002) compound the zero-borrow bug across adjacent columns.
learnerActions: Set out 3456 + 878 using place-value headers or grid paper, placing the 8 of 878 under the ones column (not under the left of 3456).
Add column by column; when the ones make 14, write 4 and carry one ten to the tens column rather than writing a two-digit entry in the ones.
Set out 6250 - 483, anchoring the 3 under the ones column, and subtract, exchanging from the next column left wherever the top digit is too small.
For each answer, round both numbers to estimate first, then check the exact result with the inverse operation.
activities.intendedInsight: Digits are added or subtracted by matching place value, anchored from the ones column on the right regardless of how many digits each number has; a column result of ten or more is carried, and a column that is too small to subtract requires exchanging from the next column left.

activities.title: Check it two ways: estimate and inverse
feedback: If the child simply redoes the original subtraction, scaffold the estimate (round both numbers) and the inverse addition separately; do not reteach the algorithm itself.
If the estimate is far from the exact answer, treat that as a signal to re-check alignment or an exchange, not to accept the exact answer anyway.
Confirm success when the child produces a rounded estimate near 2600 AND an inverse sum that returns the original minuend 4002.
activities.rationale: Pupils commonly treat checking as re-running the sum, which cannot catch a systematic procedural bug; the DfE requires both estimation and inverse operations, and separating these from the algorithm keeps them as genuine independent checks.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils are taught to 'add and subtract numbers with up to 4 digits using the formal written methods of columnar addition and subtraction where appropriate' and to 'estimate and use inverse operations to check answers to a calculation' (statutory).
learnerActions: After solving 4002 - 1367, round both numbers (about 4000 - 1400 = 2600) on a number line or strip and say whether 2635 is reasonable.
Check the same answer a second, independent way by adding the result to the number subtracted: 2635 + 1367 should return 4002.
Answer: 'What if it had been 4000 - 1367 instead — does that change how you borrow?' and explain.
Compare the two forms of checking and say what each one catches that the other might miss.
activities.intendedInsight: Checking is not redoing the same subtraction: estimation catches place-value-scale slips, and the inverse addition independently confirms the exact answer. They are complementary, not repetition.

constraints: Keep the base-ten exchange rationale explicit throughout — a carry is 'ten of these make one of those', a borrow is the reverse — so the algorithm does not become a symbol-pushing trick.
Deliberately include at least one across-zero subtraction (e.g. 4002-1367): it is the most diagnostic and most-failed case.
Use place-value column headers or grid paper so digits of unequal length align correctly (e.g. 878 under the right-hand end of 3456), anchoring from the ones column on the right.
Estimate first by rounding so a place-value slip is caught, and check every answer with the inverse operation.

A fill-in-the-column or reveal-the-exchange practice format can assess and rehearse the carried/borrowed digits and the rounded estimate, but it cannot verify a child's handwritten column ALIGNMENT, so include some set-it-out-on-paper work where the child chooses the layout.

A tap-to-reveal worked-example reference can show the ten-for-one exchange behind each carry/borrow mark, but it does not let the child perform the exchange, so it supplements rather than replaces active regrouping.

Screen-based base-ten models and physical blocks offer different experiences; either can make the exchange visible, and neither is required over the other. Physical cubes have thickness and can be handled; a screen model is an idealised representation of the same grouped quantities.

Why did you have to change the top number in the tens and hundreds when subtracting 4002 - 1367?
What if it had been 4000 - 1367 instead - does that change how you borrow?
How could you use addition to check your subtraction is right?

A shallow procedure fails visibly at the zeros or the alignment while sailing through the clean addition.

topic.description: Fluently add and subtract within 1000 using strategies and algorithms based on place value, properties of operations, and the relationship between addition and subtraction

pedagogy.summary: Fluency within 1000 is NOT just 'do columnar faster' — it is the flexible, adaptive choice of the most efficient method for THESE particular numbers (Threlfall; NCETM 'intelligent practice'). The child should have three tools in play — the standard columnar algorithm, mental strategies (compensation, near-doubles, place-value partitioning), and counting up on an empty number line for close subtractions — and pick well. Efficiency and the add/sub inverse relationship (checking) are the goals, not a single rote procedure.
bestPractices: Contrast strategies explicitly: put the same problem up and ask 'clever way vs plod way?' — build adaptive expertise rather than defaulting to the algorithm
Use counting-up on an empty number line for close subtractions (300-298, 401-399) so difference-as-distance is felt
Teach compensation for near-multiples (525+199 = 525+200-1) alongside the algorithm
Always link subtraction to addition for checking (inverse), not re-counting
Reserve the standard columnar algorithm for problems where no shortcut helps (456+287)
keyRepresentations: Place-value columns / base-ten exchange (the algorithm's meaning)
Empty number line (counting up for difference)
Part-whole bar model
Hundred square / place-value chart for +/-10, +/-100 jumps
commonMisconceptions: Reaches for the column algorithm for every problem even when counting up or compensating is far quicker (strategy inflexibility)
Smaller-from-larger subtraction bug — subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in a column regardless of position
Cannot decompose to subtract when a column is zero (borrow-across-zero)
Treats subtraction as unrelated to addition — re-counts to check instead of using the inverse

learn.summary: Fluency within 1000 is adaptive strategy choice, not just faster column arithmetic: pupils match the most efficient method to the particular numbers. The child should hold three tools and pick well — the standard columnar algorithm (for problems where no shortcut helps, e.g. 456+287), mental strategies (compensation 525+199 = 525+200-1, near-doubles, place-value partitioning), and counting up on an empty number line for close subtractions (300-298, 401-399). Subtraction is linked to addition for checking (inverse), not re-counting. Learners also need to handle known systematic subtraction bugs: smaller-from-larger, and borrow/decompose across a zero.

activities.title: Two-track strategy bench: match the method to the numbers
feedback: If the child reaches for columns on 300-298: put the two numbers on an empty number line and ask 'how far apart are they?'; contrast the steps each method took. Build the habit of glancing at the numbers before choosing.
If the child uses the algorithm well on 456+287: affirm that this is exactly where the column method earns its place.
When checking, if the child re-does the subtraction: prompt them to add the answer back using the item's own numbers — for 300-298, does 2 + 298 return 300? — to make the inverse-check routine.
activities.rationale: Running two tracks side by side lets the child feel the cost of a poor method choice and the payoff of a good one; reversing with 456+287 keeps the algorithm valued rather than discarded. A live recomputing bench with a visible timer is one concrete way to make the cost of the choice visible; a paper version (solve both ways, compare, time with a clock) can serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: The defining standard for fluency within 1000 is strategic, not rote: pupils 'fluently add and subtract within 1000 using strategies and algorithms based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction' — a range of algorithms may be used.

Adaptive expertise — choosing a strategy suited to the specific numbers (e.g. counting up for close subtractions, compensation for near-multiples) — is a distinct, teachable goal beyond executing the standard algorithm.
learnerActions: Meet a problem such as 300-298. Before computing, glance at the numbers and predict which method will be quickest.
Solve it two ways side by side: an empty-number-line track (count up from 298 to 300) and a column-algorithm track (set up and exchange across the zero). Time or step-count both.
Compare: on 300-298 the number line jumps the gap in one hop of 2 while the column track is still exchanging across the zero (and may trip over it).
Now try 456+287 the same way and compare: no obvious shortcut stands out for these numbers, so the column algorithm is a sensible, efficient choice here.

Add a check step using the inverse, with this activity's own numbers: for 300-298, add your answer (2) back to 298 and confirm you reach 300; for 456+287 (=743), subtract one addend from the total to recover the other.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means matching the method to the numbers, not grinding one algorithm; close numbers favour counting up, near-multiples favour compensation, and messy numbers favour the column algorithm.

activities.title: Sort first, then solve: which method would you choose?
feedback: If a problem is mis-sorted, ask the child to say how far apart the numbers are, or how close one is to a round number, then re-sort.
If the child sorts correctly but reverts to one method when computing, point back to their own sort and ask them to honour the chosen method.
For 502-5, if the child tries to count up the whole gap or reaches for column borrowing, point out that only 5 is subtracted, so counting back 5 or compensating is far quicker.
activities.rationale: A categorise-then-compute task drills adaptive selection explicitly and makes the selection step visible. Sorting and justifying is recognition-plus-reasoning; it checks classification but does not itself elicit the computation, so pair it with actual calculation so selection is tested against real arithmetic.
sourceClaims: Adaptive expertise — choosing a strategy suited to the specific numbers (e.g. counting up for close subtractions, compensation for near-multiples) — is a distinct, teachable goal beyond executing the standard algorithm.
learnerActions: Sort 8 problems into three piles: 'count up' (close numbers), 'compensate' (near a multiple like +199), and 'column' (no shortcut helps).
For each problem, state in one phrase why it belongs in that pile ('these two are close, so I count up').
Then compute the answers.

Transfer: given a new pair such as 502-5, decide which method is quickest — note the two numbers are far apart but only 5 is taken away, so counting back 5 or compensation beats a column borrow across the zero.
activities.intendedInsight: Strategy selection is a distinct, assessable skill: you can name and justify why a particular method fits particular numbers before doing any arithmetic.

activities.title: Fix the subtraction bugs: smaller-from-larger and borrow across zero
feedback: If the child writes 265 (smaller digit taken from larger in the ones and tens): return to concrete base-ten exchange on the failing columns, showing that 8 cannot be taken from 3 and 6 cannot be taken from 0 without exchanging, and that the hundreds must then drop from 7 to 6.
If the child stalls at the zero, writes 0 in the tens, or borrows incorrectly: model exchanging one hundred into ten tens first (703 = 6 hundreds, 9 tens, 13 ones) with blocks before the digits.
Finish with the inverse check: add the answer (135) back to 568 and confirm you reach 703.
activities.rationale: Smaller-from-larger and borrow-from-zero are documented, stable subtraction bugs, so targeted concrete exchange work on the exact failing column addresses a known error source rather than a one-off slip.
sourceClaims: Smaller-from-larger and borrow-from-zero are systematic, documented, STABLE subtraction bugs: borrow-from-zero (change a 0 to 9 but fail to keep borrowing left) is the single most common bug in Brown & Burton's data (107/1325); smaller-from-larger was used by 54; ~40% of students showed consistently buggy behaviour.
learnerActions: Work 703-568 with base-ten materials (or place-value chips) before writing digits: exchange one hundred into ten tens, then one ten into ten ones, so 703 becomes 6 hundreds, 9 tens, 13 ones.
Check each column: confirm you cannot take 8 from 3 in the ones without exchanging — you do not simply subtract the smaller digit from the larger.
Complete the written algorithm, keeping the borrow moving left across the zero (the answer is 135).

Compare your answer with a wrong answer like 265 and explain which columns were mishandled (265 comes from taking the smaller digit from the larger in each column: the ones (3 take 8) and tens (0 take 6) skipped their exchanges, so the hundreds was never reduced from 7 to 6; the ones digit 5 matches the correct answer only by coincidence).
activities.intendedInsight: Column subtraction requires exchanging by place value; a top digit smaller than the bottom digit means you must decompose, and when a zero column must give to the column on its right (as in 703-568), it first needs an exchange from the hundreds — not leaving the column as 0.

activities.title: Strategy-menu reference and 'convince me' justification
feedback: If the child cannot justify a choice beyond 'that's how you do it', ask them to compare the number of steps their method took with an alternative.
Use the menu wall as a reference, not a crutch: encourage the child to predict the pick before consulting it.
activities.rationale: A static menu offers a useful reference but cannot by itself let the child experience the cost of a choice; a justification exchange surfaces reasoning. Both support, rather than replace, actually doing and comparing the methods in the bench activity.
sourceClaims: Adaptive expertise — choosing a strategy suited to the specific numbers (e.g. counting up for close subtractions, compensation for near-multiples) — is a distinct, teachable goal beyond executing the standard algorithm.
learnerActions: Build or use a strategy-menu wall with three worked examples, one per method (count up, compensate, column), each labelled with when it is the smart pick.
After solving a problem, explain to a partner or coach why your chosen method was quickest for those numbers.
Respond to a challenge ('convince me your method was quickest') by pointing to the number features that made your choice efficient.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to articulate why a method fits particular numbers consolidates adaptive expertise and exposes whether a choice was reasoned or habitual.

constraints: The goal is efficient, adaptive method choice plus the add/sub inverse for checking — not speed at a single rote procedure.
A static strategy-menu poster is a reference only: it cannot let the child experience the choice or feel its cost, so pair it with activities that involve actually doing and comparing methods.
A sort/categorise step checks selection reasoning but should be paired with real computation so pupils also execute the chosen method correctly.
A justification dialogue surfaces reasoning but does not replace actually doing and comparing the methods; keep real computation central.
Subtraction checking should use addition (inverse), not re-counting the subtraction, and each check should use the numbers of the problem actually solved.
Reserve the standard column algorithm for problems where no shortcut helps (e.g. 456+287); do not treat it as the default for every problem.
Base-ten cutouts/blocks are concrete approximations of place-value structure; use the exchange physically before the written digits for borrow-across-zero.
Computation within 1000 is planar place-value work; the proposed number-line and column representations are sufficient here — a third spatial dimension is not required for this topic.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched this session. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source marks the Threlfall/NCETM 'intelligent practice' claim as not fetched this session (verified:false); treat the adaptive-expertise principle as plausibly supported but unverified here.

Worked arithmetic check: 300-298 = 2 (one hop of 2 by counting up); 525+199 = 525+200-1 = 724; 456+287 = 743; 703-568 = 135 (703 = 6 hundreds, 9 tens, 13 ones; the buggy 265 arises from smaller-from-larger/flip errors). These arithmetic facts were verified during this rewrite; no source effectiveness claims were verified.

The original 'only a live 2D bench can let the child pick a method and FEEL the cost', 'dialogue cannot provide', and '3D adds nothing' claims were softened to narrowly-scoped affordances with limits; the comparative-necessity wording is not established by the cited sources. Stopwatch timing is likewise one concrete scaffold, not a requirement.

502-5 is used as a transfer item; it is a 'small takeaway from a round-ish number' where counting back or compensation is quick, NOT a close-numbers/difference-as-distance case. The original gap note's 'these are close' phrasing is loose; confirm the intended discriminating feature when authoring.

Inverse checks are scoped to each activity's own problem numbers: the 300-298/456+287 bench uses its own numbers, and the 703-568 inverse check (135+568=703) sits in the subtraction-bug activity where that problem is actually worked.

probeDeeper: Which of those four was quickest for you, and why?
Could you have done 456 + 287 a cleverer way, or was the column method best there?
What about 502 - 5 - column method, or something quicker?
Show me how you'd check the 703 - 568 answer without redoing the subtraction.

Justifies each choice by the numbers ('these two are close, so I counted up').

topic.name: Adding and subtracting (age 9+)

Choose between mental and written methods for each step and explain why

topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a multi-step problem — like planning a budget where money is added and spent in several steps — can they decide which operations to use at each stage and explain their thinking?

pedagogy.summary: Multi-step (three or more step) contextual problems with five-digit numbers, where the child decides which operations and methods to use and why. This extends two-step problem-solving: the demands are now holding several steps in a plan, tracking intermediate quantities without mistaking one for the answer, and choosing per step between mental and written methods (25,000 - 20,822 is a counting-up job; 12,450 + 8,372 wants columnar). Situation-modelling, not keyword-spotting, remains the crux.
bestPractices: Represent the whole problem with a bar model before computing - structure first
Plan and label every step; explicitly name intermediate results so they are not offered as the final answer
Choose a method per step by the numbers (counting up for 25,000 - 21,000-ish; columnar for awkward sums)
Estimate the final answer up front so a dropped step or wrong operation shows up
Check reasonableness against the story at the end
keyRepresentations: Multi-bar model (running total / comparison)
Empty number line for counting-up steps
Step planner (step 1 -> step 2 -> step 3)
Jottings for method-per-step decisions
commonMisconceptions: Keyword strategy - picks operations from words rather than the situation
Drops a step - solves two of three steps and stops
Offers an intermediate quantity as the final answer
Uses a written method where counting-up is far quicker (25,000 - 20,822), or vice versa
Does not estimate, so a missing step or wrong magnitude goes unnoticed

learn.summary: Year 5 learners (age 9-10) solve multi-step (two or more step) contextual addition/subtraction problems with five-digit numbers, deciding which operations and methods to use and why. The core demands are: modelling the situation (not keyword-spotting), holding several steps in a plan, tracking intermediate quantities without mistaking one for the final answer, choosing per step between mental and written methods (e.g. 25,000 - 20,822 suits counting up; 12,450 + 8,372 suits a column method), and estimating up front plus checking reasonableness at the end.

activities.title: Plan-then-compute with a multi-bar model
feedback: If you offered 20,822 as the answer: re-read and underline what the question actually asks. 20,822 is the two-week total; the question asks how many MORE are needed to reach 25,000, so the final step 25,000 - 20,822 = 4,178 is still missing.

If you reached for column subtraction on 25,000 - 20,822: try counting up on a number line (20,822 -> 21,000 -> 25,000, which is 178 then 4,000, so 4,178). Compare how many steps each method takes; the numbers are close, so counting up avoids borrowing across the zeros.
If your answer is far from your up-front estimate, a step may have been dropped, an operation or calculation may be wrong, or the estimate itself may be off; retrace each labelled step on the bar.
activities.rationale: Visual/strip-bar representations support correct operation choice and comparison problems, and genuine problem solving is situation-modelling rather than executing memorised key-word shortcuts. Making intermediate results explicit guards against the common error of stopping at a running total.
sourceClaims: Teaching students to use visual representations (Recommendation 3, rated STRONG evidence from six middle-school studies) improves problem solving; strip/bar diagrams are suited to comparison and fraction problems, and genuine problem solving is 'not the execution of memorized rules or shortcuts, such as using key words'.
Problem structure, not surface keywords, drives multi-step difficulty; situation-modelling with bar models supports correct operation choice.
learnerActions: Before calculating, lay out the whole problem as a bar model: for the bottle problem, draw Week 1 (12,450) and Week 2 (8,372) as combining bars, then set that combined bar against the 25,000 target bar with the shortfall shown as an unknown gap.
Label every step and name each intermediate result explicitly (e.g. write '20,822 = two-week total, NOT the answer').
State an up-front estimate of the final answer (e.g. 'about 25,000 - 21,000 = roughly 4,000 more').
Choose a method for each step by looking at the numbers: count up for 25,000 - 20,822; use a column method for an awkward sum like 12,450 + 8,372.
Answer the actual question asked (how many MORE are needed = the gap, 4,178) and check it against your estimate and the story.
activities.intendedInsight: A multi-step problem is not finished until the final question is answered; the structure of the situation, modelled before computing, determines which operations and in what order, while the numbers determine the best method per step.

activities.title: Walk me through your plan: justify each step and method
feedback: If steps come out of order or an add appears where the story removes: narrate the story event by event, mapping each event to one operation in sequence.
If a method is chosen without justification: compare the cost of the two methods on these specific numbers and explain which is quicker and why.
Correct worked plan for the shop problem: 41,000 - 18,650 = 22,350, then 22,350 + 9,200 = 31,550, choosing a method per step and explaining each choice.
activities.rationale: The statutory objective requires pupils to decide operations and methods 'and why'; a justify-your-plan dialogue exercises exactly that reasoning and makes method-per-step choice and step order explicit.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should be taught to 'solve addition and subtraction multi-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why', and to 'use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy' (verbatim statutory wording).
Problem structure, not surface keywords, drives multi-step difficulty; situation-modelling with bar models supports correct operation choice.
learnerActions: Take a multi-step scenario (e.g. the two-step problem 'A shop had £41,000 in the bank, spent £18,650, then took £9,200 in sales. How much is in the bank now?', or a longer one with three or more steps) and, out loud or in writing, say which step comes first and why.
For each step, state the operation and whether you will use a mental or written method, and justify that choice from the numbers.
Say what each intermediate number means in the story before moving on (e.g. '22,350 is the balance after spending, not the final answer').

Answer the probing follow-ups: 'What is the question actually asking for?', 'Roughly how much should it be before you calculate exactly?', 'For this subtraction, would you take away or count up — which is quicker here?', 'Why did you subtract first to follow the story, and would adding the £9,200 first give the same final balance?'
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding which operations and methods to use AND WHY is the explicit objective; articulating the plan and justifying each method choice surfaces the reasoning that number-grabbing hides.

activities.title: Sequence the steps and choose the method for each
feedback: If you choose the keyword-suggested operation: ask what actually happens in the story at that point, not which word appears.
If you choose the intermediate value as the final answer: the question asked for something beyond that number; identify the remaining step.
If you choose a column algorithm for a near-value subtraction: a short count-up is often fewer steps and, when the larger number has zeros (like 25,000), avoids exchanging across zeros.
activities.rationale: Selection/ordering tasks can efficiently check that learners attend to structure and method choice, including deliberate keyword and intermediate-as-answer distractors. As a recognition format it checks discrimination but does not by itself require the learner to construct and carry out a fresh plan.
sourceClaims: Problem structure, not surface keywords, drives multi-step difficulty; situation-modelling with bar models supports correct operation choice.
learnerActions: Given a multi-step problem (two or more steps), put the steps in the correct order rather than accepting the order the words appear.
For each step, select the operation and the better method (mental counting-up vs written column), and give a one-line reason.
Spot and reject a keyword-trap option (an operation suggested only by a word like 'more' or 'total') and an intermediate-as-answer distractor (e.g. choosing 20,822 instead of 4,178).
Estimate the final answer before committing and use it to sanity-check the chosen sequence.

activities.title: Study and annotate a worked multi-step example

learn.summary: Extend the standard columnar algorithm to whole numbers with more than four digits. Estimation-first and inverse checking matter more because a single misaligned digit is now worth thousands.

activities.title: Borrowing across a row of zeros (500,000 − 234,178)
feedback: If the child stalls at the zeros or does not carry the exchange through every column (e.g. 265,832, where the tens was left as 10 instead of 9, or 275,822, where the ten-thousands was left as 10 instead of 9), model with place-value counters: exchange one hundred-thousand and walk it down column by column so each 0 becomes 9 with a ten passed on until the ones hold 10.
If a smaller digit is subtracted from a larger one regardless of position, do a concrete exchange on the failing column and reassert that you cannot take more than is there without borrowing.
If the child checks only by redoing the same subtraction, scaffold the estimate (round both numbers) and the inverse addition, or a counting-up number line, instead of reteaching the algorithm.
activities.rationale: Borrow-from-zero is a well-documented systematic subtraction bug that intensifies when a minuend has several adjacent zeros, so a deliberate round-number case targets the most-failed large-number hazard. A live place-value/counters model can animate the exchange as the child performs it; physical counters, squared paper, or a counting-up number line serve the same rationale without requiring a specific tool.
sourceClaims: Borrow-from-zero is the single most common systematic subtraction bug (Brown & Burton, 1325 students, 107 occurrences): the student changes a 0 to 9 but fails to continue borrowing leftward. When a minuend has several adjacent zeros (e.g. 500,000) the exchange must cascade through them, and this zero-borrow bug intensifies; smaller-from-larger (54 students) persists at scale. These are stable procedural bugs — ~40% of students showed consistently buggy behaviour — not carelessness.
Composing/decomposing (exchange) is the conceptual basis of the columnar algorithm regardless of digit count; DfE Appendix 1 sets out the formal written methods.

Year 5 pupils are taught to 'add and subtract whole numbers with more than 4 digits, including using formal written methods (columnar addition and subtraction)' and to 'use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy' (statutory).
learnerActions: Set out 500,000 − 234,178 in columns aligned by place value, from the ones on the right.
Before computing, estimate by rounding (about 500,000 − 234,000 = 266,000) and note the expected size of the answer.

At the ones there is nothing to take 8 from, and every column to the left is 0; work the exchange by taking one hundred-thousand and walking it down column by column so each 0 becomes 9 as a ten is passed along, until the ones finally hold 10.
Complete the subtraction to get 265,822.
Check with the inverse: 265,822 + 234,178 should return 500,000, and compare to your estimate (~266,000).
Optionally model the same subtraction as counting up on an empty number line — jump from 234,178 up to 500,000 and total the jumps — as an independent alternative that should also give 265,822.
Optionally repeat with an easier round-number case such as 500,000 − 234,000 and discuss why that borrow is simpler.
activities.intendedInsight: A single exchange can cascade through a row of zeros — each zero becomes a 9 as the ten is passed along, and the ones finally hold 10 — so a wall of zeros is not a dead end.

activities.title: Adding three numbers of up to five digits: when the carry is more than one
feedback: If the child carries only 1 from a column totalling 20 or more (e.g. 9 + 8 + 7 = 24), total the column aloud, separate it into 4 ones and 2 tens, and make the size of the carry explicit.

If a three-number sum is too small by exactly one (or more) in the column just above a heavy column (e.g. 10 too small when the ones totalled 24 but only 1 was carried), this may point to an undersized carry. Recount that column and check how many tens it holds.
If numbers of different lengths are misaligned so place values don't line up, use squared paper or place-value headers anchored from the ones on the right.
activities.rationale: A child drilled only on two-addend sums tends to assume a carry is always 1; a three-addend column that totals into the twenties surfaces and corrects that assumption. The original diagnostic problem does not actually create such a column, so a correctly chosen example is used for the larger carry while the given problem still serves alignment and repeated-carry practice. A part-whole bar can make the multi-addend structure explicit. A fill-in-the-blank format on carried digits plus a rounded estimate can assess this at scale but cannot verify handwritten alignment, so paper setup should also be observed.

Year 5 pupils are taught to 'add and subtract whole numbers with more than 4 digits, including using formal written methods (columnar addition and subtraction)' and to 'use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy' (statutory).
learnerActions: Set out 12,340 + 8,706 + 15,058 in a single column layout, aligning by place value from the ones on the right (numbers of different lengths must still line up); optionally show the three addends as parts of a part-whole bar whose whole is the total.
Add the ones column aloud and name the full total (0 + 6 + 8 = 14): write 4, carry 1.

Work through the rest of this sum: note that every carry here is only 1 (column totals including carries: tens 10, hundreds 11, thousands 16; the ten-thousands totals 3 with no carry), finishing at 36,104. This is good practice at keeping three different-length addends aligned and tracking repeated carries.

Now tackle a case that genuinely produces a larger carry, e.g. 36,489 + 27,858 + 15,937: the ones column totals 9 + 8 + 7 = 24, so write 4 and carry 2 (not 1); completing it gives 80,284, with several columns (ones, hundreds and thousands) carrying 2.
Compute 34,567 + 28,945 = 63,512 as a clean two-addend check that the basic algorithm is intact.
Estimate by rounding before computing so a place-value slip in the thousands or ten-thousands is caught.
activities.intendedInsight: When a column of three or more addends totals 20 or more, the carry can be 2 (or more), not automatically 1. (Not every three-addend sum reaches that — 12,340 + 8,706 + 15,058 only ever carries 1 — so a case whose column actually totals into the twenties is needed to surface the larger carry.)

activities.title: Worked-example reference and estimate-then-check routine
feedback: If the child's answer is far from the estimate, that gap is the signal to recheck alignment and exchanges (and quickly confirm the rounding in the estimate itself). Do not simply change the estimate to match the answer.
A revealed worked example is reference only; the child should then set out and solve a fresh case themselves on paper.
Praise specifically when the child catches their own error via estimate or inverse, reinforcing why that beats redoing the sum.
activities.rationale: Rounding-to-check is a statutory expectation and a reliable guard against single-digit place-value slips at scale; the inverse operation is independent of the original method, so it catches errors a re-run would reproduce. A revealed worked example is a useful static reference but exercises recognition rather than independent construction, so it must be paired with the child doing the work.

Fluency here means flexible, place-value-based mental strategies, not doing the column algorithm in one's head.

learn.summary: Year 5 mental addition and subtraction with increasingly large numbers, built from place-value knowledge and derived facts rather than running a written column algorithm in the head. The central move is to scale a known small-number fact by place value (knowing 6 + 4 = 10 lets you reach 6,000 + 4,000 = 10,000; knowing 45 + 8 = 53 gives 45,000 + 8,000 = 53,000) while tracking the zeros, and to choose an efficient strategy for the numbers at hand: partitioning, compensation, near-doubles, and counting up from the smaller to the larger number for subtraction from round numbers (10,000 - 3,200 = 6,800). Fluency means flexible, place-value-based mental strategies and the ability to explain the choice, not silent reproduction of column working.

activities.title: Scaling bench: a small fact with zeros bolted on
feedback: If the digits are right but the magnitude is wrong (e.g. 5,300 or 53,00 for 45,000 + 8,000), name it as a place-value slip: re-slide 45 + 8 = 53 up the chart saying the unit each step so '53' becomes '53 thousand'.
If the learner recomputes from scratch at each scale instead of reusing the known fact, pause and ask 'which small fact is hiding inside this one?' before continuing.
activities.rationale: Deriving new facts from known facts scaled by place value is an explicit mental-calculation strategy; making the scaling literal (chart row by row, watching zeros) targets the common zero-misplacement error directly.
sourceClaims: Subtraction can be done by complementary addition ('shopkeeper's method') - counting up from the smaller to the larger number, bridging through round-number 'landmarks'; 'many children find it easier to subtract by counting up rather than by counting back', and the answer is the total of the jumps, not a point on the line. Mental calculation rests on deriving new facts from known facts scaled by place value (e.g. 140 + 150 = 290 via 14 + 15 = 29; 680 + 430 via 68 + 43).
learnerActions: State a known small fact first, e.g. 6 + 4 = 10, then scale it up a place-value row at a time: 60 + 40 = 100, 600 + 400 = 1,000, 6,000 + 4,000 = 10,000, saying aloud how many zeros the answer gains.
Repeat the scaling with a fact that bridges, e.g. 45 + 8 = 53, to reach 450 + 80 = 530 and 45,000 + 8,000 = 53,000; say the unit explicitly ('45 thousand plus 8 thousand is 53 thousand').

Check each scaled answer keeps '53' as its non-zero digits and changes only in magnitude, matching the size of the numbers being added (530 is 53 tens; 53,000 is 53 thousands); flag an answer that loses that digit pattern (e.g. 125,000) or that keeps the digits but lands at the wrong magnitude (e.g. 5,300 instead of 53,000) as a scaling slip, not a new sum.
activities.intendedInsight: A 'big' calculation is often a small fact the learner already owns, with place value shifting the whole fact up predictably; the zeros are bookkeeping, not extra arithmetic.

activities.title: Counting up from a round number
feedback: If the learner gives the landing point instead of the total of the jumps, remind them the answer is the sum of the hops (800 + 6,000 = 6,800), not 10,000.
If the learner describes 'borrowing' across the zeros and pauses or errs, model the gap on a number line instead: frame it as measuring the distance between the two numbers.
For 20,000 - 19,850, if the learner starts a full decomposition, prompt 'how far apart are these two numbers?' to surface the single small jump of 150.
activities.rationale: Complementary addition (counting up through round-number landmarks) is documented as a mental subtraction strategy many children find easier than counting back, and it sidesteps the exchange-tracking error that arises when picturing the column method across zeros.
sourceClaims: Subtraction can be done by complementary addition ('shopkeeper's method') - counting up from the smaller to the larger number, bridging through round-number 'landmarks'; 'many children find it easier to subtract by counting up rather than by counting back', and the answer is the total of the jumps, not a point on the line. Mental calculation rests on deriving new facts from known facts scaled by place value (e.g. 140 + 150 = 290 via 14 + 15 = 29; 680 + 430 via 68 + 43).
learnerActions: Subtract 3,200 from 10,000 by counting up on an empty number line: jump +800 from 3,200 to 4,000, then +6,000 from 4,000 to 10,000; the answer is the TOTAL of the jumps, 6,800 (not the point you land on).
Try 20,000 - 19,850 the same way: notice the numbers are close, count up +150 from 19,850 to 20,000, and decide this gap is tiny so counting up is clearly quicker than decomposing.
Say aloud whether counting up or taking away felt easier for each, and why the numbers made that choice sensible.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtraction from a round number is a short journey measured by adding the jumps; counting up avoids the error-prone mental 'borrowing' across a string of zeros, and the size of the gap signals when it is the smart choice.

activities.title: Choosing a strategy to fit the numbers
feedback: If the learner reaches a correct answer by one slow default method throughout, accept the answer but ask 'what did you notice about these two numbers?' to prompt near-doubles or counting up.
If the learner cannot name any strategy, work one example together and have them re-explain it in their own words before the next item.
activities.rationale: The target is flexible strategy choice (scaled fact, counting up, near-doubles, compensation), so activities should require naming and justifying the method, since a correct answer by an inefficient route still signals strategy inflexibility. Sorting a strategy can check that a learner classifies it, though classification alone does not require independently constructing and carrying out the calculation, so the main work stays learner-generated.
learnerActions: Look at 2,500 + 2,600 and spot the near-double: double 2,500 = 5,000, then add 100 to get 5,100, rather than partitioning digit by digit.
Sort a mixed set of calculations into 'count up' versus 'partition' versus 'near-double/compensate', saying what feature of the numbers triggered each choice.
After solving each item, explain the method used; compare a partitioning route and a near-doubles/counting-up route side by side for the same item to see which was fewer steps.
activities.intendedInsight: Efficient mental calculation is about reading the numbers and picking a strategy that fits them, not applying one default method to everything.

activities.title: Explain your mental shortcut
feedback: If the explanation reveals an inefficient route despite a correct answer, affirm the answer then model the more efficient strategy for comparison.
Use 'talk me through it' to catch a right answer reached by mentally running the column algorithm, and redirect to scaling or counting up.
activities.rationale: Asking the learner to articulate a strategy is a design proposal intended to support metacognition and to help distinguish an efficient, place-value-based method from a laborious one; the counting-up and derived-fact strategies being explained are themselves documented, but the source does not establish that explaining them aids learning. Explanation is intended to support fluency and does not replace repeated practice.
learnerActions: After doing a calculation in your head, talk a listener through HOW you did it, step by step, so the method is audible, not just the answer.

Answer prompts such as: 'How does knowing 45 + 8 help with 45,000 + 8,000?', 'For 10,000 - 3,200, did you take away or count up, and which was easier here?', and 'What did you notice about 2,500 and 2,600 that let you use a double?'
Transfer the explained method to a fresh case (e.g. 20,000 - 19,850) and predict which strategy will be quickest before solving.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the strategy aims to consolidate it and to expose whether a right answer came from an efficient, place-value-based method or a laborious one.

constraints: These are mental strategies: the aim is flexible place-value reasoning, not reproducing the written column algorithm in the head.
Jottings such as an empty number line should support the mental method, not replace it with full written working.

Sorting tasks and fill-in-the-blank recall can rehearse and check scaled facts and strategy classification, but recognising or categorising a strategy is not the same as independently constructing and carrying out the calculation; keep the main work learner-generated and spoken/explained.

A reference poster or tappable fact-family display is useful as a lookup, but on its own it does not require the learner to perform the scaling or the counting up; use it alongside active calculation.

A linked place-value chart that slides a fact up a row while the answer gains zeros, and a number line showing counting-up hops that total the answer, are helpful ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are optional supports, not required apparatus.
Do not ban or time-pressure a child who still counts on in ones for parts of a calculation; this matures as derived-fact fluency grows. Keep modelling place-value jumps and let the counting recede.

The counting-up answer must be the TOTAL of the jumps, not the number landed on; this is emphasised in the activity to pre-empt a known slip, consistent with the source claim.

Activity 4 (explain your shortcut) cites no source: the source documents counting-up and derived-fact strategies but does not establish that having learners explain them improves learning, so that efficacy framing is left as a design proposal.

topic.description: Solve addition and subtraction multi-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why, with numbers up to 10,000,000 and decimals
evidence: Solve a two-step word problem involving addition and subtraction of numbers beyond 1,000,000
Choose between mental, written, and calculator methods for a multi-step problem and justify the choice
Interpret a real-life context to identify which addition/subtraction operations are needed across multiple steps
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a complicated word problem involving large numbers or decimals — like calculating the total cost of several items — can they plan and carry out all the steps correctly?

pedagogy.summary: The capstone add/subtract problem-solving node: multi-step problems in real contexts with numbers up to 10,000,000 and decimals, where the child decides which operations AND which method — mental, written, or calculator — to use for each step, and justifies the choice. Beyond the multi-step reasoning inherited from earlier years, the distinctive demands are (1) choosing the calculator wisely (for genuinely awkward large/decimal computation, not for steps doable mentally) and (2) checking calculator/written output for reasonableness with an estimate, because a single keying or place-value slip is now worth millions.
bestPractices: Model the whole problem (bar model) and plan every step before computing
Choose method per step by the numbers: mental for round/near steps, written for structured ones, calculator for awkward large/decimal arithmetic - and say why
ALWAYS estimate the expected result so a calculator keying error (missed digit, misplaced point) is caught
Track intermediate quantities and re-read the actual question so the final step is not dropped
Interpret the answer back in context (units, sense, magnitude)
keyRepresentations: Multi-bar / running-total model
Step-and-method planner (step | operation | method | why)
Estimate strip for the reasonableness check
Real contexts: populations, money, distances, measures (decimals)
commonMisconceptions: Offers an intermediate quantity as the final answer, or drops a step
Word-spots operations rather than modelling the situation
Over-relies on the calculator (keys in steps doable mentally) or refuses it for genuinely awkward computation
Trusts the calculator display without an estimate, so a keying/place-value error goes unnoticed
Loses track of the decimal point or a period (thousands/millions) in large or decimal numbers

learn.summary: Year 6 capstone for add/subtract multi-step problem solving in real contexts with numbers up to 10,000,000 and decimals. The distinctive demands beyond multi-step reasoning are: choosing a method per step (mental, written, or calculator) and justifying it, and checking any calculator/written output against an estimate so a keying or place-value slip (now worth millions) is caught. Learners must model the whole situation, track intermediate quantities, and answer the actual question rather than report a running total.

activities.title: Charity accounts mission planner
feedback: If a learner keys 345,000 where about 3,450,000 was expected, prompt: 'that's ten times too small - check the place value: have you missed a zero or put the decimal point in the wrong place?'
If the final answer equals an intermediate (e.g. the post-March figure), prompt: 're-read the question; which steps are still marked on your bar? Is the April-costs step included?'
If a learner keys in +2,000,000 on a calculator, ask: 'could you do this one in your head?' - discuss method fit without reteaching the arithmetic.
If a learner hand-grinds the awkward 675,450.75 subtraction unnecessarily, ask whether a calculator would suit that step and why.
activities.rationale: The national curriculum requires pupils to solve addition and subtraction multi-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why, and to use estimation to check answers and judge an appropriate degree of accuracy. Making method choice and a reasonableness gate the core loop targets exactly this content. An optional interactive version can hold the estimate and flash a magnitude warning when the entered result is an order of magnitude off, and can feed each result into a visible running bar; these are illustrative mechanisms, not requirements - the same loop works on paper with a planner grid and an estimate strip.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should be taught to 'solve addition and subtraction multi-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why' and to 'use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy'; Year 6 place value covers reading and ordering numbers up to 10,000,000 (verbatim statutory wording).
Estimation is essential for judging the reasonableness of calculator/written output; sensible calculator use is a taught competence.
learnerActions: Read a real multi-step problem, e.g. 'A charity had 3,450,000 pounds. In March it spent 1,280,000 pounds and received donations of 2,000,000 pounds. In April its costs were 675,450.75 pounds. How much does it have at the end of April?'
Before computing, model the whole problem with a running-total bar and mark every event as a signed change on the bar.

Build a running estimate first: estimate each step's expected result as well as the final total (about 3.45m - 1.28m + 2m - 0.68m is roughly 3.5m, with intermediate ballparks of about 2.17m then 4.17m along the way).
For each step, choose mental, written, or calculator, carry out the computation, and write one sentence saying WHY that method fits those numbers.
After any calculator or written step, compare that result's order of magnitude against your estimate for that same quantity before accepting it.
Re-read the original question and give the end-of-April balance (3,494,549.25 pounds), interpreted back in context, not an intermediate total.
activities.intendedInsight: A calculator does not free you from thinking: the estimate is what tells you whether to trust the display, and the final answer must answer the question asked, not report a running total.

activities.title: Defend your plan and tool choices
feedback: If justification is vague ('it just seemed right'), press for the specific feature of the numbers that makes the chosen method fit.
If the learner cannot say the expected ballpark, send them back to build the estimate before defending the tool choice.
activities.rationale: The topic explicitly requires justifying which operations and methods to use and why; an in-role defence dialogue exercises that judgement directly. A spoken, responsive defence can surface reasoning that a written answer alone may not reveal.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should be taught to 'solve addition and subtraction multi-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why' and to 'use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy'; Year 6 place value covers reading and ordering numbers up to 10,000,000 (verbatim statutory wording).
learnerActions: After solving a multi-step problem, explain the plan aloud to a partner or character who challenges it.
Answer probing challenges: 'Why calculator there but mental here? Roughly what should this step come to? Does that final answer make sense in the context?'

Justify each method choice by reference to the specific numbers (for example, round or near-round steps often suit mental methods, structured ones written methods, and awkward large or decimal ones a calculator - but the choice is a reasoned judgement, not a fixed rule).
State the ballpark estimate and say how it would have exposed a mis-keyed result about ten times too small or too large, such as 349,454.93 or 34,945,492.50.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify which operations and methods you used - and what the answer should roughly be - is part of competent problem solving, not an optional extra.

activities.title: Sequence, method, and spot the impossible answer
feedback: If an impossible answer is accepted (e.g. one order of magnitude off), prompt the learner to compare it digit-by-place against the estimate.
If the wrong final step is chosen, ask whether the selected figure is an intermediate or the balance the question requests.
activities.rationale: Sequencing, method selection, and identifying an unreasonable result are useful checks of understanding. This format mainly assesses recognition and ordering; it does not require the learner to independently construct the plan and computation, so pair it with the planner activity for production.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should be taught to 'solve addition and subtraction multi-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why' and to 'use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy'; Year 6 place value covers reading and ordering numbers up to 10,000,000 (verbatim statutory wording).
learnerActions: Put the steps of a given multi-step problem into the correct order.
For each step, select the best method (mental / written / calculator) and give a reason.
Given an estimate for a step, identify which of several candidate calculator answers is impossible because it is the wrong order of magnitude.
Flag any answer that reports a running total instead of answering the actual question.
activities.intendedInsight: Checking an answer against an estimate lets you reject results that are impossible by magnitude, and the correct final answer is the one that matches the question asked.

activities.title: Walk through an annotated worked example
feedback: Prompt learners to explain in their own words why each annotated method was chosen before moving on, so the walkthrough does not become passive reading.
activities.rationale: A worked example displays the structure of a good solution, the bar-model representation, and the role of the estimate. As a scaffold it does not by itself require the learner to generate their own plan or method choices, so it should precede or support independent problem solving rather than replace it; comparing it to the learner's own attempt can, however, prompt reflection on method choice.
sourceClaims: Teaching students to use visual representations (Recommendation 3, rated STRONG evidence) improves problem solving; the guide frames problem solving as reasoning about structure, 'not the execution of memorized rules or shortcuts, such as using key words'.
learnerActions: Study a complete multi-step worked example; reveal, for each step, the operation used, the method chosen, and the reasonableness check applied.
Identify where the estimate was built and how it confirmed (or would have caught an error in) each computed result.
Compare the annotated plan to your own attempt and note any step you dropped or any method you would change.
activities.intendedInsight: A well-structured solution makes its operation, method choice, and reasonableness check explicit at every step.

constraints: Numbers up to 10,000,000 and decimals (e.g. pounds-and-pence) must appear so the magnitude stakes of a keying/place-value slip are real.
Problems must be modelled from the situation, not solved by word-spotting operations from keywords.
The estimate should be built before or alongside computing, not after, and as a running/per-quantity estimate so it can actually gate each calculator/written result.

Recognition and ordering tasks assess understanding but do not elicit independent construction of the plan and computation; include at least one task where the learner builds and justifies the whole solution.

The worked-example walkthrough is a scaffold: it displays structure but does not by itself require the learner to generate their own plan and method choices; pair it with a task where the learner constructs and justifies the whole solution.
Interactive magnitude-warning gates, running bars, and live checks are optional illustrative mechanisms; the same learning works on paper with a planner grid and estimate strip.
Method fit is a reasoned choice about the numbers, not a fixed rule; do not teach 'always use a calculator' or 'never use a calculator'.

The IES/WWC visual-representations claim is rated STRONG for visual representations and reasoning-about-structure generally; it does not independently establish the efficacy of the worked-example walkthrough format, which is proposed as a scaffold.

The original catalog rationale implied non-interactive formats 'cannot' let the child plan or make method choices; this has been softened to scope-limited statements about what each format exercises, without asserting universal necessity of the interactive format.

topic.description: Add and subtract decimals to hundredths using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate strategies to written methods and explain reasoning
evidence: Correctly compute 3.45 + 2.78 and explain regrouping across decimal places
Use a number line or base-ten blocks to model 5.03 − 2.67
Explain why the standard algorithm works for decimal addition by connecting to place-value understanding
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} add or subtract decimal amounts like '4.73 + 2.68' or '10.00 − 3.47', lining up the decimal points and working through the columns correctly?

pedagogy.summary: Adding and subtracting decimals to hundredths, understood as the SAME place-value system as whole numbers continued rightward past the point. The algorithm is identical — align by place value, compose ten hundredths into a tenth on carrying and decompose a tenth into ten hundredths on borrowing — the only new hazard is that alignment must be by the DECIMAL POINT (tenths under tenths), not by right-edging the digits, and 'ragged' decimals (3.4 + 2.78) must be equalised with a placeholder zero. Children should relate the strategy to the written method and explain WHY it works from place value.
bestPractices: Align by the decimal point; write in placeholder zeros so both numbers have the same number of places (3.4 -> 3.40)
Use base-ten blocks re-scaled (flat = 1, rod = 0.1, small = 0.01) so ten-hundredths-make-a-tenth mirrors ten-ones-make-a-ten
Estimate first (3.45 + 2.78 is about 6) to catch a misplaced point
Explicitly connect the decimal algorithm to the whole-number one - 'same exchange, new columns'
Ask the child to explain why lining up the points (not the digits) is necessary
keyRepresentations: Place-value columns with a fixed, aligned decimal point (Th... O . tenths hundredths)
Re-scaled base-ten blocks (1 / 0.1 / 0.01)
Number line for counting up (5.03 - 2.67)
Money and metric-measure contexts (pounds.pence, metres.cm)
commonMisconceptions: Aligns the digits by the right edge instead of by the decimal point (3.4 + 2.78 set up wrongly)
Treats the digits after the point as a separate whole number ('longer decimal is bigger', so mis-orders/mis-sets)
Loses or misplaces the decimal point in the answer
Fails to borrow across the tenths, especially with a zero (5.03 - 2.67)
Thinks appending or dropping a trailing zero changes the value

learn.summary: Add and subtract decimals to hundredths by treating the decimal point as the fixed marker of where the same place-value columns continue rightward. The written algorithm is identical to whole-number column arithmetic — align by place value, compose ten hundredths into a tenth when carrying, decompose a tenth into ten hundredths when borrowing — with one new hazard: columns must be aligned by the DECIMAL POINT (tenths under tenths), not by right-edging the digits, and 'ragged' decimals such as 3.4 + 2.78 must be equalised with a placeholder zero (3.40). Learners should estimate first to place the point, compute correctly in both directions including across a zero, and explain WHY lining up the points (not the digits) is necessary.

activities.title: Decimal exchange bench: aligning by the point and trading ten-for-one
feedback: If a learner right-edges 3.4 under 2.78 (lining the 4 under the 8), stop and insist on lining up the decimal points and inserting a placeholder zero (3.40); a highlighted empty hundredths slot can prompt this, and the re-scaled blocks show tenths sitting under tenths.
If a learner cannot take 7 hundredths from 3 hundredths in 5.03 − 2.67, model the exchange with blocks first (one whole → ten tenths, one tenth → ten hundredths) before working the digits.
If the point is lost or misplaced in the answer, anchor it with the estimate: for 3.4 + 2.78, 'about 6, so it's 6.18, not 61.8 or 0.618'.
Confirm the carry explicitly: ten hundredth-pieces fuse into one tenth-piece, which slides one column left — the same move as ten ones making one ten.
activities.rationale: A fixed-point column layout with re-scaled base-ten blocks makes 'align by the point' and the hundredths→tenths exchange concrete and connects the decimal procedure to the whole-number regrouping learners already know, supporting the standard's call to use concrete models and place-value strategies and to relate the strategy to a written method.
sourceClaims: Pupils 'add, subtract, multiply, and divide decimals to hundredths, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used' (5.NBT.B.7, cluster: perform operations with decimals to hundredths).

Decimal addition/subtraction is formally established in Year 5: pupils 'practise adding and subtracting decimals, including a mix of whole numbers and decimals, decimals with different numbers of decimal places, and complements of 1' (Year 5 fractions/decimals notes and guidance).
learnerActions: Set up 3.4 + 2.78 in place-value columns with the decimal point fixed in a central column; notice that 3.4 has an empty hundredths slot (to the right of the 4, above the 8), and add the placeholder zero so it becomes 3.40 with tenths under tenths and hundredths under hundredths.

Compute 3.45 + 2.78: the hundredths total 13, so fuse ten hundredth-pieces into a single tenth-piece and carry it one column left — exactly the ones-to-tens carry already known. Record the answer 6.23.
Solve 5.03 − 2.67 by decomposing: exchange one whole into ten tenths and one tenth into ten hundredths so you can take 7 hundredths from 3 hundredths; record 2.36.
Before each calculation, estimate roughly (3.45 + 2.78 is about 6) and use the estimate to check the point is in the right place afterward.
Re-scale base-ten blocks so a flat = 1, a rod = 0.1, and a small cube = 0.01, and physically trade ten small cubes for one rod to mirror ten-ones-make-a-ten.
activities.intendedInsight: Decimals are not a new arithmetic: the point just marks where the columns keep going, and the ten-for-one exchange across every boundary (hundredths→tenths, tenths→ones) is unchanged from whole numbers. You must line up tenths under tenths and hundredths under hundredths because you can only add like to like.

activities.title: Confronting 'longer-is-larger' with ragged decimals
feedback: If a learner judges 4.11 larger than 4.9 because it has more digits, rebuild the comparison with equal places (4.11 vs 4.90) on a number line or with hundredths blocks, reading tenths and hundredths explicitly.

If a learner claims 2.78 is larger than 3.4 because it has more digits or a bigger part after the point, compare the ones first (2 ones vs 3 ones). Then rewrite with equal places (2.78 vs 3.40) and show on a number line or with blocks that 2.78 is smaller, even though 0.78 is more than 0.40. If they treat .45 and .4 as 45 and 4, compare 0.40 versus 0.45 (forty versus forty-five hundredths).
If a learner believes 6.180 differs from 6.18, establish directly that the extra zero adds zero thousandths, so the values are identical.
activities.rationale: 'Longer-is-larger' is a documented decimal misconception that is exposed specifically by ragged decimals of unequal length, and above all by cases where the longer decimal is actually the smaller one (e.g. 4.11 vs 4.9); equalising places and comparing on a shared model directly targets it, whereas a case where the longer decimal is also larger would let the misconception pass undetected.
sourceClaims: 'Longer-is-larger' is a well-documented decimal misconception in which children treat the digits after the point as a separate whole number (e.g. '4.11 is larger than 4.9 as it is longer'); it is exposed only by 'ragged' decimals of unequal length, and about half of Year 5 students make such errors. The classification traces to Sackur-Grisvard & Leonard (1985), Nesher & Peled (1986) and Resnick et al. (1989).
learnerActions: Decide which is larger, 4.11 or 4.9. Many children wrongly pick 4.11 because it 'looks longer' — but 4.9 is larger. Rewrite with equal places (4.11 vs 4.90) and read them as eleven hundredths versus ninety hundredths to see why.

Decide which is larger, 0.4 or 0.45, and whether 0.4 and 0.40 are equal or different. Then rewrite 0.4 as 0.40 (forty hundredths) to compare the same number of places directly (forty hundredths versus forty-five hundredths).
Build or mark both numbers with hundredths blocks or on a number line, lining up equal place values, and state which is larger and why.
Check the claim 'is 6.18 the same as 6.180?' and justify the answer from place value (appending a trailing zero adds zero in the next place, so the value is unchanged).

Explain in your own words why 2.78 is smaller than 3.4 even though it has more digits and a larger part after the point (0.78 vs 0.40): compare the ones first (2 < 3). Explain why you cannot judge decimal size by counting digits.
activities.intendedInsight: The digits after the point are not a separate whole number, so a 'longer' decimal is not automatically larger — 4.9 (nine tenths) is larger than 4.11 (eleven hundredths) despite having fewer digits, while 0.45 (forty-five hundredths) is larger than 0.4 (forty hundredths). You must compare the same place values. Trailing zeros do not change value because they add nothing to any place.

activities.title: Explain why the points must line up
feedback: A strong response aligns by the point using placeholder zeros, regroups correctly in both directions including across a zero, uses the estimate to place the point, and explains WHY the points must align; probe further if the learner solves equal-length items but cannot yet state the reason.

If a learner solves 3.45 + 2.78 but mis-aligns the ragged 3.4 + 2.78 or fails the borrow across the zero in 5.03 − 2.67, return to the exchange bench for that specific hazard before re-asking for the justification.
activities.rationale: Articulating why alignment follows from place value is the standard's 'explain the reasoning' strand and distinguishes procedural fluency from genuine understanding; dialogue can elicit and check this justification alongside the computation.
sourceClaims: Pupils 'add, subtract, multiply, and divide decimals to hundredths, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used' (5.NBT.B.7, cluster: perform operations with decimals to hundredths).
learnerActions: Answer the question 'why must the decimal points line up — what goes wrong if they don't?' in your own words, referring to place value.
Work 5.03 − 2.67 and explain what you did to be able to take 7 hundredths from 3 hundredths (decomposing across the tenths and the zero).
Estimate 3.45 + 2.78, 3.4 + 2.78, and 5.03 − 2.67 (about 6, 6, and 2) and describe how each estimate tells you where the point belongs in the exact answer.
Transfer the reasoning to a fresh ragged or zero case you have not seen, setting it up, computing it, and justifying the alignment.
activities.intendedInsight: You can only add tenths to tenths and hundredths to hundredths, so aligning by the point keeps like place values together; estimating first lets you catch a misplaced point. Full mastery means justifying the algorithm from place value, not just following steps.

constraints: The computation is a doing skill: learners must actually set up, regroup, and compute, not merely recognise correct setups. Fill-in-the-blank or slider-estimate items can assess column setup, regrouped digits, and estimates, but recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of the algorithm.

Always include at least one ragged-decimal item (e.g. 3.4 + 2.78) and one borrow-across-a-zero item (e.g. 5.03 − 2.67); clean equal-length items alone confirm only the basic algorithm and hide the decimal-specific hazards.

When checking 'longer-is-larger', include at least one comparison where the longer decimal is the smaller value (e.g. 4.11 vs 4.9); a comparison where the longer decimal is also larger (e.g. 0.4 vs 0.45) does not discriminate the misconception on its own.

A tap-to-reveal worked example (tap the point to reveal 'tenths under tenths'; tap the carry to reveal ten hundredths = one tenth) is useful as fixed reference, but a fixed example cannot be re-set by the learner, so pair it with hands-on setup and computation.
Re-scaled base-ten blocks (1 / 0.1 / 0.01) are an approximation: the physical pieces have thickness and the scaling is a convention, so keep the mapping (flat = 1, rod = 0.1, cube = 0.01) explicit.
Money (pounds.pence) and metric-measure (metres.cm) contexts are helpful, but watch that the two-place convention of money does not reinforce 'always two digits after the point'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Arithmetic checked: 3.45 + 2.78 = 6.23; 3.4 + 2.78 = 6.18 (via 3.40); 5.03 − 2.67 = 2.36. Estimates about 6, 6, and 2 are consistent. These match the source's stated correct answers.

Activity 2 keeps the discriminating comparison 4.11 vs 4.9 (the longer decimal 4.11 is actually smaller), taken from the source's own misconception example. The original candidate's 0.4 vs 0.45 does not expose 'longer-is-larger' because there the longer decimal is genuinely larger; it is retained only for the trailing-zero/equal-places teaching.

Activity 2 feedback was corrected so the remediation numbers match the learner's actual error: the '2.78 bigger after the point than 3.4' confusion is rebuilt as 0.78 vs 0.40, while '.45 and .4 as 45 and 4' is rebuilt as 0.40 vs 0.45.

The source assessment's reteach note phrased a comparison as an ambiguous question ('0.4 = 0.40 = forty hundredths, larger than 0.45? No'); the intended point is that 0.40 equals forty hundredths and is NOT larger than 0.45 (forty-five hundredths). The activity states this plainly.

The original artefact-fit notes claimed a third dimension 'adds nothing' to this planar place-value work; this is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law, so it is omitted rather than asserted. A 3D representation is simply unlikely to be necessary here, not proven worthless.
The 'glowing empty hundredths slot' and 'blocks fusing/sliding' are retained as optional, illustrative concrete feedback, not mandatory implementations.

The DfE Year 5 claim is kept on Activity 1 because that activity practises ragged and mixed whole/decimal cases ('decimals with different numbers of decimal places'); it supports the activity content rather than the choice of concrete representation.

probeDeeper: Roughly what should 3.45 + 2.78 come to, before you work it out exactly?

topic.description: Estimate the answer to a calculation and use inverse operations to check answers; apply to increasingly large numbers using rounding and inverse reasoning
evidence: Round numbers to the nearest 10 or 100 to estimate a sum or difference before calculating
Use addition to check a subtraction answer, or vice versa
Identify when a calculated answer is unreasonable based on the estimate

Use addition to check a subtraction answer and vice versa
