topic.assessmentPrompt: Before {{name}} works out a calculation, can they make a sensible rough guess — and then check their answer using the opposite operation?

pedagogy.summary: Estimating and checking is a habit of mind, not a calculation: before working something out, round to get a ballpark; after, judge whether the exact answer is reasonable against that ballpark, and verify using the inverse operation. The point is epistemic — how do I know my answer is sensible? — so estimation must come BEFORE calculating (to be a genuine check, not a rationalisation) and the inverse must be understood as an independent re-derivation, not a repeat of the same sum.
bestPractices: Estimate FIRST by rounding (to the nearest 10/100), then calculate, then compare — order matters or it isn't a check
Teach the inverse as a genuinely independent check: add the answer back to test a subtraction (and vice versa), rather than redoing the identical operation
Use deliberately wrong 'answers' and ask 'sensible or silly?' so the estimate earns its keep by catching nonsense
Discuss reasonableness openly — why 121 can't be right for 412+389 — rather than marking it
Build on the inverse relationship (add undoes subtract) and place-value rounding
keyRepresentations: Number line / rounding scale (which ten or hundred is it nearest?)
Bar model showing the inverse (whole minus part returns the other part)
'Sensible or silly?' answer cards to judge
Estimate-then-exact two-column jotting
Fact-family triangle (linking + and − for the inverse check)
commonMisconceptions: Treating estimation as pointless — 'you can't know until you do the real sum'
Estimating AFTER calculating, bending the estimate to match the answer already found (confirmation)
'Checking' by repeating the identical operation (which reproduces the same error) instead of using the inverse
Rounding erratically so the estimate isn't a fair ballpark

learn.summary: Estimation and checking are habits of mind for judging whether an answer is sensible, not extra calculations. Learners round FIRST to get a ballpark, then calculate, then compare; and they check using the inverse operation (adding the answer back to test a subtraction) understood as an independent re-derivation, not a repeat of the same sum. Aimed at ages 7-9 working with sums and differences of two- and three-digit numbers.

activities.title: Sensible or silly? Judge before you compute
feedback: If a learner refuses to judge without computing exactly, prompt: 'You don't need the exact answer — about how big should it be? Could 121 possibly be right for 412 + 389?'
When they correctly flag 121 as silly, name what they did: 'You rounded to about 800 and saw 121 was far too small — that's the check working.'
If they only estimate after seeing the exact answer, discuss why the estimate must come first to be a real check rather than a confirmation of what they already found
activities.rationale: Estimation is a distinct competency from exact calculation, and ordering it before the calculation is what makes it a genuine check rather than a rationalisation. Deliberately wrong candidate answers force the estimate to earn its keep by catching nonsense, and the two-column jotting makes the estimate-versus-exact comparison explicit.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils estimate the answer to a calculation and use inverse operations to check answers, and identify unreasonable answers by comparing to an estimate.

Computational estimation and judging reasonableness are distinct competencies from exact calculation; effective checking uses the inverse operation as an independent verification rather than repeating the original procedure.
learnerActions: Look at a calculation paired with a proposed answer, e.g. 412 + 389 = 121, and decide quickly whether it is 'sensible' or 'silly' BEFORE working out the exact answer
Say aloud the rounded ballpark you used: '400-and-something plus about 390 is roughly 800, so 121 can't be right'
Judge a batch of items, some with reasonable answers (e.g. 801) and some deliberately wrong, flagging the silly ones
Record your estimate and the exact answer side by side in two columns, so you can compare the ballpark against the worked result
Only after committing to your judgement, work out or reveal the exact answer and see whether your estimate caught the nonsense
activities.intendedInsight: A rounded ballpark, formed before calculating, is enough to catch a wildly wrong answer — so estimation is a genuine check, not busywork or a guess made after the fact.

activities.title: Check by adding back: the inverse as an independent test
feedback: If a learner 'checks' by subtracting again, ask: 'If you made a slip the first time, would doing exactly the same thing catch it? What could you do instead that works a different way?'
When they add the answer back and reach the start number, affirm: 'Getting back to 623 shows the subtraction was right — you tested it a different way.'
If the inverse relationship itself is shaky, revisit how add undoes subtract using the bar model and fact-family triangle before returning to checking
activities.rationale: Effective checking uses the inverse as an independent verification; understanding it as a different route (not a repeat) is the conceptual core. The bar model and fact family make the inverse relationship concrete.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils estimate the answer to a calculation and use inverse operations to check answers, and identify unreasonable answers by comparing to an estimate.

Computational estimation and judging reasonableness are distinct competencies from exact calculation; effective checking uses the inverse operation as an independent verification rather than repeating the original procedure.
learnerActions: Take a completed subtraction, e.g. 623 − 178 = 445, and check it by adding the answer back: 445 + 178
Confirm that the sum returns to the starting number (623) — if it does, the subtraction is verified
Contrast this with simply redoing 623 − 178 again, and explain why repeating the identical operation can easily repeat the original mistake, while adding back tests the answer a different way
Use a bar model (the whole minus one part returns the other part) and a fact-family triangle linking the three numbers to see how addition and subtraction undo each other
activities.intendedInsight: Checking with the inverse operation is an independent re-derivation of the answer, whereas repeating the same subtraction just reproduces the same potential error.

activities.title: How do you KNOW it's right? Reasoning discussion
feedback: Draw out reasoning rather than marking: value 'about 800, so 121 is far too small' over a bare right/wrong label
If a learner says 'you can't know until you do the real sum', surface that a rounded ballpark already rules out 121 — you knew without the exact calculation
Probe the limit honestly: an answer near the estimate (e.g. 790 vs ~800) could still be slightly off, so the estimate narrows the range rather than proving exactness
activities.rationale: The topic is epistemic — how do I know my answer is sensible? — so open discussion that probes justification suits it and exposes the misconception that only exact recomputation can establish correctness. This is explicitly a discussion to elicit reasoning, not a scored task.
sourceClaims: Computational estimation and judging reasonableness are distinct competencies from exact calculation; effective checking uses the inverse operation as an independent verification rather than repeating the original procedure.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt such as: 'A friend adds 412 + 389 and gets 121; another gets 801. Without working out the exact sum, how could you tell which answer must be wrong?'
Explain how to check a subtraction like 623 − 178 WITHOUT just doing the same subtraction again
Discuss: if your estimate and your exact answer disagree, which do you trust, and what do you do next?
Consider whether an answer could be close to the estimate but still wrong — so what does an estimate tell you, and what does it not?
activities.intendedInsight: An estimate bounds roughly how big an answer should be and flags gross errors, but it does not guarantee exactness; the inverse gives a separate confirmation. Knowing an answer is sensible is a matter of reasoning, not only recomputation.

activities.title: Rounding to a fair ballpark
feedback: If rounding is inconsistent, point to the number line: 'Is 178 nearer 170 or 180? Round both numbers the same careful way.'
Reinforce that the goal is a quick, fair approximation — not another exact sum
Note that rounding choices (nearest 10 vs nearest 100) change how tight the estimate is; a looser estimate still catches a wildly wrong answer
activities.rationale: Place-value rounding is the prerequisite skill that makes estimation a fair check; a static rounding scale is useful reference, and practising consistent rounding addresses the 'erratic rounding' misconception.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils estimate the answer to a calculation and use inverse operations to check answers, and identify unreasonable answers by comparing to an estimate.
learnerActions: Round two- and three-digit numbers to the nearest 10 and the nearest 100, e.g. 412 → 410 (nearest 10) or 400 (nearest 100); 389 → 390 (nearest 10) or 400 (nearest 100); 178 → 180 (nearest 10) or 200 (nearest 100)
Use a number line or rounding scale to see which ten or hundred a number is nearest to
Form an estimate for a sum or difference by rounding each number to the SAME place, e.g. 623 − 178 ≈ 620 − 180 ≈ 440 (both to nearest 10)
Compare estimates formed with consistent rounding against erratic rounding to see why fair, consistent rounding gives a trustworthy ballpark
activities.intendedInsight: A reliable estimate depends on rounding each number fairly to the same place; erratic rounding produces a ballpark you can't trust.

constraints: Estimation must come BEFORE calculating to function as a genuine check; estimating afterwards invites bending the estimate to match the answer already found (confirmation).

The inverse check must be understood as an independent re-derivation; repeating the identical operation is a weak check because it can easily repeat the original error (especially a misunderstanding of the method), even though it sometimes catches a careless slip.

An estimate bounds how big an answer should be and catches gross errors, but does NOT prove exactness — an answer close to the estimate can still be slightly wrong. Do not teach 'close to the estimate = correct'.
Treat the reasoning probes as discussion to surface thinking, not as scored right/wrong items; what matters is the quality of the epistemic reasoning.
A static rounding scale, bar model or fact-family triangle is a useful reference but does not by itself exercise the judging habit — pair reference tools with active judging and checking.

A timed 'buzz silly before the answer reveals' format is an optional motivational scaffold (short time pressure forces rounding over computing); it is not required, and the core objective is the estimate-first reasoning, which can also be done untimed on paper or aloud.
Prerequisite: the inverse relationship (add undoes subtract) and place-value rounding should be reteachable if shaky before checking work can succeed.

All original examples hold.

The bar model and the estimate-then-exact two-column jotting representations from the original were restored into the inverse-check and judging activities respectively, having been dropped in an earlier draft.

pedagogy.summary: A metacognitive topic: using rounding/estimation as an INDEPENDENT check on the reasonableness of a calculation, and judging the appropriate degree of accuracy for a context. Two ideas intertwine — (1) an estimate sets a ballpark that can DISPROVE an exact answer in seconds (if 47,832 + 23,156 is about 71,000, an answer of 3,988 must be wrong), and (2) the right level of accuracy depends on purpose (a stadium crowd is honestly '52,000'; a shop bill must be exact). The habit being built is 'is this answer sensible?', not another calculation.

Discuss real contexts where precision is spurious (crowd sizes, distances) vs essential (money, counts that must balance)
Frame accuracy as a decision with reasons, not 'more digits = better'

learn.summary: Learners build the habit of asking 'is this answer sensible?' by using rounding/estimation as an INDEPENDENT check on a calculation, and by judging the level of accuracy a context actually needs. Two intertwined ideas: (1) an estimate sets a ballpark that can disprove an exact answer in seconds (if 47,832 + 23,156 is about 71,000, an answer of 3,988 must be wrong), and (2) the right precision depends on purpose (a stadium crowd is honestly '52,000'; a shop bill must be exact). The two ideas are one habit, not separate tricks, and the check is deliberately NOT a re-computation of the same sum.

activities.title: The estimate as a lie-detector: prove an answer wrong without redoing it
feedback: If a learner says 71,000 is 'wrong' because the exact answer is 70,988: an estimate is meant to be near, not equal; being close is exactly what you want, and its job is to catch big errors, not to match digit for digit.

If a learner reaches for the full algorithm to check: redoing the same method can easily repeat the same mistake (especially if it comes from how you do the method), so the error may go undetected; a quick, independent estimate can catch large errors that repeating the method might miss.

If a learner rounds a five-digit sum to the nearest 10,000: that grain is often too coarse to catch errors of a few thousand (50,000 + 20,000 = 70,000 would still expose 3,988, but would not show up an answer like 74,000 as suspicious) - match the rounding grain to the question, coarse enough to be quick but fine enough to still discriminate.
When an answer IS close to the estimate, note that 'close' does not guarantee correctness; the estimate rules out large errors, not small ones.
activities.rationale: Treating estimation as a check done independently of the exact method targets the core misconception of recomputing to verify, and the use of a deliberately wrong answer makes 'how can you tell without redoing it?' concrete; choosing between nearest 100 and nearest 1,000 practises matching the grain to the context.

Computational estimation is a distinct competence used to judge reasonableness (order-of-magnitude checking), and appropriate precision is context-dependent
learnerActions: Take a completed sum with its answer, e.g. 47,832 + 23,156 = 3,988.
Round each number to a useful grain (nearest 1,000: about 48,000 and about 23,000) WITHOUT recomputing the exact sum.
Add the rounded numbers to get a ballpark of about 71,000.
State whether the given answer is possible: 3,988 is nowhere near 71,000, so it must be wrong - perhaps a place-value, alignment or copying slip; the estimate shows that it is wrong, not why.
Decide, for a stated context, whether a nearest-100 or a nearest-1,000 estimate is the better grain, and justify which keeps enough discrimination to be a useful check.
Repeat with other answers, including one that is close to the estimate (e.g. 70,988) and judge whether 'close' is enough to trust.
Explain, in your own words, why this check catches the error faster than redoing the full algorithm.
activities.intendedInsight: An estimate is an independent order-of-magnitude check: it can PROVE an answer impossible in seconds without ever doing the exact calculation. An estimate is a deliberate ballpark, not a rival exact answer.

activities.title: Honest precision: choosing the right level of accuracy for the purpose
feedback: If a learner insists the exact figure is always best: ask who the figure is for and what they'll do with it; nobody counted every head in a crowd, so extra digits imply a certainty that doesn't exist.
If a learner accepts 'about 52 pounds' for a shop bill: money must balance exactly, so here precision is the point, not a preference.
If a learner rounds too coarsely or too finely: match the grain to the purpose - '50,000' may erase a meaningful difference, while rounding a crowd to the nearest 10 is pointlessly precise.
activities.rationale: Directly addresses the 'more accuracy is always better' misconception by framing accuracy as a justified choice across contrasting real contexts where precision is either spurious or essential.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy
Computational estimation is a distinct competence used to judge reasonableness (order-of-magnitude checking), and appropriate precision is context-dependent
learnerActions: Consider a context, e.g. a newspaper reporting a football crowd. Decide whether it should print '52,000' or '51,847', and say why.
Argue that a crowd figure is inherently approximate, so '52,000' communicates the scale honestly while '51,847' implies a false precision nobody actually counted.
Contrast with a shop totting up a customer's bill: decide whether 'about 52 pounds' is acceptable and explain why money (and any count that must balance) needs exactness.
Rank several context cards (crowd / money / distance / stock count) by how much precision each honestly needs, giving a reason for each.
Identify a case where rounding a crowd to '50,000' would be TOO rough - when might that coarse figure hide something that matters?
activities.intendedInsight: The right level of accuracy is a decision with reasons tied to purpose and audience - not 'more digits is always better'. Spurious precision can be misleading; appropriate rounding can be more honest.

activities.title: Convince the sceptic (spoken reasoning)
feedback: Reward reasoning that separates the ballpark role of the estimate from the exact answer, and that ties precision to purpose.
Press any claim that an estimate 'failed' because it wasn't equal, or that exactness is universally better.

If a learner treats estimate-checking and choosing accuracy as unrelated tricks, prompt them to see both as one question - 'is this number sensible for its purpose?' - so they can transfer the habit to a new context.
activities.rationale: Reasonableness and appropriate-accuracy judgements are genuinely dialogic; an in-role 'convince me' exchange exercises the justification directly, surfaces thinking for discussion, and targets the partial-level state of holding the two ideas apart.
sourceClaims: Computational estimation is a distinct competence used to judge reasonableness (order-of-magnitude checking), and appropriate precision is context-dependent
learnerActions: In role with a sceptical editor/partner, justify out loud why a proposed answer must be impossible, using only an estimate.
Argue, when challenged, why '52,000' is the honest figure to print for a crowd and why a bill demands exact pounds and pence.
Respond to follow-up challenges: 'Could an answer be close to your estimate and still be wrong?' and 'How close is close enough to trust?'
Explain how the estimate check and the accuracy choice are the same underlying habit - asking whether a number is sensible for its purpose.
activities.intendedInsight: Judging reasonableness and defending a level of accuracy is reasoning you can articulate and defend, not just a computed value; the two moves are one habit, not separate tricks.

activities.title: Quick checks: spot the impossible answer and sort by needed precision
feedback: For a correct selection, ask the learner to say how they knew without the exact sum.
A recognition response shows which option was chosen but does not by itself show the learner could build the estimate or justify the accuracy level, so always ask for the 'why'.
activities.rationale: Selection items make the curriculum skills (rounding to check, choosing accuracy) assessable, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the independent construction of an estimate or a justified accuracy choice, so pair them with brief reasoning.

learnerActions: Given an estimate, select which of several proposed answers is impossible (e.g. an answer near 4,000 when the estimate is about 71,000).
Sort contexts into 'needs an exact figure' vs 'a rounded figure is honest'.

activities.intendedInsight: Recognising impossible answers and matching precision to context are checkable skills; adding a short reason connects them to the underlying judgement.

constraints: Estimation must be taught as a CHECK performed independently of the exact method - never by repeating the exact calculation, which can easily repeat the same error (especially a misunderstanding of the method) and so may not catch it.

Round to a level that keeps useful discrimination (e.g. nearest 1,000 for five-digit sums, not nearest 10,000); choosing between nearest 100 and nearest 1,000 is itself a reasoned, context-dependent decision.
An estimate is a deliberate ballpark; being near the exact answer is correct, not an error. 'Close to the estimate' rules out large errors but does not guarantee the exact answer is right.
Accuracy is a decision justified by purpose and audience, not 'more digits = better'; both spurious precision and over-coarse rounding are wrong for their context.

Recognition/selection tasks confirm a choice but do not by themselves show the learner can independently generate an estimate or justify a precision level - pair them with spoken or written reasoning.

Scaffolds such as a gauge, dial, number-line bracket, or tap-to-reveal poster are aids to make the mechanism visible; the objective is the learner's own judgement, so fade them as learners articulate the reasoning unaided.
Treat estimate-as-check and accuracy-by-purpose as one connected habit; a learner who performs each in isolation but cannot link them has only a partial grasp.
Context-dependent precision claims (e.g. whether '50,000' is too rough) depend on the specific purpose and must be reasoned per case, not applied as a fixed rule.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 47,832 + 23,156 = 70,988 (exact); 48,000 + 23,000 = 71,000 (estimate) - consistent across the source. The impossible answers 3,988 and 3,421 each sit well over an order of magnitude below 71,000 and ~50,000 respectively, consistent with a place-value/alignment slip; retained as given.

The source's evidence line 'Identify that a calculated answer of 3,421 cannot be correct because the estimate gives approximately 50,000' names no addends, so the ~50,000 estimate cannot be independently checked here; used only as a generic 'order of magnitude out' illustration and kept out of any learner-facing option.

Interactive examples from the original (answer-checker 'bench', gauge swinging to a red IMPOSSIBLE zone, context dial for money/crowd/distance, number-line bracket, tap-to-reveal poster) are preserved as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not as mandatory mechanisms.

Original 'poor fit' claim that a 3D/spatial treatment 'adds nothing' was not carried over as a universal law; the topic is simply judgement about number, so spatial manipulation is not the focus here.
The source's partial response level (treating estimate-as-check and accuracy-by-purpose as separate tricks) is addressed in the dialogic activity's actions and feedback.

Activity 4's cited curriculum claim supports naming the assessed skills only; the recognition-only limitation is stated as an objective affordance, not as claimed source-backed efficacy of any medium.

probeDeeper: Your estimate was about 71,000 and the real answer is 70,988 - does that small difference mean your estimate was wrong?
Could an answer be close to your estimate and still be wrong? How close is 'close enough' to trust it?
When would rounding a crowd to '50,000' be TOO rough - when might that hide something that matters?
For a shop totting up a customer's bill, would 'about 52 pounds' be an acceptable level of accuracy? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: Strong reasoning rounds each number (about 48,000 + 23,000 = 71,000), so any answer near 4,000 is impossible - it is an order of magnitude out, probably a place-value or alignment slip - and this is spotted WITHOUT the exact sum. On accuracy: a crowd figure is inherently approximate, so '52,000' communicates the scale honestly and '51,847' implies a false precision nobody counted; but for money, or counts that must balance, exactness is the point. The right level of accuracy depends on the PURPOSE, not on having more digits.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss: an estimate is a deliberate ballpark, not a rival answer; its job is to catch big errors, and being near (not equal) is exactly right.

responseLevels.gap: Can only check by recomputing exactly; treats accuracy as 'more digits is better'; cannot use an estimate to judge an answer.
responseLevels.full: Uses the estimate as an independent order-of-magnitude check AND justifies the level of accuracy by purpose/audience, transferring to a new context (money exact, crowd rounded) and explaining why.
responseLevels.partial: Can produce an estimate and see 3,988 is wrong, OR can say a crowd figure is approximate - but treats these as separate tricks; lists the ideas without connecting estimate-as-check to accuracy-fits-purpose, and cannot choose the right grain for a new context.
